4.8 Reading a dated operational report
NCC's communiqué for its Board meeting of 9 September 2026 reports 8,526 deployments against
12,179 committed coverage and capacity sites, approximately 70%. It also records concern about
disruption associated with fibre cuts. The report describes the Device Management System as live
and schedules the Telecommunications Identity Risk Management System for October 2026. It
records planned education-access launch and service dates of 10 September and 1 October
respectively. These are dated Board statements; a scheduled event is not proof that it subsequently
occurred. Source: NCC, communiqué of the 110th Board meeting, 9 September 2026.
The interpretation discipline is broader than this particular report. A commitment establishes an
intended action. A deployment report provides implementation evidence. A service measurement

NCC Promotion Study Guide   26
provides performance evidence. A demonstrated improvement for users provides outcome evidence.
Each supports a different claim, so an answer should say exactly what the evidence establishes.
There is also a difference between delivery and attribution. An operator may install a facility while a
regulator creates conditions, monitors commitments or intervenes on compliance. Both roles may
matter, but they should not be collapsed into a claim that the regulator physically constructed the
operator's network. State who performed the activity and how it relates to the institution's
responsibilities.

4.9 Indicators, targets and sound interpretation
An indicator is a defined measure used to assess a condition or progress. A baseline records the
starting position. A target states the intended result and its deadline. Actual performance records
what occurred. Variance is the difference between the intended and observed result. An informative
report states these elements together and explains material differences.
Definitions are essential. An application-processing measure may begin when an application is first
submitted or only when it is complete. It may end when assessment finishes, when approval is
granted or when the applicant receives the decision. Those choices can produce different results
from the same workflow. A useful indicator specifies the event, time window, exclusions and
responsible data owner.
Consider an illustrative complaint exercise, unrelated to reported NCC performance. A team begins a
month with 120 open cases, receives 80 new cases and closes 100. With no reopened cases or other
adjustments, the ending backlog is 120 plus 80 minus 100, which equals 100. Closures exceed new
arrivals, so the backlog falls by 20. However, this arithmetic does not establish that the oldest cases
were resolved, customers accepted the remedy or closures were properly justified.
Pair volume with quality and timeliness. Record the age of outstanding cases, the proportion
reopened, the reasons for delay and whether resolution addressed the actual complaint. An average
can conceal a small group of extremely old cases. A high closure count can conceal premature
closure. Measurement should help identify the service condition rather than reward an attractive
number detached from that condition.
For investment or infrastructure work, distinguish an input such as expenditure from an output such
as installed equipment. An outcome concerns the resulting change in service or access. Wider impact
concerns longer-term effects such as improved participation in education or commerce. Attribution
becomes more difficult farther along this chain because other factors also influence the result.

4.10 Reporting progress and recommending action
A strong progress report states the intended result, the work completed, the evidence supporting
completion, the remaining constraint and the action required. It also identifies the responsible party
and realistic next milestone. Descriptions such as ongoing or being handled are insufficient where a
decision-maker needs to understand whether intervention is necessary.
For a delayed system implementation, explain the material dependency. User acceptance may be
incomplete because test data are unavailable; an integration may be blocked because an interface
specification has not been agreed; deployment may depend on an authorised security review. These
explanations enable targeted action. Simply asking all parties to expedite does not identify the cause
or the owner of the next step.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   27
A recommendation should connect to the objective without overstating the expected result. If
recovery testing has not been completed, recommend a defined test with responsibilities and
acceptance criteria. Do not claim that the service is resilient merely because backup software was
purchased. If data quality is unreliable, recommend reconciliation and validation rather than
presenting an inaccurate dashboard as evidence of improved oversight.
In an examination answer, the same discipline produces a coherent response: establish the mandate
and objective; explain the mechanism; distinguish intended and completed work; assess the
evidence; identify risks and dependencies; and state a proportionate next action. This demonstrates
how strategic understanding informs the work of an officer.

4.11 Practice questions and explained answers
Question 1. Does a Strategic Vision Plan create a new statutory power?
Answer. No. It organises priorities and delivery within the applicable legal framework. A planned
intervention still requires an enabling power, an authorised decision-maker and the required
procedure. Strategic desirability does not cure a lack of legal authority.
Question 2. Why must a strategy be identified by its edition and period?
Answer. Targets and priorities belong to a defined planning context. An earlier target cannot be
silently presented as a current commitment. A leadership speech, annual action plan and adopted
institutional strategy are related documents with different purposes. Identify which one the question
concerns before answering.
Question 3. How can an internal Information Technology function support a regulatory
outcome?
Answer. It can provide reliable records, secure access, functioning applications, integrations, audit
trails and tested recovery arrangements. These capabilities support the substantive work of
regulatory departments. The connection should be explained through the service enabled; it does not
mean Information Technology assumes the legal decision-making role of the user department.
Question 4. A system has been installed. What additional evidence is needed before
describing service improvement?
Answer. Establish that it passed appropriate acceptance testing, users can operate it, data are
reliable, responsibilities are assigned and support arrangements function. Then compare relevant
service measures with the baseline. Installation is an output; improved service is a separate outcome
requiring evidence.
Question 5. Why does an operator’s infrastructure deployment not automatically establish
better consumer experience?
Answer. Location, demand, power, transport capacity, configuration and continuity affect the resulting
service. The deployed facility must operate effectively in the network. Performance and user evidence
are needed to assess improvement; counting assets alone cannot establish every aspect of
experience.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   28
Question 6. Explain why a planned go-live date and a live system are different statuses.
Answer. A planned date records an intention. A live system has reached an operational stage
supported by evidence. Even then, the scope of participation, functionality and actual results must be
established separately. Avoid describing a scheduled launch as completed or limited implementation
as universal coverage.
Question 7. In the illustrative case, what does the fall from 120 to 100 open complaints
prove?
Answer. Given 80 new cases, 100 closures and no other adjustments, it proves a net backlog
reduction of 20. It does not prove that remedies were adequate or the oldest cases were addressed.
Age, reopening and resolution-quality measures are needed alongside the volume calculation.
Question 8. Distinguish a strategic alignment claim from an achievement claim.
Answer. Alignment explains why an activity supports an objective: for example, tested recovery
arrangements support continuity. Achievement states what has actually been completed or improved.
The first requires a reasoned connection; the second additionally requires evidence of the claimed
result, its scope and its date.
NCC Promotion Study Guide   29

Chapter 5
Telecommunications and network foundations
A communications service depends on a complete path between a user and a destination. This
chapter starts with the information being carried, explains how networks transport it, and then follows
access, transport, core and service functions. The purpose is to understand the mechanism before
applying the terminology to spectrum, licensing, interconnection and service quality.

5.1 Information, data and physical signals
Communication begins with information: meaning that one person or system wants another to
receive. A spoken sentence, photograph and payment instruction are different kinds of information,
but a communications system must represent each in a form that equipment can process and
transmit.
From meaning to bits
Digital systems encode information as binary digits. A bit can take one of two logical states. Groups of
bits represent numbers, characters, samples of sound, pixels and instructions. Encoding does not
make the information travel; it provides a disciplined representation that later stages can package,
protect and transmit.
Signals carry representations
A signal is a physical variation used to carry information. In a fibre, pulses of light represent data. In
copper, changing electrical conditions do so. In radio, an electromagnetic wave is varied through
modulation. The receiving equipment measures the variation and reconstructs the encoded
information.
Term   Meaning   Common mistake
Analogue   A continuously varying representation.   Assuming analogue means old or poor.
Digital   Information represented using discrete values,
usually bits.
Assuming bits travel without a physical
signal.
Modulation   Varying a carrier so it conveys information.   Confusing the carrier frequency with user
data rate.
Bandwidth   A range of frequencies or, in ordinary service
language, available carrying capacity.
Using frequency bandwidth and throughput
as exact synonyms.
Throughput   Useful data successfully delivered per unit of
time.
Treating the advertised maximum as every
user's result.
Noise, loss and error
Signals weaken and become distorted. Other transmissions and electrical activity may interfere.
Receivers therefore need adequate signal quality, error detection and sometimes retransmission. A
usable service depends not merely on whether energy arrives, but whether the intended information
can be reconstructed accurately and promptly.
More signal strength does not automatically mean more capacity or faster Internet.
Strength, signal quality, channel resources, congestion and the rest of the path all matter.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   30
Units and a worked download example
A bit is a binary digit. A byte contains eight bits. Telecommunications data rates are commonly stated
in bits per second, while file sizes are often stated in bytes. Using decimal units, a 100-megabyte file
contains 800 megabits. At a sustained useful transfer rate of 20 megabits per second, the ideal
transfer time is 800 divided by 20, or 40 seconds. Real transfer time may be longer because of
overhead, interruptions, retransmissions and changing capacity. Binary file-size units such as
mebibytes use a different scale.
Frequency bandwidth and data rate are different quantities. A radio channel may occupy a range of
frequencies measured in hertz, while useful delivery is measured in bits per second. The number of
bits carried depends on the signalling method, signal quality, coding, scheduling and other conditions.
A channel width cannot be read directly as a guaranteed user speed.

5.2 Circuits, packets and shared resources
Traditional telephony is commonly taught through circuit switching: network resources are arranged
as a relatively dedicated path for the duration of a call. Modern Internet Protocol networks use packet
switching: information is divided into labelled units that can share links with packets from many users.
Why packets are powerful
Many applications transmit in bursts. Packet switching lets users share link capacity rather than
reserve a complete path for each session. Packet headers carry protocol-specific control information,
such as network addresses. Sequencing and recovery depend on the protocol: they are not features
supplied by every packet header. Internet Protocol forwarding alone does not guarantee ordered or
reliable delivery.
What sharing introduces
Packets may wait in queues when demand exceeds immediate link capacity.
Different packets can experience different delays or routes.
Packets may be lost, duplicated or delivered out of order and must be handled by protocols.
Applications have different tolerance: an email can wait; an interactive voice call is sensitive to delay
and variation.
Measure   Question answered   Consumer effect
Throughput   How much useful data is delivered each
second?
Download and streaming speed.
Latency   How long does a transfer or round trip take?   Responsiveness of calls, games and web
use.
Jitter   How much does packet delay vary?   Uneven voice or video playback.
Packet loss   What proportion never reaches the
destination?
Gaps, freezes and retransmissions.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   31
Congestion
Congestion occurs when offered traffic exceeds available processing, radio or transmission capacity
for a period. Queues grow, delay rises and buffers may discard packets. Capacity expansion can
help, but congestion management also includes scheduling, traffic engineering, caching and efficient
protocols.
Packet networks turn quality into a resource-allocation problem. Regulation should examine
demand, capacity, prioritisation, measurement conditions and consumer impact rather than rely on
one headline speed.
A capacity example
Suppose a simplified link can deliver 100 megabits per second of useful traffic and ten equally active
users share it equally. Each would receive 10 megabits per second in that deliberately simplified
case. With fifty equally active users, the same division gives 2 megabits per second. Real networks
do not necessarily divide resources equally: demand, radio conditions, scheduling, entitlements and
protocol behaviour affect the result. The example shows why a service can slow during busy periods
without losing signal coverage.
Delay also has several causes. Propagation delay concerns travel through the medium. Transmission
delay concerns the time needed to place the data on a link. Processing consumes time in equipment,
while queueing delay depends on congestion. Increasing link capacity can reduce transmission and
queueing effects, but does not remove the physical distance to a remote destination. A speed test
and a delay test consequently measure different aspects of service.

5.3 How mobile generations developed
The progression from first to fifth generation explains changes in architecture and service capability. It
is a history of technical development, not a claim that every Nigerian network adopted each feature at
the same time or that the latest generation automatically gives every user the best result.
First-generation mobile systems were principally designed for analogue voice. Second-generation
systems moved mobile voice to digital techniques and supported messaging. Global System for
Mobile Communications, usually called GSM, is a second-generation technology family. A Base
Transceiver Station is the radio equipment associated with the GSM access network; the familiar
abbreviation is BTS. The term should not be used as the exact technical name for every radio node in
every later generation.
Packet-data enhancements, including General Packet Radio Service and Enhanced Data rates for
GSM Evolution, improved the ability of second-generation networks to support data. These are
commonly referred to as GPRS and EDGE. Labels such as 2.5G describe the transitional stage
rather than a complete replacement of the underlying second-generation system.
Third-generation systems supported more capable mobile data alongside voice services.
Fourth-generation deployment made packet-based mobile broadband central. Long Term Evolution,
or LTE, is the technology name commonly associated with that transition. Managed voice over LTE
requires compatible service support; a data indication alone does not prove that the voice service is
registered and usable.
Fifth-generation radio is called New Radio. Deployment architecture matters: a non-standalone
arrangement can use fourth-generation infrastructure as an anchor, while a standalone arrangement
uses a fifth-generation core. Therefore a fifth-generation radio connection does not by itself establish

NCC Promotion Study Guide   32
that a network offers every capability associated with a standalone system. Low delay and high
capacity depend on the complete deployment, service path and load.
Several generations can coexist. Users have different handsets, operators have different coverage
footprints, and moving a service to another generation requires suitable devices and supporting
arrangements. A network change must consider voice continuity, coverage and affected users, rather
than assume that the presence of a newer technology makes every older service unnecessary.

5.4 Radio links, cells and mobility
A mobile phone communicates with the network without a cable by transmitting and receiving
radio-frequency energy. The operator may use only spectrum it is authorised to use, under technical
conditions intended to manage interference and support efficient national use.
Coverage begins with a link budget
The useful signal leaving a transmitter loses strength as it travels. Distance, frequency, antenna
characteristics, terrain, buildings, vegetation and weather can affect propagation. The receiver also
has a sensitivity limit. Engineers assess whether enough usable signal should remain at the
destination after gains and losses.
Uplink and downlink
Downlink is transmission from the network towards the device; uplink is from the device towards the
network. The paths can perform differently. A user may hear the other party clearly while the other
party cannot hear the user because the handset's lower-power uplink cannot reach the site reliably.
Radio idea   Plain meaning   Regulatory relevance
Cell   A geographic service area associated with
radio resources at a site or sector.
Coverage maps and capacity planning.
Frequency band   A defined portion of spectrum.   Allocation, assignment, licence conditions
and interference.
Channel   A usable portion or resource arrangement
within a band.
Capacity and coordination.
Interference   Unwanted energy that impairs reception.   Monitoring, enforcement and technical
conditions.
Handover   Moving an active connection between cells
or technologies.
Mobility quality and dropped sessions.
Why cells are reused
Radio resources are limited. Frequencies can be reused across cells when interference is managed;
modern networks may reuse the same carrier in neighbouring cells. Cellular design divides coverage
into manageable areas, enabling the same spectrum to support many users. Densifying a network
with additional cells can increase capacity, but requires sites, power, transmission, planning and
interference coordination.
A mast is physical support. It is not by itself a base station, cell, Radio Access Network or
complete mobile network.
A cell boundary changes with conditions; it is not a fixed circle drawn around a

mast is physical support. It is not by itself a base station, cell, Radio Access Network or
complete mobile network.
A cell boundary changes with conditions; it is not a fixed circle drawn around a mast. Terrain,
buildings, interference and the device’s capabilities influence the usable service area. Cell reselection

NCC Promotion Study Guide   33
commonly concerns a device choosing a suitable cell while idle, whereas handover concerns
maintaining an active connection as its serving radio resources change. Both involve measurements
and network rules, not simply proximity to the nearest tower.

5.5 Base stations and the Radio Access Network
The base-station site is the device's principal entry point into a mobile operator's infrastructure.
Antennas transmit and receive. Radio units generate and process radio-frequency signals. Baseband
or distributed processing functions perform coding, scheduling and protocol work. Modern
architectures may separate or virtualise some of these functions.
Why 'Radio Access Network' is larger than the tower
The Radio Access Network includes interconnected radio sites and control or processing functions
that provide wireless access. It manages radio resources, schedules users, supports mobility and
passes traffic towards the transport and core networks. The site compound may also contain power
systems, batteries, cooling, security and transmission equipment.
A device seeking service
The device searches supported frequency bands and detects suitable network signals.
It reads broadcast information describing the network and cell.
It requests access using prescribed signalling procedures.
The network evaluates the request and coordinates authentication with core functions.
Radio resources are scheduled for signalling and user traffic.
As the device moves, measurements support reselection or handover to a better cell.
Coverage versus capacity
Situation   What the user may see   Likely interpretation
No adequate signal   No service or emergency-only
indication.
Coverage, power, site availability, device
band or interference issue.
Strong signal, crowded cell   Full bars but slow or unstable data.   Coverage exists; radio capacity may be
constrained.
Good radio, failed transport   Signal bars remain but services fail.   Radio site is visible, but traffic cannot reach
the core reliably.
Good network, slow
application
Other services work normally.   Destination server, content path or
application may be the bottleneck.
Signal bars are a device-vendor display, not an end-to-end quality certificate. A complaint
investigation needs objective radio and service measurements.
The Subscriber Identity Module, or SIM, supports subscriber identity and authentication through its
credentials. It does not generate coverage. Detecting a cell, registering a subscription, establishing a
data session and reaching an application are distinct stages. A device can complete

credentials. It does not generate coverage. Detecting a cell, registering a subscription, establishing a

and fail at a later one. This is why an investigation should ask what succeeded before asking why the

5.6 Transport, aggregation and backhaul
Once the access network has received user traffic, that traffic must travel from the site to aggregation
points and the operator's core. This connecting segment is commonly called backhaul. Transport is
the broader system of links, switching and routing that moves aggregated traffic across the operator's
network.
Medium   Strength   Constraint or risk
Fibre optic cable   Very high capacity, long distance and low
delay.
Cuts, route concentration, right-of-way,
construction time and repair access.
Microwave radio   Rapid deployment and useful where fibre is
unavailable.
Line-of-sight, spectrum coordination,
weather at some bands and finite channel
capacity.
Satellite   Wide reach and value in remote or rapidly
served locations.
Propagation delay for some orbits, capacity
economics and gateway dependence.
Copper   Uses existing physical infrastructure in some
fixed networks.
Distance and condition limit performance.
Aggregation
One site may carry traffic for hundreds or thousands of devices. Transport networks combine traffic
from many sites into progressively larger links. A failure at an aggregation point can therefore affect a
wide area even though every local radio site remains powered.
Resilience
A resilient design provides alternative paths, protected equipment, spare capacity, power continuity
and restoration procedures. Two fibre cables do not provide genuine diversity if both occupy the
same duct or bridge. Physical-route evidence matters as much as a logical network diagram.
Fibre cut diagnosis
Identify alarms and the affected span.
Determine which sites, services and other operators depend on the route.
Switch to a diverse path where available.
Protect the repair area and mobilise the responsible owner.
Communicate impact and restoration estimates accurately.
After repair, reconcile traffic and examine root cause, route protection and repeat incidents.
Backhaul is not the Internet. It is the transport connection from access infrastructure
towards aggregation and core functions; Internet access comes later in the service path.
Fixed access reaches the network through a different local arrangement. Fibre may extend to a
building or home, where an optical

infrastructure
towards aggregation and core functions; Internet access comes later in the service path.
Fixed access reaches the network through a different local arrangement. Fibre may extend to a
building or home, where an optical terminal converts between the optical access system and the
customer’s equipment. A local router may then serve devices over cables or Wi-Fi. Wi-Fi is the local
wireless connection; it is not necessarily the upstream Internet service. Poor performance can arise
inside the premises even when the provider’s access link is functioning, or upstream while the local
wireless signal remains strong.
NCC Promotion Study Guide   35

5.7 Core functions, authentication and session control
The core network is the operator's central service-control and connectivity environment. It determines
whether a subscription is recognised and permitted, establishes communication sessions, tracks
mobility at a broader level, applies policy and charging controls, and routes traffic towards its
destination.
Control plane and user plane
The control plane exchanges signalling needed to establish and manage service: registration,
authentication, mobility, session setup and policy. The user plane carries the subscriber's actual
voice, video or application data after the necessary control decisions. Separating the two helps
diagnosis: successful registration does not prove that user traffic can reach the service.
Function   Plain-language purpose
Subscriber data   Stores or retrieves the authorised service profile and related identifiers.
Authentication   Tests whether the subscription can prove possession of valid credentials.
Mobility management   Maintains enough location state to reach and serve a moving device.
Session management   Creates and controls the data connection and its parameters.
Policy control   Applies service, quality, roaming and charging rules.
User-plane forwarding   Moves actual subscriber traffic towards internal or external destinations.
Charging records   Creates usage information for billing, settlement and assurance.
A core fault can affect large numbers of users across many radio sites. Geographic breadth,
signalling alarms and multi-service symptoms help distinguish it from a local access fault.
Authentication and authorisation are different decisions. Authentication establishes confidence in the
credentials presented; authorisation determines which requested services are permitted. A valid
subscription may still lack an entitlement, have a restriction or encounter a failed session-creation
process. Usage records also need to correspond to the applicable charging rules: the fact that traffic
moved does not by itself prove that the resulting bill is correct.

5.8 Voice, data and service platforms
A network connection is not yet a completed service. Voice requires call control, addressing, media
handling and interconnection. Internet access requires addressing, name resolution, routing and
external connectivity. Messaging, mobile money and other services rely on their own platforms and
interfaces.
Voice over Long-Term Evolution
Fourth-generation radio and core networks are packet based. Voice over Long-Term Evolution
carries managed voice using Internet Protocol mechanisms and the Internet Protocol Multimedia
Subsystem. The system must register the voice service, establish a session, reserve appropriate
treatment and exchange media. If unavailable, some deployments historically moved the device to an
earlier-generation network for voice.
Internet service journey
The device obtains addressing and service parameters from the operator.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   36
A Domain Name System resolver translates a human-readable name into an address.
Routers select paths towards the destination network.
The traffic may pass through an Internet exchange, transit provider, content-delivery network or cloud
platform.
The destination application processes the request and sends a response.
Security, congestion and server performance can affect every stage.
Service symptom   Possible layer
Calls fail but data works   Voice registration, call control, interconnection or voice policy.
One website is slow   Application, content-delivery or route-specific problem.
All Internet services fail   Session, addressing, name service, gateway or upstream connectivity.
On-net calls work; off-net fail   Interconnection or routing between operators.
Internet Protocol does not mean public Internet. An operator can use Internet Protocol
internally for controlled voice and management services that are not ordinary public web
access.

5.9 Other networks, Internet routing and content
An operator's customers need to communicate beyond that operator. Interconnection is the physical,
logical, commercial and regulatory arrangement through which communications networks exchange
traffic. Internet connectivity is similarly an ecosystem of peering, transit, routing and content
relationships.
On-net and off-net
On-net traffic begins and ends on the same operator. Off-net traffic must cross to another network.
The originating network identifies the destination, selects an interconnection route and hands the
communication to the terminating network under agreed and regulated conditions.
Element   Why it matters
Point of interconnection   Defines where networks exchange traffic and responsibility changes.
Capacity   Insufficient ports or links can cause congestion even when both access networks
are healthy.
Signalling   Networks must exchange valid control information to establish and clear
communications.
Number routing   The destination number must be mapped to the correct serving network, including
ported numbers.
Termination and settlement   Commercial arrangements account for traffic and applicable charges.
Quality monitoring   Operators and NCC need evidence to locate degradation and disputes.

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.topic: 5.9 Other networks, Internet routing and content
metadata.section: 5.9 Other networks, Internet routing and content

chunks.content:
NCC Promotion Study Guide   37
Peering and transit
Internet networks may exchange traffic directly through peering, often at an Internet exchange point,
or pay a transit network to reach destinations they do not connect to directly. Local peering and
caching can shorten paths and reduce international dependence, but only where the desired content
and networks participate.
Border Gateway Protocol
The Border Gateway Protocol distributes reachability information among autonomous networks. It
helps networks decide which external paths to use. A routing leak, withdrawal or misconfiguration can
make services unreachable even though radio, transport and core equipment remain physically
operational.
Interconnection supports consumer choice and competition. Without it, subscribers would be
trapped in isolated network islands.
A Content Delivery Network distributes service content across servers so suitable material can be
delivered from a location closer to the user. Cached local content may perform well even if an
international route is impaired. Conversely, one remote service may be slow while local services
remain healthy. Comparing several destinations is therefore more informative than treating one
application as a complete test of the access network.
An Internet Exchange Point enables participating networks to exchange traffic. It does not guarantee
that every domestic communication stays within the country: participation, peering agreements,
routing policy and the location of the requested content still matter. Border Gateway Protocol
exchanges reachability information between autonomous networks. The selected route reflects policy
and available information, not a universal promise of the geographically shortest or least delayed
path.

chunks.content:
5.10 Protocol layers and encapsulation
The Open Systems Interconnection model divides communication into seven conceptual layers. The
Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol model groups the practical Internet protocol suite into
fewer layers. Neither is a literal drawing of one operator's departments. Their value is disciplined
separation of functions.
OSI layer   Core question   Example
7 Application   What service does the user or software need?   Web, email, name resolution or signalling
application.
6 Presentation   How is information represented or protected?   Encoding, compression and encryption
format.
5 Session   How is an interaction organised and maintained?   Dialogue establishment and recovery.
4 Transport   How do endpoints manage delivery?   Transmission Control Protocol or User
Datagram Protocol.
3 Network   How are packets addressed and routed?   Internet Protocol and routing.
2 Data link   How is a local link shared and framed?   Ethernet or a radio link-layer function.
1 Physical   How are bits represented in a medium?   Radio energy, light or electrical signal.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   38
Encapsulation
As application data moves downward through a protocol stack, each layer adds control information
needed for its function. At the receiver, corresponding layers interpret and remove that information.
This is why a packet capture contains nested headers and why one user message can generate
several protocol exchanges.
Use the models carefully
A fibre cut is a physical-path problem, but it can trigger routing changes at higher layers. A Domain
Name System failure is an application-layer service problem, yet users may describe it as 'the
Internet is down'. Layers interact; classification is a starting point for evidence, not a ban on
cross-layer causes.
The OSI model has seven conceptual layers; the practical TCP/IP model is commonly
shown with four or five. Do not force every modern mobile-network function into one
perfect box.
The Open Systems Interconnection model is commonly shortened to OSI. The Internet protocol suite
is commonly called TCP/IP, after Transmission Control Protocol and Internet Protocol. In a four-layer
teaching model, application functions sit above transport, Internet and link functions. The mapping
below relates responsibilities; it is not an assertion that the two models are identical.
Seven-layer model   Common four-layer Internet
model
Relationship
Application, presentation, session   Application   Application protocols and software carry out
functions described separately in the upper
conceptual layers.
Transport   Transport   Endpoint communication, including
transport protocols and their delivery
behaviour.
Network   Internet   Internet Protocol addressing and forwarding
between networks.
Data link and physical   Link   Local delivery, framing, media access and
physical transmission.
Transmission Control Protocol provides reliable, ordered delivery of a byte stream using mechanisms
including sequence numbers, acknowledgements and retransmission. User Datagram Protocol
provides a datagram service without those delivery guarantees; an application can add its own
mechanisms. Reliability at one layer does not mean that an application can never fail. A connection
may be interrupted or an application may reject data that arrived correctly. Technical basis: Internet
Engineering Task Force,

own
mechanisms. Reliability at one layer does not mean that an application can never fail. A connection
may be interrupted or an application may reject data that arrived correctly. Technical basis: Internet
Engineering Task Force, RFC 9293, Transmission Control Protocol.
Internet Protocol version 4 uses 32-bit addresses, while version 6 uses 128-bit addresses. The larger
address space supports many more addressable interfaces. An address is used for network delivery;
it is not automatically proof of a person's identity. A device may have several interfaces and
addresses, and shared-address arrangements can complicate attribution. Technical basis: Internet
Engineering Task Force, RFC 8200, Internet Protocol Version 6 Specification.
Encapsulation can be followed through a web request. The application creates a request. The
selected transport protocol supplies its own delivery information. Internet Protocol supplies
addressing for routing. The local link carries the resulting data using its framing and physical medium.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   39
At a router, local link information can change as the packet is forwarded onto another link. At the
destination, the receiving protocol functions interpret the information intended for them. A layer model
helps explain this process without requiring every physical appliance to perform only one function.

5.11 Coverage, capacity, service quality and experience
These four concepts are related but must not be collapsed.
Concept   Question   Evidence
Coverage   Can an adequate service signal reach the
location?
Prediction maps, drive/walk tests, signal
measurements and availability.
Capacity   Can available resources serve the offered
demand?
Utilisation, congestion, scheduler and
transport statistics.
Quality of Service   Does measurable service performance
meet applicable requirements?
Accessibility, retainability, throughput, delay,
loss and availability indicators.
Quality of Experience   What does the user actually perceive in
context?
Application tests, surveys, complaints, device
and content conditions.
Full bars, slow Internet
A nearby cell may provide strong signal but share limited radio capacity among many users. The
transport link may be congested. A core gateway or external route may be overloaded. The
application server may respond slowly. The device itself may support limited bands or processing.
The correct investigation moves through the path and tests each hypothesis.
Accessibility, availability and retainability
Accessibility asks whether a user can start the service. Retainability asks whether it remains available
until properly completed. A network may permit call setup but drop calls during handover; it therefore
performs differently on the two dimensions. Availability concerns whether the relevant service or
component is operational during a defined period. A powered site may be available as equipment
while a particular service remains inaccessible; the measurement definition determines what is being
assessed.
Measure, diagnose, act
Measure the symptom using reproducible methods and relevant indicators.
Locate the affected users, times, technologies, services and network layers.
Correlate field results with operator alarms, configuration and capacity evidence.
Identify the controllable root cause rather than the nearest visible symptom.
Require proportionate remediation and verify improvement after action.
Quality regulation should connect an indicator to a cause, responsible actor, corrective action and
verified consumer outcome.
A measurement needs a defined location, time, device, technology, service and method. Indoor and
outdoor results may differ, as may busy-hour and quiet-period results. A national average

verified consumer outcome.
A measurement needs a defined location, time, device, technology, service and method. Indoor and
outdoor results may differ, as may busy-hour and quiet-period results. A national average can
conceal a locality with persistent problems. Comparing measurements is meaningful only when
differences in conditions and scope are accounted for. Numerical legal thresholds belong with their

5.12 Power, resilience and network operations
Communications equipment requires dependable power. A radio site may rely on grid supply,
rectifiers, batteries, generators, solar systems and automatic switching. Core and data-centre sites
require high-availability power, environmental control, fire protection and redundant infrastructure.
A failure chain
Grid power fails. Batteries carry the site temporarily. If backup generation does not start or fuel is
unavailable, voltage falls and radio equipment shuts down. Neighbouring cells absorb additional
users, become congested and may themselves experience power or capacity stress. One physical
event therefore produces coverage, capacity and quality effects.
Resilience control   Purpose
Redundancy   Provide an alternative component, link or path.
Diversity   Ensure alternatives do not share the same hidden point of failure.
Protection switching   Move traffic automatically or rapidly when a fault is detected.
Monitoring   Detect degradation before complete failure and support diagnosis.
Spares and field support   Reduce restoration time after equipment failure.
Disaster recovery   Restore critical systems and data after a major disruption.
Business continuity   Maintain priority services and organisational operations during disruption.
Network Operations Centre
A Network Operations Centre observes alarms, performance and incidents; coordinates field teams;
communicates impact; escalates major outages; and records restoration. It does not replace
engineering, security, customer care or regulatory oversight, but it is a central evidence and
coordination point.
Mean Time to Repair
Mean Time to Repair summarises restoration duration across relevant incidents. Averages can hide
severe outliers, repeated failures or differing incident classes. NCC should examine definitions,
distributions, causes and affected consumers rather than accept one average without context.
Redundancy is not diversity. Two systems can be redundant yet fail together because they
share power, a route, software or physical location.
NCC Promotion Study Guide   41

Regulatory response ladder
Confirm the scope and protect urgent consumer or safety interests.
Preserve reliable, time-stamped evidence from independent and operator sources.
Identify the obligation, licence condition, regulation or quality rule engaged.
Separate root cause from contributing factors and external dependencies.
Require a corrective and preventive action plan with owners and deadlines.
Verify restoration and sustained improvement rather than closing on assertion.
Escalate repeated, serious or non-compliant conduct through the lawful enforcement process.
A Level 10 answer
Begin with the end-to-end service, identify the likely layer, request the evidence that could prove or
disprove the hypothesis, connect the finding to the responsible actor and regulatory obligation, and
propose proportionate remediation followed by verification. This structure demonstrates technical
understanding without pretending that an officer can diagnose a live network from a complaint
sentence alone.

chunks.content:
5.14 Practice questions and explained answers
Question 1. A phone shows full bars but a website is slow. Has the operator proved good
service?
Answer. No. Signal bars concern part of the radio connection. The cell may be crowded, transport
may be constrained, a core function may be impaired or the destination may respond slowly. Test
more than one service and compare relevant radio, transport and application evidence before
attributing the cause.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   42
Question 2. Explain the difference between a mast, a base station and a Radio Access
Network.
Answer. The mast provides physical support. The base station supplies radio equipment and
processing that communicate with devices. The Radio Access Network comprises the wider access
functions, sites and associated processing. None alone is the complete path to an Internet application
or another operator’s customer.
Question 3. How long would a 100-megabyte file take at a sustained useful rate of 20
megabits per second?
Answer. With decimal units, multiply 100 megabytes by eight to obtain 800 megabits. Divide by 20 to
obtain 40 seconds. This is an ideal calculation at the stated useful rate; additional interruptions or a
lower actual rate increase the duration. Do not divide bytes directly by bits per second.
Question 4. Does packet switching guarantee that every packet arrives in order?
Answer. No. Packet networks can lose, duplicate or reorder traffic. Delivery behaviour depends on
the protocols involved. A reliable ordered transport can recover from some network effects, while a
datagram application may use different mechanisms or tolerate some loss. Packet switching and
reliable delivery are different concepts.
Question 5. A subscription registers successfully but Internet use fails. Why is that
possible?
Answer. Registration establishes only part of the service. A data session, addressing, policy,
forwarding, name resolution and destination access must also work. Distinguishing control signalling
from user traffic helps identify which stage has succeeded and where to investigate next.
Question 6. Why can calls fail while mobile data works?
Answer. Managed voice requires its own registration, call control, service entitlement and media path.
Interconnection may also be needed. A working data session does not establish that every
voice-service function is operational. Compare on-net and off-net calling, relevant service registration
and the affected devices.
Question 7. Why are two fibre links in one duct insufficient evidence of route diversity?
Answer. A single excavation or

function is operational. Compare on-net and off-net calling, relevant service registration
and the affected devices.
Question 7. Why are two fibre links in one duct insufficient evidence of route diversity?
Answer. A single excavation or physical incident may cut both links. They provide two links but share
a failure location. Check actual physical routes, entry points, power dependencies and switching
arrangements before describing the design as diverse.
Question 8. What does a working Wi-Fi connection establish?
Answer. It establishes some degree of local wireless connectivity, not complete Internet reachability.
The router’s upstream connection, addressing, name resolution, provider network and destination still
matter. Compare local and external access and test the upstream service separately.
Question 9. Why does a fifth-generation indicator not prove a complete standalone
fifth-generation service?
Answer. The radio may be deployed in a non-standalone architecture using fourth-generation
infrastructure as an anchor. Features also depend on the core, transport, device and service
configuration. The indicator alone does not establish the whole architecture or a guaranteed
performance level.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   43
Question 10. Calls drop repeatedly at one point on a road. What evidence should be
obtained?
Answer. Locate the event and compare radio measurements, neighbouring cells, handover attempts,
resource availability and transport alarms. Repeat under comparable conditions and consider
device-specific effects. A geographic pattern suggests hypotheses but does not itself prove a
particular fault.
Question 11. A busy-hour improvement followed a capacity upgrade. What is needed
before attributing success?
Answer. Compare measurements using consistent locations, load periods, devices and service
definitions; examine relevant utilisation and fault data. Determine whether the improvement persists
and whether other changes explain it. A completed upgrade is implementation evidence, while
improved service requires performance evidence.
Question 12. Describe a Level 10 regulatory response to a widespread outage.
Answer. Establish scope and immediate service impact; preserve time-stamped evidence; identify
shared dependencies and the responsible entities; connect findings to the applicable obligations;
require restoration and corrective action through the lawful process; and verify sustained recovery.
Communicate confirmed facts and uncertainty accurately.
NCC Promotion Study Guide   44

Chapter 6
Spectrum: technical foundations and regulatory
management

Chapter 5 explained how radio provides access to a communications network. Spectrum
management determines how many different users and services can use radio frequencies under
compatible conditions. This chapter connects the physical properties of radio with institutional
authority, assignment decisions, monitoring and the evolution of spectrum use.

chunks.content:
6.1 The resource and the reason for coordination
Radio spectrum is the usable range of electromagnetic frequencies through which wireless
systems transmit information. It is not a physical substance stored in a warehouse. The scarce
regulatory resource is the ability to use particular frequencies, at particular places, times, powers
and technical conditions, without causing or receiving unacceptable interference.
Why regulation is unavoidable
Two transmitters can impair each other when their emissions, locations, timing and receiver
characteristics conflict. No operator can create a nationally and internationally compatible frequency
environment alone. Public management coordinates uses, protects safety and essential services,
supports competition, promotes efficient utilisation and enables innovation.
Question   Spectrum answer
What is managed?   Rights and conditions for using defined frequencies.
Why scarce?   Many desired uses compete for combinations of frequency, geography, time and
interference tolerance.
Who benefits?   Mobile, broadcasting, satellite, aviation, maritime, defence, emergency, scientific
and other services.
What is the goal?   Efficient, interference-managed use aligned with public interest and international
obligations.
Do not memorise band numbers without understanding propagation, bandwidth, ecosystem,
assignment method and policy purpose. A frequency is useful only within a complete technical and
regulatory context.
A transmission does not permanently consume a frequency in the way that an engine consumes fuel.
Reuse is possible across geography, time and technical arrangements. Scarcity arises when desired
uses compete under conditions in which interference or other constraints prevent them from
operating satisfactorily together. Spectrum policy therefore concerns practical rights and
compatibility, as well as the frequency range itself.

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.chapter: Chapter 5 explained how radio provides access to a communications network. Spectrum

metadata.section: 6.1 The resource and the reason for coordination

chunks.content:
6.2 Frequency, wavelength and bandwidth
An electromagnetic wave carries energy through changing electric and magnetic fields. Frequency is
the number of cycles completed each second and is measured in hertz. Wavelength is the physical
distance occupied by one cycle. In free space, higher frequency corresponds to shorter wavelength
because wave speed is approximately constant.

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.chapter: Chapter 5 explained how radio provides access to a communications network. Spectrum

chunks.content:
NCC Promotion Study Guide   45
The relationship
Wave speed equals frequency multiplied by wavelength. Therefore wavelength equals wave speed
divided by frequency. This relationship helps explain why antenna dimensions and propagation
behaviour differ across bands.
Term   Meaning   Practical importance
Hertz   One cycle per second.   Base unit of frequency.
Kilohertz   One thousand hertz.   Used for lower-frequency services and
channel descriptions.
Megahertz   One million hertz.   Common for broadcasting and mobile band
references.
Gigahertz   One billion hertz.   Common for microwave, satellite, wireless
local-area and mobile bands.
Wavelength   Distance between corresponding wave
points.
Influences antenna size, diffraction and
interaction with objects.
Frequency is not speed
A higher carrier frequency does not mean that information travels through space faster.
Electromagnetic waves propagate at similar fundamental speed in the same medium. Service
performance changes because available bandwidth, signal loss, antenna design, propagation,
technology and network capacity differ.
Bandwidth
Frequency bandwidth is the width of a frequency range. A wider authorised channel can support
greater potential data capacity when combined with suitable technology and signal quality. It does not
guarantee user throughput because spectrum must be shared, network implementation matters and
the end-to-end path can constrain service.
Frequency, frequency bandwidth and data throughput are related but not interchangeable.
For an approximate free-space calculation, take wave speed as 300 million metres per second. At
900 million cycles per second, wavelength is about one third of a metre. At 3.5 billion cycles per
second, wavelength is about 0.086 metre, or 8.6 centimetres. These examples explain the
relationship between frequency and wavelength; they do not specify an operator's current
assignment.
Centre frequency identifies the position of a channel, while bandwidth describes its span. An
illustrative channel from 3,400 to 3,420 megahertz is 20 megahertz wide. Another from 3,500 to 3,520
megahertz has the same width at a different position. Different centre frequencies do not necessarily
mean different bandwidths or user speeds.

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.chapter: Chapter 5 explained how radio provides access to a communications network. Spectrum

chunks.content:
6.3 Capacity, spectral efficiency and duplexing
Spectral efficiency expresses the amount of information carried per unit of frequency bandwidth
under specified conditions. Better modulation, coding and antenna techniques can improve it when
signal conditions support them. Weak or noisy conditions may require more robust transmission with
fewer information bits for the same radio resource. More ambitious signalling is therefore not always
the better choice for a difficult link.

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.chapter: Chapter 5 explained how radio provides access to a communications network. Spectrum

chunks.content:
NCC Promotion Study Guide   46
An illustrative efficiency of 2 bits per second per hertz across 10 million hertz gives 20 million bits per
second before any additional deductions assumed by the example. This is a calculation based on the
stated efficiency, not a guaranteed subscriber rate. Protocol overhead, scheduling, control resources
and sharing affect the result delivered to each user.
Capacity can also be increased by adding cells, improving sectorisation, using suitable
multiple-antenna techniques, reducing interference or moving appropriate traffic onto other access
networks. Each choice has dependencies. New cells need sites, power and transport; additional radio
bandwidth cannot remove a bottleneck in backhaul. The regulatory assessment should identify the
actual limiting resource.
A large contiguous block may be easier to use than the same total bandwidth split into separated
pieces. Carrier aggregation can combine supported carriers, but this depends on compatible network
equipment, devices and band combinations. Adding the sizes of all an operator's assignments is not
enough to establish the capacity available to one user at one location.
Duplexing separates the two directions of communication. Frequency Division Duplex, usually
shortened to FDD, normally uses paired frequency resources for uplink and downlink. Time Division
Duplex, or TDD, separates the directions in time on the same frequency resource. Uplink carries
traffic from the device towards the network; downlink carries it towards the device.
Time-based separation permits different amounts of time to be used for the two directions, but
neighbouring systems need compatible timing or other protection arrangements. Otherwise one
network's downlink transmission can interfere with another network's uplink reception.
Frequency-based separation also requires suitable filters, separation and equipment. Neither
arrangement eliminates interference management.
Multiple access answers a related but different question: how several users share resources.
Systems can distinguish users by frequency, time, code, subcarriers, spatial processing or
combinations. Duplexing concerns directions; multiple access concerns users. Guard bands and
emission limits help neighbouring uses coexist, but protective separation may

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master

chunks.content:
share resources.
Systems can distinguish users by frequency, time, code, subcarriers, spatial processing or
combinations. Duplexing concerns directions; multiple access concerns users. Guard bands and
emission limits help neighbouring uses coexist, but protective separation may reduce the bandwidth
available for ordinary traffic.

chunks.content:
6.4 Propagation and the coverage-capacity relationship
Radio waves interact with terrain, buildings, vegetation, the atmosphere and other objects.
Regulatory decisions therefore cannot be made from a frequency number alone.
Effect   Plain meaning   Network consequence
Free-space loss   Signal power spreads and weakens with
distance.
Limits link range and requires adequate power
and antenna gain.
Reflection   A wave bounces from a surface.   Creates alternative paths and coverage
variation.
Diffraction   Energy bends around edges.   Helps reach behind obstacles, especially at
longer wavelengths.
Refraction   A changing medium bends the path.   Can alter terrestrial or atmospheric link
behaviour.
Scattering   Small or irregular objects redirect energy.   Creates diffuse signals and fading.

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.chapter: Chapter 5 explained how radio provides access to a communications network. Spectrum

chunks.content:
NCC Promotion Study Guide   47
Effect   Plain meaning   Network consequence
Absorption   Materials convert part of the energy.   Walls, rain or vegetation may attenuate signals
depending on frequency.
Lower and higher bands
Lower-frequency mobile bands generally travel farther and penetrate buildings more effectively,
making them valuable for wide-area and rural coverage. Higher bands can offer large contiguous
bandwidth and high capacity but usually require denser infrastructure and are more sensitive to
blockage. These are tendencies, not absolute rules; antenna systems, power, terrain and technology
remain important.
Coverage-capacity trade-off
A regulator may use lower bands to promote wide coverage and higher bands to add urban capacity.
Mid-bands can provide a compromise. A balanced portfolio therefore supports coverage, capacity
and innovation rather than treating one auction band as a complete national broadband strategy.
A higher-frequency assignment is not automatically better spectrum. Its value depends on
the intended service, ecosystem, available bandwidth, deployment cost and propagation
needs.

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.chapter: Chapter 5 explained how radio provides access to a communications network. Spectrum

chunks.content:
6.5 International coordination and Nigerian institutions
Radio waves cross borders and equipment markets are global. Spectrum management therefore
operates through connected international, regional and national layers.
Layer   Role
International Telecommunication
Union Radiocommunication Sector
Maintains the Radio Regulations, conducts World Radiocommunication
Conferences and supports global allocation and coordination.
Regional coordination   African and West African bodies help develop common positions,
harmonisation and cross-border cooperation.
Federal policy and national allocation   Nigeria determines national policy and reflects international obligations in its
frequency allocation framework.
NCC sector administration   NCC plans, licenses, assigns, prices, monitors and enforces spectrum use
within its communications mandate, while coordinating with other competent
authorities.
Licensee and user   Uses assigned frequencies within authorised service, geography, power,
technology and other conditions.
Radio Regulations
The International Telecommunication Union Radio Regulations form the treaty-level framework for
international frequency allocation, notifications, coordination and protection. They do not by
themselves hand a Nigerian operator a domestic assignment. National authorisation is still required.
National Frequency Allocation Table
A national table maps frequency ranges to radiocommunication services and national arrangements.
It is a planning instrument: an allocation to a service category creates the framework within which
more specific national uses and assignments can be made.

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.chapter: Chapter 5 explained how radio provides access to a communications network. Spectrum

chunks.content:
NCC Promotion Study Guide   48
Cross-border coordination
Signals near borders can cause harmful interference or constrain neighbouring networks.
Administrations coordinate frequencies, sites, powers and technical parameters. An assignment valid
domestically may still require coordination before operation in a border area or satellite context.
International allocation, national allocation and operator assignment are different decisions made
at different levels.
The National Frequency Management Council has national and trans-sectoral responsibilities. NCC
exercises communications-sector responsibilities within the statutory framework. A regional
coordination body supports cooperation; it does not replace Nigeria’s domestic licensing authority. An
officer should first establish whether a problem concerns national planning, a communications
assignment, another sector’s use or a cross-border coordination obligation.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 5 explained how radio provides access to a communications network. Spectrum

chunks.content:
6.6 Allocation, allotment, assignment and authorisation
Term   Meaning   Example
Allocation   Entry in a frequency table designating a band for
one or more radiocommunication services.
A range allocated to mobile and/or
fixed service.
Allotment   Designation of a channel or block for use in an
area or by a country under a plan.
A planned channel associated with a
geographic area.
Assignment   Authorisation for a station or licensee to use a
frequency under stated conditions.
An operator receives a defined block
for authorised deployment.
Primary and secondary services
The Radio Regulations can identify services as primary or secondary in a band. A secondary service
generally must not cause harmful interference to primary services and cannot claim protection from
them. The precise status comes from the applicable table and footnotes; do not infer it from
commercial importance.
Exclusive and shared use
An assignment can provide exclusive use within defined conditions, but spectrum is increasingly
shared across services, geography, time or technical frameworks. Sharing requires compatibility
analysis and enforceable rules. It is not permission for everyone to transmit without coordination.
Licence-exempt does not mean unregulated
Some devices may operate without an individual frequency assignment when they comply with
general authorisation, power, band and equipment conditions. Users receive convenience, not a
guarantee of interference-free operation or permission to exceed technical limits.
Allocation does not give a company an operating right; assignment does not transfer
ownership of the electromagnetic spectrum.
A service licence and a frequency licence address different permissions. A business may be
authorised to provide a communications service but still require an appropriate frequency
authorisation for a proposed radio deployment. Conversely, access to a frequency does not by itself
permit every commercial service. Check the activity, resource, applicable exemption and licence
conditions together.

6.7 The Act’s spectrum provisions: sections 121–127
Section 121 vests the Commission with responsibility for managing and administering frequency
spectrum for the communications sector and the associated licensing and regulatory powers. This
must be read with the national frequency-management arrangements already explained in Chapter 3.
It does not make the Commission and the National Frequency Management Council the same body.
Section 122 addresses intentional transmission to provide a service without the required frequency
licence, subject to applicable exemptions. Its offence provisions include licence-fee-related fines,
imprisonment of up to one year or both, and forfeiture on conviction of the property and equipment
used for the service. The monetary provisions refer to the relevant initial licence fee, rather than one
universal fixed sum for every case. Where a contravention causes death or physical harm, the Act
also preserves exposure under the applicable criminal law.
Section 123 permits regulations on matters in the chapter and identifies auction, tender and a
Commission-determined fixed price among possible spectrum-assignment procedures. These are
examples within the statutory framework. The provision does not require every assignment to be
auctioned or establish identical award conditions for every band.
Section 124 provides for NCC, in consultation with and on behalf of the Council, to develop the
national frequency plan. The Commission must liaise with different spectrum users, including military,
security, maritime and aviation interests. Planning must consider the Act's objectives, existing users
and applicable international standards and agreements. This explains why a proposed change in a
band needs more than a list of interested commercial applicants.
Section 125 permits the issue or renewal of a frequency licence subject to prescribed fees and
imposed conditions. The rights concern specified bands or the operation of a specified kind of
network facility within specified frequencies. Issue and reissue must conform to the national
frequency plan and the relevant determination of bands for assignment. A fee payment does not
override those planning requirements.
Section

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.chapter: Chapter 5 explained how radio provides access to a communications network. Spectrum

chunks.content:
kind of
network facility within specified frequencies. Issue and reissue must conform to the national
frequency plan and the relevant determination of bands for assignment. A fee payment does not
override those planning requirements.
Section 126 concerns compulsory acquisition of assignments in accordance with a reassignment
policy consistent with the national frequency plan or in the national interest. The section permits
reasonable compensation where an assignment is acquired before expiry. The statutory wording is
discretionary: it should not be rewritten as an unconditional promise that compensation must always
be paid.
Section 127 concerns failure to use assigned spectrum by the specified deadline or to renew a
frequency licence when due. The Commission may, at its discretion, require forfeiture, after which the
assignment reverts to it for reassignment. No compensation is payable for forfeiture under that
subsection. Compulsory acquisition and forfeiture therefore have different grounds and compensation
treatment. Source: Nigerian Communications Act 2003, sections 121–127.

6.8 Managing the assignment throughout its life
Stage   Regulatory work
Demand identification   Assess services, technology, coverage, capacity, public safety and innovation needs.
Planning   Review international allocations, national policy, incumbent use, equipment ecosystem
and coexistence.
Clearing or coexistence
design
Determine whether incumbents move, remain, share or receive protection.
Valuation and award design   Choose administrative assignment, auction, comparative process or another lawful
method.
Assignment   Define block, geography, duration, power, rollout and other conditions.
Deployment   Licensee builds within site, equipment, coordination and authorisation requirements.
Monitoring   Measure utilisation, emissions, interference and compliance.
Enforcement   Correct unauthorised or non-compliant use through lawful processes.
Renewal, transfer or trading   Review continued use and any permitted change of rights.
Refarming or re-planning   Reorganise use for greater efficiency, new technology or policy objectives.
Surrender or expiry   Recover and prepare rights for future use where appropriate.
Why assignment is not the finish line
An award starts a regulatory relationship. NCC may need to verify payments, rollout obligations,
coordination, utilisation, interference control, reporting, consumer outcomes and licence conditions.
An unused assignment can carry opportunity cost because other services cannot readily use the
same rights.
Spectrum inventory
Effective management requires reliable records linking bands, blocks, licensees, locations, transmit
parameters, authorisation dates, obligations, monitoring results and interference cases. Poor records
can create conflicting assignments and weaken enforcement.
Manage spectrum as a lifecycle, not an auction event.
An information system supporting spectrum administration should preserve the relationship between
the legal instrument and the technical record. A changed database entry is not itself approval for a
changed assignment. Record who authorised the change, its effective date, the affected parameters
and any consequential obligations. Versioned records help explain which conditions applied when an
interference event occurred.

6.9 Award methods and competition safeguards
Method   Best suited where   Risk to control
Administrative assignment   Demand is limited, use is specialised or
coordination is the main issue.
Opacity, inconsistent treatment or weak
valuation.
First-come process   Applications are comparable and scarcity
is not acute.
Strategic queueing and unfair information
advantage.
Comparative selection   Policy objectives require qualitative
assessment.
Subjectivity and challenge to evaluation.
Auction   Scarce commercial rights attract
competing qualified bidders.
Overbidding, concentration, collusion and
design failure.
Beauty contest plus price   Technical or policy commitments combine
with financial competition.
Complex scoring and enforcement of
promises.
Dynamic/shared access   Use can be coordinated by database,
geography, time or sensing.
Reliability, incumbent protection and
accountability.
Auction is a means, not the objective
An auction can discover market value transparently and allocate scarce rights among qualified
bidders, but maximum immediate revenue is not the only public-interest objective. Competition,
coverage, investment capacity, spectrum caps, rollout and long-term consumer welfare may shape
design.
Reserve price and spectrum cap
A reserve price establishes a minimum acceptable bid or value safeguard. A spectrum cap limits how
much a participant can acquire to address concentration. Poorly calibrated values can deter
participation, encourage speculative acquisition or undermine competition.
Post-award risk
A bidder can win but deploy slowly, fail to finance the network or warehouse rights. Award documents
and licences therefore need payment, rollout, reporting, default and enforcement provisions. The
regulator must distinguish legitimate deployment challenges from strategic delay.
Highest bid does not automatically equal best regulatory outcome; the award method and
licence conditions must serve the defined policy objective.
The methods above describe regulatory design options. Their inclusion is not a statement that every
option is available for every Nigerian band. The applicable instrument and award documentation
determine the actual process. Eligibility, evaluation and default conditions must be known before
treating a payment or commercial announcement as completion of an award.

chunks.content:
6.10 Pricing, investment and efficient use
Spectrum has economic value because authorised access can enable revenue, reduce deployment
cost or provide strategic capacity. Value varies by propagation, bandwidth, ecosystem, geography,
duration, obligations, interference environment and market structure.
Pricing component   Purpose
Application or processing fee   Recover defined administrative work where applicable.

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.chapter: Chapter 5 explained how radio provides access to a communications network. Spectrum

chunks.content:
NCC Promotion Study Guide   52
Pricing component   Purpose
Assignment or licence fee   Charge for authorised spectrum access under the prescribed framework.
Auction payment   Reflect competitive bids for scarce rights.
Annual spectrum fee   Support ongoing administration and reflect authorised holdings or use.
Monitoring or coordination cost   Recover specified technical work where lawfully provided.
Penalty or interest   Address breach or late payment under lawful authority; not ordinary pricing.
Administrative Incentive Pricing
Administrative pricing can encourage efficient holding by reflecting opportunity cost and technical
characteristics. It should be transparent and predictable. A high fee may release underused rights but
can also weaken rural investment if it ignores obligations and economics.
Spectrum is not sold outright
A payment normally purchases a time-limited, conditional right of use, not private ownership of the
national resource. Renewal, transfer, technology and geographic rights remain governed by the
instrument and regulatory framework.
Efficiency has several meanings
Technical efficiency: more useful communication from limited interference and bandwidth.
Economic efficiency: rights flow to uses producing high social and commercial value.
Allocative efficiency: bands are directed to appropriate services and users.
Dynamic efficiency: the framework supports innovation and future reconfiguration.
Social efficiency: public safety, inclusion and national development are considered.
Price is one management tool. Monitoring, conditions, competition safeguards and refarming are
equally important.

6.11 Interference investigation and monitoring
Interference is unwanted radio-frequency energy that degrades reception. Harmful interference is
defined and assessed within the applicable regulatory context; not every detectable signal constitutes
unlawful harmful interference.
Type   Cause   Evidence
Co-channel   Two systems use the same or overlapping
channel incompatibly.
Frequencies, locations, timing, power and
receiver impact.
Adjacent-channel   Energy spills into or receivers admit a
nearby channel.
Emission masks, filters, separation and
equipment performance.
Intermodulation   Signals combine in nonlinear equipment to
create new products.
Site inventory, frequencies and equipment
tests.
Spurious emission   Unwanted transmitter output outside
necessary bandwidth.
Spectrum analyser measurements and
equipment conformity.
Jamming   Intentional interference with reception.   Direction finding, timing, motive and
authorised records.

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.chapter: Chapter 5 explained how radio provides access to a communications network. Spectrum

chunks.content:
NCC Promotion Study Guide   53
Type   Cause   Evidence
Natural/electrical noise   Lightning, machinery or faulty electronics.   Field measurements and source isolation.
Investigation sequence
Record complainant, service, frequency, time, location and impact.
Check assignments and authorised technical parameters.
Measure the signal with calibrated equipment and preserve traceable records.
Use direction finding, site inspection and controlled tests to identify the source.
Distinguish transmitter fault, receiver weakness, poor planning and unauthorised use.
Protect safety-critical services and coordinate urgent mitigation.
Apply proportionate lawful correction and verify that interference has ceased.
Monitoring network
Fixed and mobile monitoring facilities observe occupancy, emissions and interference. Monitoring
also reveals unauthorised transmissions and supports planning. A measurement without method,
calibration, location and time has limited evidential value.
The loudest signal near the complainant is not automatically the source. Direction, timing,
modulation and controlled tests matter.
Spectrum monitoring examines radio emissions and use. Quality-of-service testing examines
delivered service performance. A clean radio observation cannot establish that backhaul has
sufficient capacity, while a slow data result cannot establish that an unlawful transmitter exists. The
two investigations can inform one another, but the measurements and conclusions must remain
distinct.
