6.12 Refarming, sharing and trading
Refarming reorganises spectrum use so a band can support a new technology, service or more
efficient arrangement. It can involve moving incumbents, changing channel plans, modifying licences
or permitting technology-neutral use.
A defensible refarming process
Define the public-interest and efficiency problem.
Identify incumbents, equipment, users, investments and dependencies.
Conduct compatibility and market analysis.
Consult affected stakeholders and assess alternatives.
Decide transition timing, costs, protection and continuity measures.
Amend assignments and coordinate equipment migration.
Monitor implementation and resolve interference or competition effects.
Mechanism   Meaning   Control
Technology neutrality   Licensee may choose among compliant
technologies within defined rights.
Emission, interference, competition
and service obligations remain.

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.chapter: Chapter 5 explained how radio provides access to a communications network. Spectrum

chunks.content:
NCC Promotion Study Guide   54
Mechanism   Meaning   Control
Spectrum sharing   Several uses coexist by geography, time,
power, database or technical rules.
Compatibility and enforceable priority
are essential.
Spectrum trading   Permitted transfer or lease of rights under
regulatory approval and conditions.
Concentration, hoarding, transparency
and original obligations.
Surrender   Licensee voluntarily returns rights under the
governing framework.
Liabilities, fees and continuity must be
settled.
Trading is not an unregulated sale
Because assignments are conditional public-resource rights, a transaction may require NCC approval
and competition review. The regulator should examine the buyer's eligibility, spectrum concentration,
use plan, outstanding obligations and effect on consumers.
Refarming does not mean simply changing a label from one generation to another. It is a
managed technical, legal, commercial and consumer transition.
The 2022 Spectrum Trading Guidelines add transaction-specific controls. Their eligibility provisions
require an appropriately licensed buyer, consenting Board resolutions, at least one year of holding by
the seller and, where applicable, achievement of at least 25% of the licence rollout obligation. They
also specify two years of good regulatory and financial standing and restrictions affecting spectrum
subject to forfeiture notice or licence breach. These requirements must be read together; satisfying
one is not sufficient. Source: NCC, Spectrum Trading Guidelines 2022, section 4.
Consider a proposed trade involving an underused band. First determine the legal form of the
transaction and whether the rights are eligible. Then examine the parties, approval requirements,
original obligations and any competition or technical concern. A signed agreement demonstrates
commercial intention. The authorised transaction, updated records and fulfilment of conditions
establish a different stage. Do not let a private agreement obscure the continuing public obligations
attached to spectrum use.

6.13 Satellite systems and non-terrestrial uses
Satellite communications combine radio-frequency use with orbital resources and international
coordination. The frequency, beam, earth station, satellite network filing and orbital position can all
affect interference relationships.
Orbit   Characteristic   Regulatory implication
Geostationary Earth orbit   Satellite appears fixed relative to Earth at
approximately 35,786 kilometres above
the equator.
Valuable orbital positions, long
propagation path and international
coordination.
Medium Earth orbit   Intermediate altitude and movement
relative to ground.
Constellation coordination and tracking
terminals.
Low Earth orbit   Lower altitude, moving satellites and large
constellations.
Many gateways, handovers, debris and
cross-border service issues.

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.chapter: Chapter 5 explained how radio provides access to a communications network. Spectrum

chunks.content:
NCC Promotion Study Guide   55
Filing is not a domestic licence
An international satellite network filing supports recognition and coordination but does not
automatically authorise commercial service, earth stations or spectrum use in Nigeria. Domestic
licensing, landing rights, equipment approval and applicable fees or conditions remain separate
questions.
Other protected uses
Aviation, maritime, meteorological, scientific, defence, public safety and emergency services can
require high protection and international compatibility. Commercial demand must be balanced against
safety and sovereign responsibilities.
Unmanned aircraft and private networks
New use cases can create demand for command links, payload communications and local private
networks. The regulator must determine whether existing allocations and licence categories are
suitable, how interference is controlled and whether devices meet applicable standards.
Satellite regulation requires four separate checks: international filing/coordination, national
spectrum authority, service licensing and equipment/earth-station compliance.
A user link connects a satellite system with the subscriber terminal. A feeder link connects the system
with a gateway and terrestrial networks. A satellite service can therefore depend on terrestrial power,
fibre, data centres and interconnection even where the subscriber's access path is through space.
Direct-to-device service seeks to connect suitable user devices with satellites without a conventional
terrestrial base station providing the local access link. Device compatibility, the service offered and
the permitted frequencies matter. Such a service should not be assumed to provide the capacity,
coverage conditions or functionality of every terrestrial mobile network. Protection of existing uses,
cross-border effects and domestic authorisation remain relevant.
Non-terrestrial networks are a wider category. Satellite systems and high-altitude platforms are
different arrangements within that wider discussion. Orbit type, access method and service model
describe different aspects of a system and should not be treated as synonyms.

chunks.content:
NCC Promotion Study Guide   56
Spectrum alone does not create 5G
Commercial fifth-generation service requires compatible devices, radio equipment, transport capacity,
core functions, power, sites, software, optimisation and demand. An auction or assignment is
therefore an input, not proof of nationwide rollout or user experience.
Spectrum roadmap
A roadmap should signal future availability, technology trends, international developments, incumbent
transitions and likely award sequencing. It reduces uncertainty and supports investment. It is a
planning document, not itself an assignment or guarantee that every proposed date will be achieved.
Coverage obligations
Licence conditions may use rollout, population coverage, geography, service quality or reporting
obligations to connect spectrum rights to public outcomes. Obligations should be measurable and
enforceable, while recognising infrastructure, security and right-of-way constraints.
'5G spectrum' is convenient shorthand, not permanent ownership by one technology.
Always check the band plan and licence conditions.
The historical 2021 Nigerian 3.5-gigahertz auction design offered two 100-megahertz lots using
time-division duplex arrangements. It belongs to the development of fifth-generation deployment, not
proof of every subsequent rollout or coverage claim. As with earlier mobile and broadband
assignment stages, the historical award must be distinguished from later utilisation and service
results.
The published Spectrum Roadmap for the Communications Sector 2026–2030 identifies four focus
areas: Bridging the Digital Divide; Market Driven Investment; Enhancing Quality of Experience; and
Promoting Innovation. Its short-term programme includes the 600-megahertz and
1427–1518-megahertz bands, an audit of assigned spectrum, stronger spectrum-management
capabilities and work on lower 6-gigahertz and 60-gigahertz frameworks. These are planning
commitments, not evidence that each action is complete. Source: NCC, Spectrum Roadmap
2026–2030, chapters 2 and 5.
The operational connection is to choose suitable resources for an identified service need, make
authorisation and investment conditions clear, verify actual use and assess the resulting service. That
reasoning links this chapter with network foundations, competition, infrastructure and consumer
outcomes. The Spectrum Roadmap's own focus areas must not be relabelled as the
Commission-wide Strategic Vision

6.15 Applied regulatory cases
Scenario 1 - Rural coverage gap
Worked response. Assess whether suitable low-band rights are available and used, whether rollout
obligations apply, and whether the actual constraint is spectrum, sites, power, backhaul, economics
or security. Reassigning spectrum will not repair a missing fibre route or inaccessible site.
Scenario 2 - Interference after a new site activates
Worked response. Verify both assignments, site parameters, antenna orientation, emission masks
and commissioning records. Measure the affected area, isolate the source and require technical
correction. Do not assume the newest site is automatically unlawful.

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.chapter: Chapter 5 explained how radio provides access to a communications network. Spectrum

chunks.content:
NCC Promotion Study Guide   57
Scenario 3 - Licensee holds unused spectrum
Worked response. Check licence conditions, utilisation evidence, rollout obligations, market
circumstances and reasons for delay. Consider enforcement, use-it-or-lose-it provisions, trading,
sharing, refarming or other lawful measures proportionate to the evidence.
Scenario 4 - Auction winner seeks transfer
Worked response. Review transfer authority, buyer eligibility, payment and rollout compliance,
spectrum concentration, competition effect and consumer continuity. Auction payment does not
create an unrestricted private asset.
Scenario 5 - Border interference
Worked response. Coordinate measurements, authorised parameters and affected services with the
neighbouring administration through the applicable bilateral, regional and International
Telecommunication Union framework. Domestic enforcement alone may not resolve a cross-border
source.
Scenario 6 - Satellite operator cites an international filing
Worked response. Confirm the filing and coordination status, then separately examine Nigerian
service authorisation, frequency use, earth stations, equipment approval, landing arrangements and
consumer obligations.
Scenario 7 - Public claims auction equals coverage
Worked response. Explain that assignment enables deployment but does not itself produce sites,
transport, power or devices. Report separately on assignment, rollout, coverage, capacity, adoption
and experienced quality.

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.chapter: Chapter 5 explained how radio provides access to a communications network. Spectrum

chunks.content:
6.16 Practice questions and explained answers
Question 1. Why can spectrum be scarce if transmissions do not consume it
permanently?
Answer. Scarcity concerns compatible use in particular locations, bands, times and technical
conditions. Several desired uses may interfere or compete for the same practical rights. Reuse is
possible, but it needs appropriate conditions and coordination.
Question 2. Calculate the approximate wavelength at 900 megahertz.
Answer. Use wavelength equals wave speed divided by frequency. With 300 million metres per
second divided by 900 million cycles per second, the result is about 0.333 metre. This calculation
does not establish range or throughput, which depend on other conditions.
Question 3. Distinguish frequency bandwidth from spectral efficiency.
Answer. Bandwidth is the frequency span, measured in hertz. Spectral efficiency describes
information carried per unit bandwidth under stated conditions. Together they inform potential
capacity, but the actual subscriber rate also depends on sharing, overhead, signal conditions and the
rest of the network.
Question 4. What is the difference between duplexing and multiple access?
Answer. Duplexing separates transmission directions. Multiple access organises sharing between
users. Frequency Division Duplex and Time Division Duplex describe ways of separating uplink and
downlink; they do not mean that only one user can use the network.

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.chapter: Chapter 5 explained how radio provides access to a communications network. Spectrum

chunks.content:
NCC Promotion Study Guide   58
Question 5. Does allocation of a band to mobile service grant a named company operating
rights?
Answer. No. Allocation designates a service use within a frequency table. A particular user still
requires the applicable assignment or authorisation and must comply with its conditions. International
and national planning do not themselves complete an operator licence award.
Question 6. Does section 123 require every frequency assignment to use an auction?
Answer. No. It identifies auction, tender and fixed price among possible procedures under
regulations. The relevant legal framework and award documents determine the appropriate method.
An auction is one mechanism, not the whole spectrum-management function.
Question 7. How do compulsory acquisition and forfeiture differ?
Answer. Section 126 addresses acquisition under the stated reassignment-policy or national-interest
grounds and permits reasonable compensation for acquisition before expiry. Section 127 addresses
specified non-use or failure to renew, permits forfeiture at the Commission’s discretion and excludes
compensation for that forfeiture. The facts determine which provision is relevant.
Question 8. A high fee has been paid. What does that establish about coverage?
Answer. It may establish fulfilment of a financial condition, but it does not establish deployed sites,
operational backhaul, available power or experienced service. Examine rollout and performance
evidence separately from payment and award evidence.
Question 9. An earth station reports interference after a nearby site is commissioned. Is
the new site necessarily unlawful?
Answer. No. Check both parties’ authorisations, technical parameters, receiver behaviour and
commissioning records. Measure and locate the impairment, test possible causes and assess the
applicable protection requirements before selecting a remedy.
Question 10. What should be checked before treating two spectrum rights as freely
interchangeable?
Answer. Compare band, bandwidth, geography, duration, permitted use, power, coordination and
other conditions. Similar bandwidth alone does not establish equal rights or equivalent technical
value. Any proposed change must comply with the governing authorisation and procedure.
Question 11. Does a roadmap implementation date

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.chapter: Chapter 5 explained how radio provides access to a communications network. Spectrum

chunks.content:
power, coordination and
other conditions. Similar bandwidth alone does not establish equal rights or equivalent technical
value. Any proposed change must comply with the governing authorisation and procedure.
Question 11. Does a roadmap implementation date prove completion?
Answer. No. It records the intended timing. Completion requires evidence of the relevant decision,
assignment, operational system or other deliverable. The appropriate evidence depends on the
action, and deployment outcomes may need further verification.
Question 12. How should spectrum feature in the final SVP alignment chapter?
Answer. Identify the applicable official strategic objective and explain how spectrum planning,
authorisation, monitoring or enforcement contributes to it. State whether the relationship is explicit in
the plan or is analytical. Then identify implementation and service-result evidence. Do not substitute
the Spectrum Roadmap’s focus areas for the institution-wide plan.

chunks.content:
Chapter 7
Licensing and authorisation
The preceding chapters explained the institution, networks and spectrum. Licensing connects those
subjects to a particular legal person and activity. The starting question is what the proposed business
will actually do. The answer determines the authorisation required and the obligations that continue
throughout operation. This chapter follows sections 31–52 of the Nigerian Communications Act 2003
and then applies them to practical decisions.

7.1 What a licence authorises
A communications licence is legal authorisation to operate a defined communications system or
facility or to provide a defined communications service, subject to its scope, duration, conditions
and the governing law. It is not merely a certificate issued at the beginning of a business. It creates
a continuing regulatory relationship between NCC and the licensee.
Section 31 gateway rule
No person may operate a communications system or facility or provide a communications service in
Nigeria unless authorised under a communications licence or exempted under regulations made by
NCC. The first exam question is therefore not 'Which licence?' but 'Does the proposed activity
amount to a regulated system, facility or service, and is it already authorised or exempt?'
Object   What it answers
Licence   Who may conduct which activity, where, for how long and under what conditions?
Licence condition   What obligations, limits or benefits attach to that authorisation?
Spectrum assignment   Which frequencies may be used and under what technical conditions?
Numbering assignment   Which numbers or codes may be used?
Type approval   Does the equipment type conform to applicable technical requirements?
A service licence does not automatically supply spectrum, numbers, land access or type
approval. Each regulatory object must be checked separately.
A licence is the authority to conduct an activity within its permitted scope. A condition regulates the
exercise of that authority. A business may hold a valid licence and still breach a condition; another
business may lack the required authorisation altogether. Those are different findings and must not be
described interchangeably.
The legal person matters. A corporate group can contain several companies, but authorisation held
by one does not automatically authorise every other member. Compare the applicant or operator's
identity with the licence, the proposed service, geographic scope and any relevant restrictions. A
trading name alone may not identify the legal entity that bears the obligations.
NCC Promotion Study Guide   60

7.2 The licensing requirement and exemptions: section 31
Section 31(1) establishes the prohibition. Section 31(2) makes breach an offence and provides a
range of consequences on conviction: a fine not less than the initial fee for the relevant licence; a fine
not exceeding ten times that fee; imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year; or both fine and
imprisonment. Upon conviction, the property, facilities, installations and equipment used for the
unlicensed service are also forfeited to NCC.
How to apply section 31
Identify the actual activity, not the name used by the business.
Determine whether it operates a communications system or facility or provides a communications
service.
Check NCC's current licensing classification and exemptions.
Verify the exact licence holder, scope, validity and conditions.
Separate the service from spectrum, numbering and equipment approvals.
Preserve evidence of operation, customers, infrastructure, payments and representations.
Substance over label
A company cannot avoid licensing by calling itself a platform, technology partner, reseller or
consultant if it substantively controls and supplies a regulated communications service. Conversely, a
contractor that merely maintains licensed infrastructure does not automatically become the service
provider. Examine control of the network, customer relationship, billing, service decisions and
regulatory responsibilities.
Exemption
Exemption is not self-declared convenience. It must arise under the applicable regulatory framework.
A person relying on an exemption should fall within its defined activity and conditions. When the
business model changes, the exemption analysis must be repeated.
Begin enforcement by proving the regulated activity and the absence or insufficiency of authority.
Do not begin with punishment and work backwards.

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.topic: 7.2 The licensing requirement and exemptions: section 31
metadata.section: 7.2 The licensing requirement and exemptions: section 31

chunks.content:
7.3 Licence classes and decision principles: sections 32–33
Section 32 authorises NCC to issue class and individual licences on terms it determines, taking
account of the Act's objectives and section 33(3). NCC must publish which communications services
qualify for each class or are exempt. In making a new classification, it must protect previous licence
holders from disadvantage except as permitted by the Act and subsidiary legislation.
Individual licence   Class licence
Granted to a specified person for a specified activity.   Provides standard authority for a class of persons
conducting a specified activity.
Requires an application and individual decision.   Requires registration before operation unless an
exception applies.
May contain special or additional conditions.   Uses standard terms and conditions declared for the
class.

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.topic: 7.3 Licence classes and decision principles: sections 32–33
metadata.section: 7.3 Licence classes and decision principles: sections 32–33

chunks.content:
NCC Promotion Study Guide   61
Individual licence   Class licence
Transfer, renewal, surrender, suspension and revocation
follow the individual-licence provisions.
Registration and de-registration follow sections 50-52.
Section 33 procedures
NCC must publish regulations on licensing processes and eligibility. Procedures may include auction,
selection, public tender invitation or competitive bidding. The list is not closed; the chosen method
should fit scarcity, policy, market structure and administrative need.
Six statutory principles
Transparency, fairness and non-discrimination.
Efficient use and management of radio frequencies.
Available numbers under the National Numbering Plan.
Promotion of fair competition and investment.
Modern, qualitative, affordable and readily available services throughout Nigeria.
Other necessary national-interest considerations determined by NCC.
Section 32 tells you the licence classes; section 33 governs processes and decision
principles. An auction is a possible process, not a third licence class.
The distinction between individual and class licensing concerns the authorisation framework, not
whether a provider is large or small. An individual framework allows a decision and conditions
directed to the particular applicant. A class framework standardises the authority and conditions for
qualifying participants, while requiring the applicable registration. Neither category means that
compliance is optional.
The published classification of activities determines the appropriate route. A company should not
choose a class registration simply because it appears easier if the actual service requires an
individual licence. The assessment follows the activity and applicable classification. Likewise, an
award process such as auction or tender describes a method of selection, not an additional statutory
licence class.

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.topic: 7.3 Licence classes and decision principles: sections 32–33
metadata.section: 7.3 Licence classes and decision principles: sections 32–33

chunks.content:
7.4 Conditions, consultation and continuing control: sections 34–38
Under section 34, NCC may make written declarations that an individual licence, a classification of
individual licences or a class licence is subject to stated terms and conditions or enjoys stated
benefits. The declaration must be consistent with the Act's objects and relevant provisions.
Affected licensees and procedural fairness
Before making a declaration, section 35 requires written notice to affected licensees, a draft, and an
opportunity for written submissions. The permitted submission period must be at least 30 days. NCC
must consider the submissions and section 33(3) principles. Section 36 requires registration of
declarations.
Variation
Section 37 permits NCC to amend, modify, vary or revoke licence conditions or a declaration. The
sections 34-36 procedure applies with necessary adaptations. A licence therefore operates within a
controlled but adaptable framework; regulatory change must still follow the prescribed process.

Condition area   Possible purpose
Service scope   Define authorised activity and customers.
Geographic scope   Limit or require operation in specified areas.
Rollout   Translate public-interest award objectives into measurable deployment.
Quality   Require performance, reporting and consumer safeguards.
Competition   Prevent discrimination, tying or abuse of market position.
Technical   Protect networks, spectrum, numbering and interoperability.
Reporting/audit   Give NCC evidence for continuing supervision.
Section 38
The grant is personal to the licensee. It may not be operated by, assigned, sub-licensed or
transferred to another party without NCC's prior written approval. The licensee must continually
comply with its licence, the Act and subsidiary legislation.
A share sale, merger, outsourcing or management agreement may alter effective control
even if the licence document is not physically handed over. Analyse the substance and
obtain required approval.
The minimum 30-day opportunity under section 35 is for affected licensees to make written
submissions on the proposed declaration. Their views must be considered, but the provision does not
give them a veto. A sound decision record identifies the material issues raised and explains how they
were addressed against the statutory principles.
Section 37 applies the procedure in sections 34–36 with necessary adaptations when conditions or
declarations are amended, modified, varied or revoked. Flexibility therefore has a procedural
boundary. A system administrator changing a condition field, or an officer circulating an informal
message, does not by itself complete the statutory process.
Prior written approval under section 38 has three elements: the approval must precede the relevant
operation, assignment, sub-licensing or transfer; it must be written; and it must come from the
Commission through the competent process. A private agreement, payment or verbal assurance
cannot be treated as an equivalent. Whether a corporate transaction triggers a particular approval
requirement must be assessed under the actual facts and applicable framework.

applies. Application may be withdrawn before grant or refusal.

deems the application withdrawn, without preventing a fresh application.

granted, granted with special/additional conditions, or refused with reasons.

later written approval is received.

Due diligence
A credible assessment considers legal identity, ownership and control, technical plan, financial
capability, business model, management competence, source of funds, proposed infrastructure,
spectrum and numbering needs, competition implications, consumer protection, security, data
governance and consistency with the licence category. The exact checklist remains category- and

Unique application identifier and immutable receipt date.
Role-based access and segregation of assessment, approval and issuance.
Complete-document validation without silently changing statutory timelines.
Recorded requests for additional information and deadline extensions.

Versioned recommendations, approvals and licence conditions.
Payment verification linked to the correct applicant and fee type.
Audit trail for every status change and communication.
Submission is not grant; payment is not grant; favourable assessment is not grant.
Authorisation exists only through the competent decision and issued instrument.

7.6 Digital applications and evidence of authorisation
NCC's published application instructions direct applicants to establish an e-services account and use
the Licensing Management Platform for new applications or renewals. The renewal process begins
from the existing licence record. The instructions state that licence-fee payments are made during the
application process, rather than requiring payment on e-services before beginning. Source: NCC,
Apply for a Licence, consulted 22 September 2026.
The digital workflow carries evidence of an application; it does not replace the governing law. A
submitted status proves submission, and a payment receipt proves the recorded payment. Neither
necessarily establishes that the competent authority has granted the licence. The legal decision and
its terms must be traceable to the issued instrument and relevant record.
For an internal Information Technology function, this means preserving application identifiers, receipt
times, documents, requests, recommendations, approvals and communication records. Access
controls should prevent an unauthorised user from changing an outcome. A corrected record should
retain the reason and authority for correction. Auditability supports the regulatory department's ability
to explain what happened and which obligations apply.
Business rules must also be implemented accurately. For example, a portal must not silently reset a
statutory clock merely because a file was moved between officers. A dashboard may distinguish
elapsed time, time awaiting information and an internal service target, but those measures need clear
definitions. The system should support the legal process rather than invent it.

7.7 Grant, refusal, commencement and the licence register
A grant decision should identify the legal person, authorised activity, licence category,
commencement, duration, geographic and technical scope, applicable fees, special conditions and
linked approvals. Ambiguity at issuance becomes a compliance and dispute risk later.
Refusal
Section 41 requires reasons for refusal of a qualifying non-competitive individual-licence application.
Reasons support fairness, accountability and any available review. A refusal should connect
evidence to published eligibility, legal requirements and regulatory objectives rather than rely on
unexplained discretion.
Decision risk   Control
Wrong legal entity   Verify incorporation, ownership, authorised representatives and beneficial
control.
Scope mismatch   Compare requested activity with the current licensing framework and technical
design.
Premature operation   State that application or payment does not authorise service before grant.
Condition omission   Use approved templates while documenting category-specific departures.

Some licences permit operation from grant; others require payment, performance security, rollout

Licence register
Section 48 requires registers of individual licences and associated special conditions, variations,

protect consumers, investors and enforcement teams from conflicting claims.

7.8 Renewal and pending applications: section 43
A licensee may apply for renewal not later than six months before expiry. The renewal fee determined
by NCC becomes payable on approval. Renewal is not automatic; it is a fresh regulatory decision
informed by performance and the current framework.
If NCC intends not to renew
Give written notice not later than three months from receipt of the renewal application.
Notify and publish the intention at least 30 days before expiry in at least one national daily
newspaper.
Give the affected licensee a reasonable opportunity for written submissions of not less than 14 days.
Consider the submission before the final decision.
Grounds for refusal
NCC may refuse renewal where the licensee failed to comply with licence terms, the Act or subsidiary
legislation, or an instrument issued, made or given by NCC.
Renewal review area   Evidence
Compliance   Outstanding directions, penalties, reporting and enforcement history.
Rollout/service   Obligations, coverage, quality and consumer outcomes.
Financial standing   Fees, levies and capacity to continue service.
Technical integrity   Network, spectrum, numbering and security compliance.
Ownership/control   Approved changes and current beneficial ownership.
Public interest   Competition, continuity, investment and market development.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   66
Pending renewal protection
Section 47(3) allows an expired individual licensee to continue as if the licence had not expired upon
proof that a section 43-compliant renewal application is pending. This is a specific statutory
protection, not permission for a late applicant to operate indefinitely.
Renewal application should be made not later than six months before expiry; do not
reverse this into 'within the final six months' as though last-day filing were compliant.
A renewal decision concerns continued authority beyond the existing term. A licence-condition
amendment concerns the content of authority, while a transfer concerns who may exercise it. Those
processes may arise together, but completion of one should not be assumed to complete the others.
The pending-renewal protection in section 47(3) requires proof to the Commission that a renewal
application made in accordance with section 43 is awaiting determination. The important distinction is
between a qualifying pending application and a mere intention to apply. A late filing cannot
automatically be treated as satisfying the statutory condition, and the existence of unpaid or
unresolved matters should be examined within the applicable process.

7.9 Surrender, suspension, revocation and expiry: sections 44–47
Surrender
A licensee may surrender an individual licence by written notice. It takes effect when NCC receives
the licence and notice, or on a later stated date. Surrender is irrevocable unless scheduled for a later
date and NCC allows withdrawal before that date.
Suspension or revocation grounds
Failure to pay an amount or fine required under the Act or licence.
Failure to comply with the Act, subsidiary legislation or licence conditions.
Contravention of another written law relevant to communications.
Failure to comply with an NCC instrument.
Specified insolvency, receivership, liquidation, winding-up or dissolution circumstances.
Public interest.
Rectifiable breaches
For the grounds in section 45(1)(a)–(d), the Act requires a written breach notice and a demand for
rectification, if the breach is capable of rectification, within 60 days. It also provides for notice of the
intended suspension or revocation and reasons, written submissions with at least 14 days allowed,
and consideration of those submissions. Section 45(6) addresses the 30-day period before
effectiveness following service of the specified declaration notice. Publication follows when the action
has taken effect; delayed publication does not invalidate it. Do not mechanically add every period
together without identifying the notices and sequence required by the provision.
Effects
For suspension, NCC determines duration and penalties, which may include withdrawal of assigned
spectrum allocation, taking gravity and mitigation into account. On revocation, surrender or expiry, the
right to provide the service is lost, subject to written transitional authority for winding up, customer
migration or service continuity and the pending-renewal protection.

7.10 Class registration, cancellation and records: sections 49–52
Section 49 permits NCC to grant a class licence with standard terms and conditions. Section 50
requires a person intending to operate under it to register in the prescribed form and pay the
prescribed registration fee as a condition precedent. Unless an exception applies, operation cannot
begin until NCC registers the person.
Individual regime   Class regime
Licence granted to a specified person.   Standard licence applies to qualifying persons after
registration.
Application assessed for individual grant.   Registration notice and conditions establish participation.
Renewal, surrender, suspension and revocation under
sections 43-47.
De-registration under section 51.
Register maintained under section 48.   Class licences, registrants, condition declarations and
cancellations registered under section 52.
De-registration
Section 51 permits de-registration for the specified payment, compliance, relevant-law and
regulatory-instrument failures, or in the public interest. Subsection (2) clearly states that cancellation
immediately removes the right to provide the service covered by the class licence. Its closing phrase
repeats “de-register” in a way that is internally awkward. Do not treat that phrase as an automatic
right of restoration or silently substitute a different statutory word. Any later lawful authority to resume
service must be established separately.
Why class licensing exists
Where many providers conduct a standardised, lower-scarcity activity, a class framework can reduce
administrative burden while preserving registration, conditions and enforcement. It does not mean the
activity is unregulated or that every communications business belongs in a class.
A class licence is not a licence issued personally to every registrant; the standard class
authority and the person's registration work together.

7.12 Supervision throughout the licence term
Licensing does not end at issuance. Section 38(2) requires continuing compliance with licence terms,
the Act and subsidiary legislation. Compliance is therefore the operational life of the licence.
Compliance domain   Examples
Financial   Fees, levies, contributions, approved tariffs and financial reporting.
Technical   Network standards, spectrum parameters, numbering use, security and
interoperability.
Service   Rollout, availability, quality, consumer support and continuity.
Market conduct   Competition, interconnection, access and non-discrimination.
Information   Periodic returns, incident notifications, ownership changes and accurate records.
Consumer/data   Fair terms, complaint handling, privacy and lawful data governance.
Institutional   Directions, determinations, inspections and audit cooperation.
Evidence-led supervision
Maintain obligation registers linked to licence clauses and instruments.
Define responsible licensee officers, due dates and evidence.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   69
Validate returns rather than treating submission as proof of compliance.
Correlate consumer complaints, technical measurements and financial records.
Issue notices and directions through the statutory procedure.
Escalate repeated or serious breaches proportionately.
Preserve decision, service and publication records for audit and review.
Directions
Sections 53-56 provide a related direction framework: NCC may address compliance or
non-compliance, but must notify the person, provide an opportunity to be heard, consider reasons
and then issue a written direction. Directions may be modified, varied or revoked through a similar
process; non-compliance can attract a fine.
Monitoring is not harassment and self-reporting is not self-regulation. NCC needs lawful,
proportionate and verifiable oversight throughout the licence term.

chunks.content:
7.14 Worked licensing cases
Scenario 1 - Applicant begins service after paying a fee
Worked response. Confirm the regulated activity, any exemption and the issued instrument.
Application and payment alone do not establish grant. Preserve evidence, assess consumer impact
and refer the matter through the competent enforcement process. Any cessation requirement or
penalty must have its own lawful authority and procedure.
Scenario 2 - Licensee outsources its entire network
Worked response. Examine whether the licensee retains strategic and regulatory control or has
effectively allowed another party to operate the licence contrary to section 38. Outsourcing may be
permitted, but accountability and prohibited transfer must not be disguised.
Scenario 3 - Renewal filed late
Worked response. Check the six-month statutory requirement, expiry date and any current procedural
instrument. Do not automatically extend the pending-renewal protection to a non-compliant filing.
Plan consumer continuity and lawful enforcement.
Scenario 4 - Merger announced before NCC approval
Worked response. Separate corporate announcement from regulatory effectiveness. Review control,
eligibility, competition, obligations, spectrum, numbering and continuity before any licensed rights
move.
Scenario 5 - Repeated quality breach
Worked response. Link measurements to licence and quality obligations; notify and hear the licensee;
require rectification; evaluate consumer harm, repetition and mitigation; and escalate through
directions, penalties or section 45 procedure as justified.
Scenario 6 - Class registrant assumes registration is permanent
Worked response. Explain standard class conditions and section 51 de-registration grounds. Verify
fees, instruments and compliance; provide the applicable process and update the section 52 register.
Scenario 7 - Licence expires during consumer migration
Worked response. Section 47 ends ordinary service rights but permits written transitional
authorisation for winding up, migration or continued service arrangements. Protect consumers
without creating an unrecorded indefinite licence.

7.15 Practice questions and explained answers
Question 1. A company has applied and paid a processing fee. May it start the proposed
service?
Answer. Not on those facts alone. Establish the actual activity, any lawful exemption and whether the
necessary authorisation has been granted. Submission and payment are stages in a process; they do
not themselves prove permission to operate.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   71
Question 2. Is competitive bidding a third category alongside individual and class
licences?
Answer. No. Individual and class are the licence categories under section 32. Competitive bidding is
one possible selection process under section 33. The category of authorisation and the method used
to select an applicant answer different questions.
Question 3. Can affected licensees veto a proposed condition declaration?
Answer. Section 35 gives them notice, the draft and at least 30 days for written submissions. NCC
must consider the submissions and statutory principles. This opportunity is not a veto. The final
decision must nevertheless comply with the governing authority and procedure.
Question 4. Can NCC vary a licence condition without repeating the relevant process?
Answer. Section 37 permits variation but applies sections 34–36 with necessary adaptations. The
power to change the condition does not dispense with the associated procedural requirements.
Question 5. Does notification of a proposed transfer satisfy section 38?
Answer. No. The provision requires prior written approval for the specified operation, assignment,
sub-licensing or transfer. Notification informs the regulator; approval authorises the relevant act.
Neither a private contract nor verbal assurance is equivalent to the required approval.
Question 6. An applicant fails to provide requested information within the permitted
period. What follows under section 40?
Answer. The application is deemed withdrawn and is not proceeded with. The right to make a fresh
application is preserved. Confirm the actual deadline and any extension before reaching that
conclusion.
Question 7. No decision arrives within 90 days on a qualifying individual application. Is it
automatically granted?
Answer. No. Section 41 provides deemed refusal, unless the applicant later receives written approval.
Its scope excludes applications subject to competitive bidding. Silence and approval are not
interchangeable.
Question 8. When should an individual licence renewal application be made?
Answer. Section 43 states not later than six months before expiry. This means the deadline precedes
expiry by six months;

approval are not
interchangeable.
Question 8. When should an individual licence renewal application be made?
Answer. Section 43 states not later than six months before expiry. This means the deadline precedes
expiry by six months; it does not authorise waiting until the final day or filing within six months after
the licence ends.
Question 9. Can an expired licensee continue because it has merely announced an
intention to renew?
Answer. No. Section 47(3) concerns proof that a section 43-compliant renewal application is pending
determination. An intention is not an application. Separately, section 47(2) permits specified written
transitional authority; it should not be invented from informal correspondence.
Question 10. Why distinguish surrender from revocation?
Answer. Surrender originates in the licensee’s written action under section 44, whereas revocation is
a Commission action under section 45. Their triggers and procedures differ even though both can
end ordinary service rights. Consumer-transition arrangements still require the relevant authority.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   72
Question 11. Does a class framework remove the need to register?
Answer. Section 50 requires registration and the prescribed registration fee, subject to the Act’s
exceptions. Standard conditions reduce the need for individually negotiated terms; they do not make
the activity unregulated or registration optional.
Question 12. How should an officer respond to a proposed service continuation after
cancellation?
Answer. Identify whether the case concerns an individual licence or class registration, the effective
event and any lawful authority for continued service. Verify the relevant record and consumer
arrangements. Do not invent a general grace period or silently correct ambiguous statutory wording to
create permission.
NCC Promotion Study Guide   73

Chapter 8
Competition, tariffs and economic regulation
Licensing permits market entry. Economic regulation asks whether firms can compete effectively after
entry, whether essential inputs are available on fair terms and whether consumers receive
sustainable value. The sequence is market structure, conduct, evidence, remedy and tariff oversight.

8.1 Why telecommunications needs economic regulation
Communications markets combine strong possibilities for rivalry with structural features that can
weaken it. Building nationwide infrastructure requires heavy capital expenditure. Much of that
expenditure is sunk: once fibre is buried or a site is built, its cost cannot be fully recovered by moving
the asset elsewhere. Spectrum and numbering are scarce public resources. Networks also exhibit
economies of scale and scope, because average cost may fall as more traffic, subscribers or services
share the same platform.
Network effects
A network becomes more useful when more people or services can be reached through it.
Interconnection allows competing networks to share that social value. Without an interconnection
obligation, a large incumbent could turn its subscriber base into a barrier: customers would prefer the
network that can reach everyone, and smaller entrants could be isolated.
Bottlenecks and duplication
Some infrastructure can be economically or physically difficult to duplicate—rights of way, ducts,
landing facilities, towers in constrained locations, local loops, switching interfaces or wholesale
capacity in a particular area. Regulation may require access or infrastructure sharing where denial
would foreclose effective competition, but should not remove the incentive to invest.
Feature   Regulatory implication
High fixed and sunk cost   Entry may be slow; sustainable pricing must still support efficient investment.
Economies of scale/scope   Large networks may be efficient, but scale can also entrench power.
Network effects   Interconnection and interoperability prevent customer-base isolation.
Scarce inputs   Transparent assignment and non-discriminatory access matter.
Vertical integration   A wholesale provider may have an incentive to disadvantage retail rivals.
Information asymmetry   Consumers need clear tariffs, quality data and comparable terms.
Switching barriers   Number portability, unlocking, contract rules and complaint systems can
strengthen choice.
Static and dynamic efficiency
Static efficiency asks whether current resources are used well and current prices reflect efficient cost.
Dynamic efficiency asks whether the framework supports future investment, innovation and better
technology. A tariff that is extremely low today may please

asks whether current resources are used well and current prices reflect efficient cost.
Dynamic efficiency asks whether the framework supports future investment, innovation and better
technology. A tariff that is extremely low today may please consumers briefly but become harmful if it
prevents maintenance, expansion or entry. Good regulation balances affordability, competition and
sustainable investment.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   74
The object is not the maximum number of firms at any cost. It is a contestable, innovative market
in which efficient firms can enter, compete and invest while consumers receive fair value.

8.2 The statutory competition framework
Section 90 of the Nigerian Communications Act 2003 gives NCC exclusive competence to determine,
pronounce upon, administer, monitor and enforce competition laws and regulations as they relate to
the Nigerian communications market. In an examination answer, state the communications-sector
mandate precisely, but do not casually convert a 2003 provision into a claim that every later
cross-sector institutional question is automatically resolved. Where the Federal Competition and
Consumer Protection Act 2018 or another later law is relevant, analyse concurrent or coordinated
responsibilities from the actual instruments and current case law.
Section 91: substantial lessening of competition
A licensee must not engage in conduct whose purpose or effect is substantially to lessen competition
in any aspect of the Nigerian communications market. NCC may clarify the test through guidelines or
regulations. The Act identifies the relevant economic market, global trends, competitor numbers and
shares, entry barriers, range of services, cost and profit structures and any other relevant matter.
Per se-style prohibitions in section 91(3)
Rate fixing: competitors coordinate price instead of deciding independently.
Market sharing: competitors divide customers, territories, services or opportunities.
Boycott of a competitor.
Boycott of a supplier of apparatus or equipment.
Boycott of another licensee.
Section 91(4) also prohibits making supply of one communications product or service conditional on
acquiring—or not acquiring—another product or service from the licensee or another person. This
addresses tying and coercive exclusivity. In a scenario, identify the separate products, the condition
imposed, the supplier's power and the foreclosure or consumer effect.
Purpose or effect
Anti-competitive purpose can be inferred from the agreement, communications, design and
commercial context. Effect asks what the conduct does or is likely to do to rivalry. The word
'substantially' excludes merely trivial effects. The analysis should examine price, output, quality,
innovation, entry, choice and access—not price alone.
Section 93 authorisation
A licensee may apply before engaging in potentially restrictive conduct. NCC may authorise it if
satisfied

trivial effects. The analysis should examine price, output, quality,
innovation, entry, choice and access—not price alone.
Section 93 authorisation
A licensee may apply before engaging in potentially restrictive conduct. NCC may authorise it if
satisfied that authorisation is in the national interest and may require an undertaking. Current
authorisations must be registered. This is not an automatic defence created after the event: the
statutory route is prior application, reasoned assessment and recorded authorisation.
Collaboration can create efficiencies, but good motives do not erase section 91. Ask
whether the restriction is necessary and proportionate to the claimed benefit and whether
prior section 93 authorisation exists.
NCC Promotion Study Guide   75

8.3 Relevant market definition
Market definition is an analytical tool for identifying the competitive constraints on a product or
service. It is not a description of the whole telecommunications sector. The relevant market normally
has a product or service dimension and a geographic dimension; time and customer dimensions may
also matter.
Demand-side substitution
Ask whether customers would switch to another service if the focal service became slightly but
significantly less attractive—for example through a small lasting price increase, lower quality or worse
terms. Voice calls and messaging applications may compete for some uses, yet differ in device, data,
reliability, emergency access and user behaviour. The answer must come from evidence rather than
assumption.
Supply-side substitution
Ask whether other suppliers could rapidly and credibly begin supplying the focal service without major
additional sunk investment or regulatory delay. A fibre operator cannot necessarily become a
nationwide mobile network operator quickly merely because both provide connectivity. Licensing,
spectrum, sites, devices, distribution and network integration may prevent immediate substitution.
Possible dimension   Evidence
Product/service   Function, customer use, price, quality, switching patterns, technology and
contract terms.
Geography   Coverage, local infrastructure, licensing scope, transport cost and regional
price or quality differences.
Customer group   Retail/wholesale, residential/business, prepaid/postpaid,
mass-market/enterprise.
Time   Peak/off-peak constraints, temporary scarcity, migration from legacy to newer
technology.
Two-sided platform   Whether users on one side attract or affect users, advertisers or developers
on another.
Hypothetical-monopolist discipline
A common conceptual test asks whether a hypothetical sole supplier could profitably sustain a small
but significant non-transitory worsening of terms. If enough customers would switch away, the
candidate market is too narrow and substitutes are added. In zero-price or regulated-price services,
quality, privacy, advertising load or innovation may be a more useful parameter than price.
Cellophane fallacy and starting point
If a firm already charges a monopoly price, customers may switch to distant substitutes after a further
increase. That does not prove those substitutes constrain the firm at competitive prices.

Cellophane fallacy and starting point
If a firm already charges a monopoly price, customers may switch to distant substitutes after a further
increase. That does not prove those substitutes constrain the firm at competitive prices. Officers must
also avoid starting with a brand name and declaring it a market. Define the economic arena from
consumer and supplier constraints.
'Mobile communications' may be too broad for one issue and too narrow for another.
Market definition is purpose-specific: termination, towers, enterprise connectivity and retail
mobile data can involve different constraints.
NCC Promotion Study Guide   76

8.4 Dominance and market power - section 92
Section 92 allows NCC to determine that a licensee is dominant in any aspect of the Nigerian
communications market and to publish guidelines or regulations explaining the test. Statutory factors
include the relevant economic market, global technology and commercial trends, market share,
independent rate-setting power, product or service differentiation and promotion, plus other relevant
matters.
Meaning in ordinary language
Market power is the ability to worsen price, quality, output, choice or innovation for a meaningful
period without being defeated by customers switching or rivals expanding. Dominance describes
substantial and durable market power. It is a position, not in itself misconduct; the concern is conduct
that uses or protects that position in a way that substantially lessens competition.
Indicator   Why it matters—and its limit
Market share   A high and stable share can indicate power, but depends on correct market
definition and conditions.
Entry barriers   Spectrum scarcity, sunk cost, site access, scale, brand, distribution and
switching barriers may protect power.
Countervailing buyer power   Large informed customers may negotiate; fragmented consumers usually
cannot.
Control of an input   A bottleneck can confer power even if retail share appears modest.
Excess capacity and expansion   Rivals able to expand quickly can discipline conduct.
Pricing independence   Persistent ability to set terms without losing business is probative.
Technology change   Innovation may erode power—or strengthen an ecosystem and its switching
costs.
Vertical integration   Control across wholesale and retail layers can enable discrimination or margin
squeeze.
Individual and collective dominance
A market may be concentrated around one powerful firm, or conditions may permit several firms to
behave with limited competitive constraint. Do not infer collective power merely from parallel prices:
similar costs, taxes or regulation may create similar outcomes. Look for transparency, retaliation,
stable demand, symmetry and barriers that make coordination sustainable.
Section 92(4)
NCC may direct a dominant licensee to cease conduct that has or may substantially lessen
competition and to

similar outcomes. Look for transparency, retaliation,
stable demand, symmetry and barriers that make coordination sustainable.
Section 92(4)
NCC may direct a dominant licensee to cease conduct that has or may substantially lessen
competition and to implement appropriate remedies. The decision should identify the market,
dominance evidence, impugned conduct, likely harm and connection between remedy and harm.
Significant Market Power is often used in sector regulation, while dominance is the Act's
section 92 term. Do not treat either as a synonym for 'largest operator' without applying the
governing legal test.
NCC Promotion Study Guide   77

8.5 Agreements, coordination and vertical restraints
Horizontal conduct occurs between actual or potential competitors. Vertical conduct occurs between
firms at different levels—such as network operator, tower company, distributor and retailer. Horizontal
price or market coordination normally presents acute risk because it directly replaces rivalry. Vertical
arrangements can improve distribution or investment but may also foreclose competitors.
Conduct   Competition concern   Possible legitimate context
Rate fixing   Eliminates independent price rivalry.   A regulated or expressly authorised
common charge must rest on lawful
authority, not private coordination.
Market sharing   Allocates territories, customers or
services.
Network-sharing geography may create
efficiency but requires careful restriction
and authorisation analysis.
Collective boycott   Cuts a rival or supplier off from the
market.
Objective technical/security standards
must be transparent and proportionate.
Exclusive dealing   Locks customers or inputs away from

May support investment or quality if

Tying/bundling   Uses power in one product to compel
another or exclude rivals.
Integrated packages can lower cost when
customers retain meaningful choice.

rivalry.

Information exchange
Competitors legitimately exchange technical information for interconnection, roaming, fraud control,
cybersecurity and standards. Risk rises when they exchange current or future prices, customer-level
strategy, capacity plans or other competitively sensitive data beyond what the purpose requires.
Controls include a defined purpose, minimum necessary data, aggregation, delay, clean teams,
access restrictions and auditable governance.
Joint infrastructure
Co-location and infrastructure sharing can reduce duplication, speed rollout and improve coverage.
But an agreement can become harmful if it coordinates retail conduct, divides territory, limits
independent capacity or excludes other access seekers. Analyse the layer being shared: passive
assets generally preserve more independent competition than active radio or core functions, though
the actual design controls.
Evidence
Contracts, memoranda, emails, meeting notes and messaging records.

An agreement need not be legally enforceable under section 91(3). Informal understandings and
coordinated arrangements can matter. Focus on the meeting of minds and competitive

8.6 Abuse and exclusionary conduct
The analytical question is whether conduct by a powerful provider competes on the merits or prevents
equally efficient rivalry through control of customers, inputs or rules. Aggressive competition—lower
prices, better quality and innovation—is normally desirable even when rivals dislike it.
Conduct   How harm may arise   Evidence needed
Refusal to supply/access   A bottleneck owner denies an
indispensable or regulated input and
forecloses downstream rivalry.
Input necessity, alternatives, capacity,
terms, reasons and downstream effect.
Discrimination   A vertically integrated firm gives its own
retail arm faster, cheaper or better
wholesale access.
Comparable transactions, service levels,
costs and internal transfer terms.
Margin squeeze   Wholesale and retail prices leave an
efficient downstream rival no viable
margin.
Correct price, cost, product, customer and
time period; avoid crude subtraction.
Predatory pricing   Below-cost sacrifice excludes rivals with a
credible route to recoupment.
Appropriate cost benchmark, duration,
strategy, entry conditions and
recoupment.
Excessive pricing   Durable power permits prices persistently
out of reasonable relation to value or
efficient cost.
Cost, risk, investment, comparators,
quality and persistence.
Tying/exclusivity   Power in one market forecloses choice or
entry in another.
Separate demand, coercion, duration,
coverage, efficiencies and foreclosure.
Cross-subsidy   Protected or dominant revenue finances
exclusionary pricing elsewhere.
Cost allocation, transfer charges,
accounts, funding flow and competitive
effect.
Essential facilities caution
The essential-facility idea should not become a shortcut requiring every useful asset to be shared.
Ask whether the input is genuinely indispensable or economically impracticable to duplicate, whether
refusal is likely to eliminate effective competition, whether access is technically feasible, whether
there is objective justification, and whether a duty would preserve investment incentives.
Non-price degradation
A dominant firm may disadvantage rivals through delayed provisioning, inferior fault repair, poor
interface information, restrictive technical standards or strategic congestion. Equal headline prices do
not establish non-discrimination if service quality, timing or information differs.
Low prices are usually the fruit of competition. Predation requires a disciplined cost and
recoupment analysis; do not

or strategic congestion. Equal headline prices do
not establish non-discrimination if service quality, timing or information differs.
Low prices are usually the fruit of competition. Predation requires a disciplined cost and
recoupment analysis; do not condemn a promotion simply because a competitor cannot
match it.
NCC Promotion Study Guide   79

8.7 Interconnection, access and bottleneck control
Competition regulation and network regulation meet in sections 96-103. Under section 96, a network
service or facilities provider receiving an interconnection request must interconnect at technically
feasible locations, under section 97 principles and terms negotiated in good faith. Interconnection
enables subscribers of different networks to reach one another; access can cover listed network
facilities, network services and other enabling facilities or services.
Statutory safeguards
Written interconnection agreements must comply with the Act and subsidiary instruments.
Principles include neutrality, transparency, non-discrimination, fair competition, universal coverage,
access to information, equality of access and equal terms and conditions.
NCC may intervene when an agreement conflicts with law, consensus fails or delays, or public
interest requires intervention.
Agreements must be registered within 30 days of execution; NCC may require revision.
Interconnection regulation may address negotiation time, quality, rates, intellectual property,
commercial information, facilities and technical information.
Disconnection requires NCC's prior written approval.
Section 101 access must be on reasonable terms; technical standard and quality must be at least the
same as or more favourable than the provider gives itself.
Termination as a bottleneck
A call to a particular subscriber normally must terminate on that subscriber's network. The originating
operator cannot readily substitute another terminating network. This can create monopoly power over
termination even for a network with a small retail share, illustrating why market definition—not
company size alone—controls the analysis.
Wholesale issue   Potential remedy
Access denial   Supply obligation with objective eligibility and capacity rules.
Price discrimination   Cost-oriented or benchmarked charge and equivalence obligations.
Quality discrimination   Service-level agreements, key performance indicators and equal treatment.
Information advantage   Reference offers, publication and simultaneous disclosure.
Delay   Negotiation/provisioning deadlines and escalation procedure.
Accounting opacity   Accounting separation, cost allocation and audit.
Interconnection, access and infrastructure sharing overlap but are not identical.
Interconnection links networks for end-to-end communication; access makes listed
facilities or services available; sharing may concern passive or active infrastructure.

8.8 Investigation and economic evidence
A defensible competition decision is a chain from allegation to evidence, theory of harm, legal test
and remedy. Start with a clear hypothesis but remain open to evidence that disproves it.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   80
Investigation workflow
Stage   Officer's work
Triage   Identify conduct, parties, affected layer, urgency and possible
consumer/market harm.
Preservation   Secure documents and data with lawful scope, chain of custody and
confidentiality controls.
Market inquiry   Map products, customers, geography, substitutes, suppliers, entry and
regulation.
Theory of harm   Explain the mechanism by which conduct could reduce rivalry, quality, output,
choice or innovation.
Counterfactual   Compare likely conditions with and without the conduct; avoid assuming the
status quo is competitive.
Quantitative analysis   Test shares, concentration, switching, price-cost relationships, quality and
entry.
Qualitative analysis   Use contracts, strategy records, customer evidence, technical constraints and
industry history.
Representations   Give affected persons notice and a fair opportunity to answer the case where
required.
Decision   Make findings, address contrary evidence and connect remedy to established
harm.
Concentration measures
Concentration ratios and the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index can describe market structure. The index
sums squared market shares, giving more weight to large firms. Neither establishes illegality. Shares
depend on the market definition; concentration may reflect efficiency; and competitive constraints,
entry and buyer power still matter.
Natural experiments and benchmarking
Price, quality or churn changes across regions, time periods or comparable services can help identify
effects. Comparators must be genuinely comparable. A before-and-after fall in competition may
instead reflect exchange rates, energy cost, tax, spectrum obligations, seasonal traffic or technology
migration.
Confidentiality and procedural integrity
Competition files often contain sensitive pricing, costs, network plans and customer data. Limit
collection to lawful need; segregate restricted material; record access; prepare non-confidential
versions where disclosure is required; and do not let confidential submissions become a channel for
competitors to exchange strategy.
Correlation begins the inquiry; it does not finish it. Explain the causal mechanism, test alternatives
and state evidential limits.
NCC Promotion Study Guide   81

8.9 Remedies and regulatory design
A remedy should restore or protect the competitive process, not punish success or redesign the
market without evidence. Section 92(4) permits NCC to direct a dominant licensee to cease harmful
conduct and implement appropriate remedies. Other powers may arise from licences,
interconnection, access, tariff and enforcement provisions.
Remedy type   Examples   Design risk
Cease-and-desist   Stop discriminatory, tying or exclusionary
conduct.
Too vague to monitor.
Access obligation   Supply wholesale input on reasonable
and non-discriminatory terms.
Price or quality may still foreclose.
Reference offer   Publish standard terms, interfaces and
service levels.
Can become stale or permit gaming.
Price control   Ceiling, cost orientation, benchmark or
model.
May suppress investment if cost/risk is
mismeasured.
Accounting separation   Separate wholesale/retail accounts and
transfer charges.
Allocation rules can be manipulated
without audit.
Functional safeguards   Independent processes, clean teams and
equivalence controls.
High compliance cost and weak cultural
adoption.
Structural remedy   Divestiture or separation in exceptional
cases under lawful authority.
Irreversibility and loss of economies of
scope.
Monitoring   Key indicators, reporting, audit and review
date.
Data burden without decision use.
Proportionality
Suitability: can the remedy address the identified mechanism of harm?
Necessity: is a less restrictive measure equally effective?
Balance: do expected benefits justify cost and investment effects?
Clarity: can the regulated party understand exactly what is required?
Measurability: can NCC test compliance with reliable data?
Reviewability: is there a review or sunset point as market conditions change?
Ex ante and ex post regulation
Ex ante obligations are imposed prospectively where market structure makes harm likely—for
example access, non-discrimination or price controls on a bottleneck. Ex post enforcement responds
to actual or attempted prohibited conduct. The tools complement each other: a mature competitive
market may justify removing prospective controls, while a persistent bottleneck may require them.
Regulatory failure
Intervention can itself create error: prices fixed below sustainable cost, obligations that deter entry,
rules captured by incumbents, or compliance burdens that favour large firms. Impact

while a persistent bottleneck may require them.
Regulatory failure
Intervention can itself create error: prices fixed below sustainable cost, obligations that deter entry,
rules captured by incumbents, or compliance burdens that favour large firms. Impact assessment,
consultation, evidence, transparent reasons and periodic review reduce these risks.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   82
A fine may deter, but it does not necessarily reopen access or repair discrimination. Match
the remedy to the competitive mechanism.

8.10 Tariff regulation - sections 108-111
Section 108 provides the core discipline for holders of individual licences. They may not impose tariffs
or charges for a service until NCC has approved them, except as otherwise provided in the Part. They
must charge approved rates, obtain prior written approval for changes and publish approved rates
and modifications.
Section 108(4) principles
Principle   Meaning
Fair and non-discriminatory   Similarly situated persons should not receive unjustifiably different treatment.
Cost-oriented   Rates should bear a rational relationship to efficiently incurred cost under the
applicable methodology.
Cross-subsidies generally eliminated   Revenue from one service should not conceal or finance distortion elsewhere,
subject to the governing framework.
No unreasonably prejudicial discounts   A discount should not impair other providers' competitive opportunities without
objective basis.
Investment-supportive structure   Rates must allow the sector to attract capital and sustain efficient networks.
International context   Applicable recommendations and regulations of organisations to which
Nigeria belongs may be considered.
Sections 109-111
Section 109 allows NCC, for good cause or public interest, to intervene in determining and setting
tariffs for non-competitive services supplied by the individual licensees covered by section 108.
Section 110 authorises rules or regulations on tariff determination and publication, including
variations, disclosures and tariff models. Section 111 requires appropriate financial penalties where
an individual licensee exceeds a duly approved tariff.
Price floor, ceiling and cap
A ceiling protects consumers from excessive charges; a floor may guard against exclusionary
below-cost pricing in appropriate circumstances; a price-cap regime can allow efficiency gains while
constraining average price movement. These are different instruments. Do not claim the Act
automatically selects one model: identify the applicable current rule or approval.
Tariff package analysis
Headline rate, billing unit and rounding.
Setup, subscription, access, usage, out-of-bundle and termination charges.
Validity, expiry, rollover and auto-renewal.
Eligibility, geography, time and network restrictions.
Taxes, levies and whether the displayed price is inclusive.
Quality or speed assumptions and fair-usage controls.
Discount funding, duration and comparison with

termination charges.
Validity, expiry, rollover and auto-renewal.
Eligibility, geography, time and network restrictions.
Taxes, levies and whether the displayed price is inclusive.
Quality or speed assumptions and fair-usage controls.
Discount funding, duration and comparison with the unpromoted rate.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   83
Affordability does not mean the lowest imaginable price. A lawful tariff framework balances
consumer value, efficient cost, investment, innovation and competition.

8.11 Costs, price models and accounting separation
Cost language becomes useful only when attached to a decision. Historical accounting cost records
past expenditure; current cost estimates the cost of an equivalent modern asset; incremental cost
asks what additional cost is caused by a defined service or output; common cost supports several
services and cannot be attributed to one alone without an allocation rule.
Concept   Plain meaning   Regulatory use
Fixed cost   Does not change immediately with traffic
or subscribers.
Network planning and cost recovery.
Variable cost   Changes with output in the relevant
period.
Promotions and short-run pricing.
Incremental cost   Cost avoided if a defined increment were
not supplied.
Cost orientation and predation analysis.
Long-run incremental cost   All inputs can adjust over the long run for
the defined increment.
Wholesale/termination modelling where
applicable.
Common cost   Shared across multiple services.   Transparent, causal and consistent
allocation.
Fully allocated cost   Direct and shared costs distributed across
services.
Accounting review, subject to allocation
limitations.
Weighted average cost of
capital
Required return reflecting debt/equity
financing and risk.
Investment allowance in a model.
Bottom-up and top-down models
A bottom-up model constructs an efficient hypothetical network from engineering and demand
assumptions. A top-down model begins with an operator's audited accounts and allocates cost.
Bottom-up can reflect efficiency but depend heavily on assumptions; top-down reflects actual
operations but may embed inefficiency. Reconciliation or hybrid approaches can test both.
Accounting separation
A vertically integrated operator can obscure whether its retail arm receives favourable internal terms.
Accounting separation creates regulatory accounts for defined business units, with documented
transfer charges and allocations. It does not necessarily create separate legal companies, but
improves visibility of discrimination, cross-subsidy and margin squeeze.
Margin-squeeze illustration
Suppose the dominant provider's wholesale input costs a retail rival 800 units per customer, while the
provider's own retail price is 900. A 100-unit gap is not automatically a squeeze. The test must
identify all relevant retail costs, discounts, customer life, efficient
