8.12 Applied level 10 scenarios
Scenario 1 - Identical tariff increases
Do not infer rate fixing from parallel movement alone. Examine independent cost shocks, timing,
communications, internal pricing papers and any exchange of future rates. If competitors agreed the
increase, section 91(3)(a) is directly engaged.
Scenario 2 - Tower owner refuses a new entrant
Define the relevant infrastructure/geographic market; test alternatives, site capacity and objective
technical reasons; examine dominance, section 101 access obligations and comparable treatment;
then consider access, timing, price and quality remedies.
Scenario 3 - Dominant operator offers a deep promotion
Consumers benefit from low prices, so test rather than assume predation. Identify the correct price
after all rebates, relevant avoidable or incremental cost, duration, target, intent evidence, entry
barriers and recoupment prospect.
Scenario 4 - Wholesale charge rises while retail price falls
Investigate possible margin squeeze. Use matched products, time periods, volumes and cost
assumptions; review internal transfer charges and whether an efficient rival has a viable downstream
margin.
Scenario 5 - Infrastructure-sharing agreement
Identify passive and active elements, geographic scope, duration and information exchange. Weigh
rollout, cost and environmental efficiencies against territorial division, capacity coordination and
exclusion. Consider whether section 93 prior authorisation is required.
Scenario 6 - Unapproved consumer charge
Verify that the supplier is an individual licensee covered by section 108, the approved tariff schedule
and the actual amount imposed. Preserve billing evidence, stop departure from the approval, ensure
publication and apply the section 111 penalty framework as appropriate.
Scenario 7 - Large operator loses share rapidly
Do not rely on an old designation mechanically. Technology, entry, switching and buyer behaviour
may have changed power. Reassess the market and durable constraints before continuing or
removing ex ante obligations.
Scenario 8 - Exclusive handset arrangement
Define handset, connectivity and distribution markets; assess duration, coverage, switching, rival
access and efficiencies. If service is conditional on acquiring another product, analyse section 91(4)
directly.
MODEL ANSWER FORMULA
Issue

8 - Exclusive handset arrangement
Define handset, connectivity and distribution markets; assess duration, coverage, switching, rival
access and efficiencies. If service is conditional on acquiring another product, analyse section 91(4)
directly.
MODEL ANSWER FORMULA
Issue   →   statutory or regulatory rule   →   market and evidence   →   application to facts   →
counterarguments/efficiencies   →   proportionate remedy   →   monitoring and review. This structure
shows judgment rather than memorised vocabulary.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   85
Provision   Recall
Section 90   NCC's competition competence for the Nigerian communications market.
Section 91   No purpose or effect of substantial lessening; rate fixing, market sharing and
boycotts prohibited; tying rule.
Section 92   Dominance determination, factors and remedial direction.
Section 93   Prior application; national-interest authorisation and undertaking; register.
Section 94   Injunction and certificate for court enforcement except injunction.
Section 95   Foreign-provider agreements: prevent substantial lessening or misuse of
market power.
Sections 96-100   Interconnection duty, principles, registration, regulation and controlled
disconnection.
Sections 101-103   Reasonable access, equal or better standard, access list and extended
safeguards.
Sections 108-111   Tariff approval, principles, intervention, rules/models and penalties.
High-value distinctions
Do not confuse   Correct distinction
Large share and dominance   Share is one indicator; durable freedom from constraint is the concern.
Harm to rival and harm to competition   The law protects rivalry and consumer outcomes, not every competitor.
Low price and predation   Predation requires the proper below-cost and foreclosure/recoupment
analysis.
Collocation and collusion   Collocation places equipment at a shared site; collusion coordinates
competitive conduct.
Interconnection and access   Network-to-network communication versus use of listed inputs/services.
Price approval and price control   Approval is the statutory gate; the control model depends on applicable rules.
Accounting and legal separation   Regulatory accounts versus separate corporate entities.
Current-status control
This unit teaches the Act and durable economic reasoning. Before the examination, reconcile it
against NCC's then-current Competition Practices Regulations or Guidelines, market studies and
dominance determinations, tariff rules and approvals, interconnection/access instruments, merger or
transfer procedures, published decisions, and the operative coordination framework with the Federal
Competition and Consumer Protection Commission. Drafts and consultations must remain labelled as
such; a new document does not repeal an older operative instrument merely by existing.
Competition analysis is a disciplined proof: define the market, establish constraint or agreement,
explain the mechanism of harm, test evidence and efficiencies, apply the correct statutory power, and
design a proportionate remedy.
NCC Promotion Study Guide   86

Chapter 9
Interconnection, access and roaming
A subscriber on one network must be able to reach services and people beyond that network. This
chapter follows the technical connection, the statutory obligation, the commercial agreement, service
performance and dispute resolution.

9.1 Section 96 - obligation to interconnect
A network-services or facilities provider receiving an interconnection request from another licensee
must interconnect its communications system with that licensee's network at technically feasible
locations, consistently with section 97 principles and on terms negotiated in good faith.
Element   What must be established
Requesting party   Is it a licensee entitled to request the relevant interconnection?
Receiving party   Is it a network-service or network-facilities provider within section 96?
Requested service   What traffic, interface, capacity, geography and date are required?
Technical feasibility   Can the location/interface operate safely and reliably, and what alternatives
exist?
Good faith   Did each party exchange necessary information, make reasoned proposals
and avoid strategic delay?
Section 97 principles   Do terms respect neutrality, transparency, non-discrimination, fair competition,
coverage, information access and equality?
Technical feasibility is evidential
A refusal needs more than the phrase 'not feasible'. It should identify equipment, interface, capacity,
power, routing, security or timing constraints; show current utilisation; examine augmentation or
another location; and treat comparable requests consistently.
Good-faith negotiation
Nominate authorised technical and commercial contacts.
Exchange forecasts, network information and draft terms under appropriate confidentiality.
Respond within applicable timelines and explain disagreement.
Separate negotiable commercial preference from genuine technical necessity.
Maintain minutes, issue logs, versions and decisions.
Escalate unresolved issues without weaponising delay.
The duty is to achieve workable connectivity on lawful terms. Neither a requester nor provider can
convert negotiation into indefinite obstruction.
NCC Promotion Study Guide   87

9.2 Sections 97-100 - the statutory sequence
Section   Core rule
97(1)   Every interconnection agreement is written and complies with the Act,
subsidiary instruments and listed regulatory principles.
97(2)   Parties primarily agree terms; NCC may make binding rulings for
inconsistency, failure/delay of consensus or public interest.
98   Either or both parties register the agreement within thirty days of execution
and supply requested information.
98(3)   NCC may require revision where terms/charges conflict with the framework or
public-network integrity.
99   NCC makes interconnection regulations, including model terms, negotiation
procedure, quality, rate methodology, information and facilities.
100   No party may disconnect or discontinue interconnection without NCC's prior
written approval, regardless of contract wording.
Private agreement, public consequence
Interconnection agreements are negotiated commercially, but they affect users, market entry and
public-network integrity. Registration is substantive oversight, not a filing formality.
Thirty-day rule
The registration clock runs from execution. Amendments affecting interconnection terms should be
treated under the applicable registration framework; an unregistered side letter should not silently
alter regulated obligations.
NCC intervention
Intervention can be party-triggered or own-initiative where public interest requires. A binding ruling
should state authority, issues, evidence, reasons, terms, implementation date and monitoring.
Disconnection
Even genuine debt does not authorise unilateral service termination. Prior written approval allows
NCC to assess debt, dispute, competition, emergency traffic and consumer continuity and to impose
controlled arrangements.
'The contract permits disconnection' is incomplete and legally unsafe; section 100 prevails
with a prior-written-approval requirement.

9.3 How an off-net voice call travels
Interconnection becomes understandable when traced as a service journey rather than an acronym
list.
Stage   Function
Originating access   Calling device reaches Network A through radio or fixed access; Network A
authenticates and authorises service.
Number analysis   Network A interprets the destination, checks portability/routing data and
chooses an outbound route.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   88
Stage   Function
Signalling   Control messages request a session, identify routing context and
communicate answer/release state.
Point of Interconnection   Defined physical/logical boundary passes signalling and media traffic between
networks.
Terminating network   Network B locates and alerts the called user, then completes the
bearer/media path.
Usage record   Each network records events for billing, settlement, quality, fraud and dispute
evidence.
Control plane and user plane
The control plane establishes, manages and releases communication; the user plane carries voice or
data content. A call can fail because signalling cannot establish it even where transmission capacity
exists, or connect with poor audio because the media path is impaired.
Origination, transit and termination
Service   Meaning
Origination   Conveying traffic from the calling end toward another network or service.
Transit   Carrying traffic through an intermediate network between origin and
destination.
Termination   Delivering traffic into the destination network to reach its subscriber/service.
Mobile Number Portability
The visible prefix may identify original allocation, not current network. Routing must consult
authoritative portability information or use the agreed method; stale data can create one-way or
network-specific failure.
Diagnose the exact stage. 'Interconnection problem' is a hypothesis until signalling, route, capacity
and destination evidence locate failure.

chunks.content:
9.4 Internet and IP interconnection
Internet interconnection differs from traditional telephone termination even though both exchange
traffic. Internet networks identify address blocks and routing paths, commonly using the Border
Gateway Protocol, and exchange traffic through private links, transit providers or Internet exchange
points.
Arrangement   Commercial/technical meaning
IP transit   One network pays another for reachability to the wider Internet; price may
depend on committed capacity and traffic.
Settlement-free peering   Networks exchange eligible customer traffic without per-unit payment under
agreed policy; it is not necessarily costless.
Paid peering   Direct exchange under a commercial payment arrangement.
Internet exchange point   Shared exchange fabric where multiple networks can peer; each relationship
still follows policy and capacity.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   89
Arrangement   Commercial/technical meaning
Private interconnection   Dedicated link between two networks or a network and large content/cloud
provider.
Content delivery/cache   Content is stored nearer users, reducing upstream traffic and latency;
placement and access terms matter.
Autonomous systems and routing
An autonomous system is a network under a common routing policy. Border Gateway Protocol
announcements indicate reachability, not guaranteed performance. Route leaks, hijacks, filtering or
misconfiguration can make services unreachable despite working physical links.
Peering versus interconnection regulation
Do not assume every Internet peering relationship is governed identically to voice termination.
Identify the licensed service, parties, facility, market power, agreement and applicable instrument.
The Act's access and competition provisions can remain relevant.
Local traffic
Domestic peering and local hosting can reduce international transit and latency, but concentration at
one exchange or facility can create failure risk. Resilience requires diverse routes, capacity and
operations.
Internet exchange membership does not guarantee that two members peer with each other
or exchange all traffic.

9.5 Points of interconnection and capacity
Design issue   Questions
Location   Where is the physical/logical demarcation and who supplies transmission to
it?
Interface   Which protocol, port speed, media, addressing, signalling and security profile
apply?
Capacity   What busy-hour traffic, growth margin, link utilisation and augmentation trigger
apply?
Resilience   Are routes, equipment, power and signalling genuinely diverse across failure
domains?
Testing   What conformance, load, failover, numbering and service tests precede
acceptance?
Operations   Who monitors, opens tickets, escalates, restores and communicates planned
work?
Measurement   Which counters, clocks, probes and record formats determine performance
and settlement?
Forecasting
Parties should exchange credible busy-hour forecasts and compare forecast accuracy.
Under-forecasting can cause congestion; strategic over-forecasting can force wasteful investment.
Capacity triggers should be measurable and allow lead time for augmentation.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   90
One-way failure
Calls or messages may work from A to B but not B to A because routes, numbering translations,
signalling rules or capacity are directional. Test both directions and multiple number ranges,
technologies and service types.
Congestion evidence
Use offered traffic, carried traffic, utilisation, blocking, answer/seizure ratios, signalling rejects, route
overflow and time patterns. A low daily average can conceal a saturated busy hour.
Demarcation
The agreement should define where responsibility changes. Demarcation aids diagnosis but does not
excuse cooperation: one party's fault can trigger alarms or consumer impact in the other network.
Capacity is not a single number. It combines engineered limit, current utilisation, service mix,
growth, resilience and provisioning lead time.

9.6 Interconnection agreement anatomy
Schedule/part   Essential content
Definitions and scope   Services, parties, licence basis, geography, technology and exclusions.
Technical   Points, routes, interfaces, signalling, numbering, synchronisation, testing and
changes.
Capacity   Forecasts, orders, augmentation, reservations and consequences of delay.
Quality   Indicators, measurement, reporting, fault priority, maintenance and service
credits.
Commercial   Rates, units, taxes, billing periods, currency, security and late payment.
Records/settlement   Usage-record format, exchange, reconciliation, disputes, audit and fraud
treatment.
Operations   Contact matrix, ticketing, escalation, planned work and emergency
restoration.
Governance   Confidentiality, data protection, intellectual property, compliance and audit.
Lifecycle   Commencement, review, amendment, suspension, termination, migration and
continuity.
Disputes   Negotiation, escalation, NCC intervention, applicable law and interim
arrangements.
Agreement hierarchy
State how the main agreement, schedules, order forms, Reference Interconnection Offer and later
amendments relate. Inconsistency rules prevent a technical annex from silently overriding a
regulatory safeguard.
Change control
Network upgrades, new number ranges, Internet Protocol migration and security changes need
notice, impact analysis, joint testing, approval and rollback. Emergency change should be recorded
and reviewed afterward.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   91
Service-level design
A service level needs definition, threshold, measurement point, exclusions, reporting, remedy and
dispute method. 'Best efforts' without these elements gives weak accountability.
An agreement can be signed yet still require NCC revision under section 98(3). Execution
does not make inconsistent terms lawful.

9.7 Reference interconnection offer
A Reference Interconnection Offer is a published or approved standard offer describing
interconnection services and baseline terms, particularly useful where a provider has significant
bargaining power or must offer equivalent access.
Purpose   Regulatory benefit
Transparency   Potential interconnectors can see products, processes, interfaces and
baseline prices.
Non-discrimination   Comparable seekers start from comparable terms; hidden affiliate advantages
become easier to detect.
Faster negotiation   Standard clauses reduce repeated bargaining while leaving justified
service-specific detail.
Regulatory monitoring   NCC can compare actual agreements and performance with the approved
offer.
Market entry   New/smaller providers can plan cost, timing and technical integration.
Typical contents
Eligible services and points/levels of interconnection.
Technical interfaces, signalling, numbering and testing.
Ordering, provisioning and capacity-expansion process.
Quality indicators, fault management and maintenance.
Charges, billing units, records, reconciliation and financial security.
Confidentiality, information exchange and data protection.
Dispute, suspension, termination and migration safeguards.
Offer versus agreement
The Reference Interconnection Offer is a baseline offer, not the final bilateral agreement itself. Parties
may negotiate objectively justified differences subject to law, approval and non-discrimination. Actual
performance must match the terms.
Affiliate equivalence
Where a wholesale provider also operates downstream, compare information, ordering, provisioning
time, quality, price and repair given to its affiliate and rivals. Formal publication alone does not prove
equivalence.
The regulatory value of a Reference Interconnection Offer lies in comparability and enforceable
implementation, not the volume of its clauses.
NCC Promotion Study Guide   92

9.8 Charges, costs and economic logic
Interconnection charges affect retail competition because one provider pays another for wholesale
traffic handling. Charges too high can foreclose entry; charges too low can weaken efficient
investment and maintenance.
Cost concept   Meaning
Incremental cost   Additional cost caused by supplying the relevant service over a defined
horizon.
Long-run incremental cost   Efficient forward-looking cost when inputs can vary over the long run.
Common cost   Shared cost not uniquely caused by one service; allocation method matters.
Fully allocated cost   Direct and shared costs allocated across services under stated rules.
Efficient operator benchmark   Models prudent technology and scale rather than reimbursing every historical
inefficiency.
Cost of capital   Reasonable return required for financed assets and risk.
Termination monopoly
For a call to a specific subscriber, only the serving network can terminate it. This can confer
bottleneck power even where retail market share is modest, supporting regulatory rate control or
symmetry analysis.
Symmetric versus asymmetric rates
Symmetry applies the same regulated rate; asymmetry may temporarily recognise objectively
different efficient costs or market conditions. It should be justified, targeted and reviewed rather than
becoming permanent protection from efficiency.
Wholesale and retail
A wholesale termination rate is not the consumer's retail call price. Retail price also reflects
origination, marketing, distribution, taxes, customer care, network and commercial strategy.
Currency and tax
Agreements should define currency, exchange-rate source, tax treatment and invoice evidence.
Ambiguity can create debt even where traffic totals are agreed.
Cost orientation does not mean reimbursement of whatever cost an operator reports. It
asks what efficient relevant cost should inform the regulated service.

9.9 Traffic records, billing and settlement
Each party generates call or session records. Settlement reconciles those independently produced
records, applies agreed rates and resolves differences.
Record element   Control
Calling/called identifier   Formatting, masking and portability treatment.
Start/answer/end time   Clock synchronisation, time zone and rounding.
Duration/volume   Billable definition, unit and minimum/step.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   93
Record element   Control
Route/Point of Interconnection   Correct service and price classification.
Release/cause code   Failure diagnosis and exclusion treatment.
Service/technology   Voice, messaging, data, transit, emergency or other class.
Record version   Immutable original, correction trail and source system.
Reconciliation process
Exchange summaries and detailed records through secure agreed channel.
Compare totals by route, service, day and exception category.
Set tolerance only for practical minor variance, not unexplained material loss.
Investigate missing, duplicate, rejected, late and differently rounded records.
Apply approved rate/version and agreed tax.
Issue adjustment, credit note or dispute with evidence.
Preserve records and sign settlement without destroying unresolved claims.
Clock problem
Unsynchronised clocks can create mismatched duration, date and sequence. Time sources, drift
monitoring and daylight/time-zone convention should be specified.
Fraud and bypass
SIM boxes, call refiling, masking and false routing can disguise origin, avoid charges or breach lawful
requirements. Detection should combine traffic patterns, signalling, device/network evidence and
coordinated investigation; unusual traffic is a lead, not automatic proof.
Financial dispute and continuity
Separate undisputed sums, disputed invoices and current traffic. Escrow, security or payment plans
can protect creditors while NCC assesses disconnection and consumer harm.
Interconnection billing is a data-governance function as much as a finance function: definitions,
clocks, lineage and version control determine the money.
NCC Promotion Study Guide   94

9.10 Quality, faults and end-to-end accountability
Indicator   Interpretation
Call setup success   Whether signalling establishes attempts; affected by routes, signalling and
destination response.
Answer-seizure ratio   Answered calls relative to seizures; user behaviour and unavailable
destinations can affect it.
Post-dial delay   Time from completed dialling to progress indication; routing/signalling delay
contributes.
Drop/release pattern   Unexpected termination after connection; locate access, core, interconnect or
destination cause.
Speech quality   Codec, packet loss, jitter, delay and transcoding can degrade audio.
Availability   Whether link/service is usable over the defined period, with controlled
exclusions.
Repair time   Time from valid detection/report to stable restoration; define pause and
priority.
End-to-end versus domain accountability
Consumers experience one communication, but each operator controls only its domain and shared
boundary. Agreements should support joint testing and evidence so responsibility can be attributed
without leaving the consumer between parties.
Fault workflow
Detect and correlate alarms, complaints and performance.
Open a unique cross-network ticket with severity and affected services.
Run directional tests and share relevant traces.
Apply workaround or reroute where safe.
Restore, test across representative routes and monitor stability.
Issue root-cause report and preventive action.
Link chronic failure to capacity, agreement or enforcement action.
Maintenance
Planned work should use notice, agreed window, risk assessment, fallback and post-test. Emergency
work may shorten notice but still requires coordination and record.
A poor answer-seizure ratio does not automatically prove network failure;
unanswered/busy users and invalid destinations can lower it. Analyse cause codes and
context.

9.11 Access under sections 101-103
Interconnection links networks to exchange traffic. Access concerns use of listed wholesale network
facilities or services needed to provide downstream network or applications services.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   95
Section 101
Subject to published exemptions, a network-facilities or network-service provider must give
reasonable-term access to items in the access list when another eligible provider makes a written
request. The technical standard and quality must be at least the same as, or more favourable than,
that supplied on the first provider's own network.
Access principle   Meaning
Written request   Define asset/service, quantity, location, interface, date and requester
authority.
Reasonable terms   Price, time, security, capacity and operations must be objectively supportable.
Quality equivalence   No inferior wholesale input to weaken downstream competitor.
Access list   NCC determines listed facilities/services and maintains the statutory register.
Sections 97-100 applied   Agreement, registration, regulation and discontinuance controls extend with
necessary adaptations under section 103.
Access list
Section 102 permits network facilities, network services and other facilities/services facilitating
network or applications services. Listing and the current register matter; not every commercially
useful asset is automatically a regulated listed service.
Access versus section 137
Sections 101-103 govern listed wholesale access. Section 137 separately addresses
licensee-to-licensee non-discriminatory access to posts, network facilities and rights of way, with
capacity/safety exceptions and a jurisdictional qualification. Cite the correct route.
Access regulation prevents a wholesale bottleneck from defeating downstream competition while
preserving objective technical and capacity limits.

9.12 Non-discrimination, dominance and margin squeeze
Risk   Evidence
Refusal   Capacity/feasibility records, alternatives, affiliate access and decision
chronology.
Strategic delay   Process milestones, comparable orders, resource assignment and internal
communications.
Quality discrimination   Provisioning, availability, repair and capacity by customer/affiliate.
Price discrimination   Comparable service, cost differences, rebates and total effective price.
Information advantage   Forecasts, launch plans and technical information given to affiliate or rival.
Margin squeeze   Wholesale input price versus provider's downstream retail price and efficient
downstream cost.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   96
Dominance
Section 92 permits NCC to determine dominance using relevant market, trends, share, independent
rate-setting power, differentiation and other relevant factors. Dominance is not itself unlawful; abusive
conduct or substantial lessening of competition attracts remedy.
Relevant market
Define product/service and geography from demand and supply substitution. A provider may lack
dominance in retail mobile service yet control termination to its own subscribers or a unique facility at
one location.
Objective justification
Differences can be justified by cost, volume, risk, location, service level or technology. The reason
must be relevant, proportionate, evidence-based and consistently applied.
Remedies
Possible lawful remedies include access obligation, Reference Interconnection Offer, transparency,
equivalence, cost-oriented rate, accounting separation, capacity augmentation, non-retaliation and
monitored delivery. Match remedy to diagnosed harm.
Equal treatment does not mean identical terms despite materially different circumstances;
it means equivalent treatment of comparable cases and objective reasons for difference.

9.13 Disconnection and continuity safeguards
Disconnection can isolate millions of consumers and disrupt emergency, financial and public
services. Section 100 therefore makes prior written NCC approval mandatory in every circumstance.
NCC consideration   Question
Legal basis   What breach, contract term and statutory authority support the request?
Debt/evidence   What is admitted, disputed, reconciled, secured or paid?
Materiality   How serious, persistent and remediable is the default?
Consumer/public harm   Which users, services, locations and emergency functions would be affected?
Competition   Would disconnection foreclose a rival or reward strategic conduct?
Alternatives   Payment plan, escrow, capacity limit, traffic segregation or supervised
transition?
Implementation   Notice, timing, scope, monitoring, communication and restoration trigger?
Approval is not automatic
NCC can refuse, condition or phase the requested action based on law and evidence. Approval
should identify exactly what may be disconnected and when; a party should not expand it beyond the
written decision.
Emergency degradation
Immediate technical action may be needed to protect network safety or integrity, but parties should
use the emergency provisions of the operative framework, minimise effect, notify/escalate promptly
and preserve evidence. Emergency engineering must not disguise a commercial disconnection.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   97
Consumer communication
Where service impact is unavoidable, communication should be accurate, timely and coordinated
without misleading blame or disclosing confidential dispute information. Alternative routes and
restoration updates should be provided where possible.
Restoration
Define the cure, confirmation and technical steps for reconnection. Settlement of debt is not useful if
configuration or testing delay keeps users offline.
Section 100 converts continuity from a private bargaining weapon into a regulated public-interest
decision.

9.14 Dispute resolution and evidence
Dispute   Minimum evidence
Feasibility/capacity   Design, utilisation, forecasts, structural/port limits, alternatives and cost/time.
Charge   Rate instrument, cost model, service definition, traffic and comparators.
Quality   Agreed indicator, raw counters, measurement points, cause codes and
outages.
Invoice   Records, clocks, tariff version, reconciliation, adjustments and payments.
Discrimination   Comparable affiliate/rival transactions and objective differences.
Delay   Dated requests, dependencies, responses, approvals, work orders and tests.
Disconnection   Default, notices, consumer impact, alternatives and continuity plan.
NCC analytical method
Define issues, parties, licences and relief precisely.
Identify Act, operative regulation, registered agreement and binding decisions.
Separate agreed facts, allegations and missing evidence.
Preserve traffic, configuration and commercial records.
Give each party material evidence and fair opportunity to respond.
Test technical, economic, competition and consumer consequences.
Make reasoned binding terms with measurable implementation.
Monitor and verify; enforce non-compliance separately.
Interim relief
Where final resolution will take time, a lawful interim measure can preserve connectivity, capacity,
payments or evidence. It should be necessary, proportionate, time-limited and without improperly
predetermining the merits.
Expert evidence
Network or cost experts should state qualifications, data, method, assumptions, uncertainty and
alternatives. A model output is not self-proving; parties must be able to challenge material inputs
subject to confidentiality protection.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   98
Commercial confidentiality does not permit a party to withhold evidence lawfully required
by NCC; it requires controlled handling and disclosure.

9.15 National roaming
What roaming means
Roaming allows a subscriber of a home network to receive service through a visited network under
technical and commercial arrangements. The subscriber retains the home relationship and identity
while the visited network supplies radio access and supporting functions.
National versus international roaming
National roaming   International roaming
Home and visited networks operate
within Nigeria.
Subscriber uses a network in another country.
Can support coverage, entry,
resilience and domestic infrastructure
efficiency.
Supports continuity while travelling and depends on cross-border commercial
arrangements.
Governed by Nigerian licensing,
competition, spectrum, consumer and
roaming rules.
Also involves foreign regulation, currency, international signalling and
settlement.
The 2021 framework
NCC's Guidelines on National Roaming in Nigeria 2021 provide the operative guideline anchor in the
controlled source set. Commercial agreements remain subject to NCC oversight and relevant licence
conditions. The guidelines should be studied as their own instrument rather than inferred from
international roaming practice.
Technical operation
The visited network detects and serves the roaming device where an agreement and coverage exist.
The home and visited networks exchange authentication and subscriber/service information.
Routing determines how voice, messaging and data traffic reach the home network or service
destination.
Usage records support wholesale settlement and the subscriber's retail bill.
Service restrictions, emergency access, quality and lawful requirements must be controlled.
Why national roaming is not infrastructure sharing
Roaming supplies service to another operator's subscribers. Infrastructure sharing supplies use of
network assets or functions. A roaming agreement can exist without tower sharing, and tower sharing
can exist without subscriber roaming.
National roaming does not transfer the subscriber permanently to the visited network and
is not the same as Mobile Number Portability.

9.16 Roaming benefits and risks
Potential benefits
Faster geographic reach for a new or smaller operator.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   99
Coverage continuity where the home network has gaps.
Reduced duplication in low-demand locations.
Resilience where reciprocal or emergency arrangements are available.
More efficient use of already-deployed radio infrastructure.
Competition risks
A host network may set excessive wholesale prices, provide inferior quality, delay integration, restrict
technologies or use roaming to learn a rival's demand. Conversely, a guest operator may rely
indefinitely on roaming and under-invest in its own licensed obligations. NCC must balance entry and
efficiency against durable infrastructure competition.
Consumer issues
Issue   Control question
Price   Is the consumer told clearly when domestic roaming changes charges or
allowances?
Quality   Can users distinguish visited-network limitations and obtain complaint
resolution?
Coverage claims   Does the home operator accurately describe where service depends on
roaming?
Emergency service   Does roaming preserve reliable access and location handling?
Privacy/security   Are subscriber and signalling data protected between networks?
Billing   Are records reconciled and disputed charges corrected promptly?
Roaming and rollout obligations
A licence may require the operator to deploy its own network. Roaming can complement but not
automatically replace that obligation. NCC should read the licence, roaming approval and rollout
milestones together.
National roaming can simultaneously promote entry and reduce investment incentives. The
regulatory answer should specify limits, quality, pricing, transparency and rollout safeguards.

9.17 Status control and applied scenarios
Operative and draft position
NCC's current regulations register lists the Telecommunications Networks Interconnection
Regulations 2007 as published, while the Communications Network Interconnection Regulations
developed through the 2024 public inquiry remain draft/proposed unless a final instrument is officially
made and published. A public-inquiry report proves consultation and regulatory development, not
commencement.
Scenario 1 - Busy-hour off-net failures
Compare on-net/off-net patterns, directional routes, Point-of-Interconnection utilisation, signalling
rejects, forecasts and augmentation orders. Direct capacity or routing correction at the responsible
boundary and verify peak-hour recovery.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   100
Scenario 2 - Refusal based on 'security'
Require specific risk, architecture and mitigation evidence; compare affiliate treatment; examine a
restricted interface or alternative location. Security is legitimate but cannot remain an untestable
phrase.
Scenario 3 - Signed agreement has discriminatory rate
Registration does not cure inconsistency. Compare service/cost and similar agreements; apply
sections 97-99, competition rules and operative rate decisions; require revision and address past
impact lawfully.
Scenario 4 - Debt and threatened midnight cut
Stop unilateral action; section 100 requires prior written NCC approval. Reconcile debt, separate
disputed amount, consider escrow/payment security, assess consumer harm and issue a controlled
continuity decision.
Scenario 5 - IP route leak
Preserve Border Gateway Protocol announcements and timing, identify source/propagation,
filter/withdraw, restore valid routes, notify affected parties and review routing-security controls. Do not
analyse it as voice termination merely because two licensees are connected.
Scenario 6 - Affiliate receives faster provisioning
Compare end-to-end order timestamps, information, staffing, internal interfaces and quality. Require
equivalence and remediate affected rivals if objective justification is absent.
Scenario 7 - Draft rule cited as law
Classify it as draft/proposed; apply the NCA, 2007 Regulations and current binding instruments. The
draft may explain policy direction but cannot independently impose an operative obligation.
MODEL ANSWER FORMULA
Define service and boundary   →   identify sections 96-103 and operative instrument   →   map technical
path   →   examine agreement, rate and quality evidence   →   assess competition/consumer harm   →
preserve continuity   →   issue measurable remedy and verify.
Provision   Recall
Section 96   Requested interconnection at technically feasible locations; section 97
principles; good-faith negotiation.
Section 97   Written agreement; statutory principles; NCC binding intervention for
inconsistency, failure/delay or public interest.
Section 98   Register within thirty days; information; NCC may require revision.
Section 99   Regulations/model terms cover procedure, quality, rates, information,
intellectual property and facilities.
Section 100   No disconnection/discontinuance without prior written NCC approval.
Section 101   Reasonable access to listed facilities/services; at least own-network technical

require revision.
Section 99   Regulations/model terms cover procedure, quality, rates, information,
intellectual property and facilities.
Section 100   No disconnection/discontinuance without prior written NCC approval.
Section 101   Reasonable access to listed facilities/services; at least own-network technical
quality.
Section 102   NCC access list and register.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   101
Provision   Recall
Section 103   Sections 97-100 extend to access with necessary adaptations.
High-value distinctions
Do not confuse   Correct distinction
Interconnection/access   Traffic exchange between networks / use of listed wholesale input.
Point/route   Defined exchange boundary / path traffic follows.
RIO/agreement   Standard baseline offer / binding bilateral terms.
Termination/retail price   Wholesale delivery to destination network / consumer charge.
Peering/transit   Direct eligible traffic exchange / paid wider Internet reachability.
Dispute/disconnection   Controversy requiring resolution / continuity-ending act requiring approval.
NCC Promotion Study Guide   102

Chapter 10
Collocation and infrastructure sharing
Networks can share sites and infrastructure without becoming one operator. Begin with the physical
arrangement, then distinguish assets, responsibilities, agreements, competition and service
resilience.

10.1 Meaning and related concepts
Collocation is an arrangement under which one communications provider places equipment at a
site, building, shelter, tower compound or other facility owned, controlled or managed by another
provider. The parties share a location and supporting facilities while remaining legally,
commercially and technically distinct.
Terminology control
Collocation, co-location and colocation are spelling variants in telecommunications. They do not
describe three different arrangements. Use 'collocation' in ordinary explanations, but reproduce the
published title of an NCC instrument or licence exactly. NCC materials themselves use more than
one spelling.
Concept   Regulatory object   Memory cue
Collocation   Shared premises, site space and
supporting facilities.
Same location.
Infrastructure sharing   Shared physical assets or network
functions.
Same asset or function.
Interconnection   Networks link to exchange
communications traffic.
Exchange traffic.
Roaming   A subscriber receives service through
another network.
Use visited network.
Why NCC cares
Collocation can accelerate deployment, reduce duplicated construction, lower cost, limit
environmental impact and improve coverage. It can also create discrimination, excessive pricing,
safety risks, confidential-information abuse and common points of failure. Regulation must enable
efficient sharing while preserving competition, resilience and accountability.
NCC Promotion Study Guide   103

10.2 Facilities at a shared site
Element   Function   Sharing issue
Land and compound   Provides the controlled physical location.   Lease rights, boundaries, access and
environmental approvals.
Tower or mast   Supports antennas at required height and
orientation.
Structural loading, wind limits and
antenna allocation.
Shelter or cabinet   Houses radio, transmission and control
equipment.
Floor space, heat, security and
separation.
Power system   Grid input, rectifiers, batteries, generator
or renewable supply.
Capacity, fuel, metering, priority and
availability.
Cooling   Maintains equipment within operating
temperature.
Load allocation, maintenance and failure
responsibility.
Transmission entry   Connects fibre or microwave backhaul.   Duct, tray, port, route and
cross-connection capacity.
Earthing and lightning
protection
Controls electrical and lightning risk.   Common standards, testing and liability.
Security and access control   Protects people, equipment and records
site entry.
Authorisation, escort, emergency access
and audit logs.
The tower is not the whole service
A tenant may have antenna space but insufficient power or transmission. A physically sound tower
can therefore host equipment that cannot deliver reliable service. Collocation analysis must examine
the complete site resource: structural, spatial, electrical, thermal, transmission, security and
operational capacity.
Renting land beside a tower is not necessarily equivalent to receiving a complete
collocation service. Identify exactly which facilities and obligations are shared.

10.3 Passive and active infrastructure sharing
Model   Examples   Main concerns
Passive sharing   Land, towers, poles, shelters, ducts,
trenches, dark fibre, power and cooling.
Capacity, safety, price, access,
maintenance and resilience.
Active sharing   Antennas, radio equipment, transmission
capacity, Radio Access Network functions
or other electronic network elements
where permitted.
Spectrum rights, control, quality, security,
competition and lawful obligations.
Wholesale capacity   Use of defined transmission or network
capacity without joint occupation of all
facilities.
Service levels, traffic separation, pricing
and dependency.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   104
Why the boundary matters
Passive sharing normally leaves each operator in clearer control of its electronics and spectrum use.
Active sharing can create greater efficiency, especially in difficult locations, but requires stronger
rules for operational control, performance evidence, security and competitive independence. The
label chosen by a contract does not decide the regulatory classification; NCC should examine what
assets and functions are actually shared.
Examples
Ask who owns the asset, who controls it, who operates it, whose licence authorises the service
and who remains accountable to the consumer.
Active sharing also needs safeguards against excessive coordination between competitors.
Operators may share defined technical assets without becoming one commercial undertaking. Retail
pricing, customer information and competitive decisions should not be pooled merely because part of
the infrastructure is shared. The regulatory assessment therefore considers both the efficiency gained
and the independence that must remain.

10.4 Participants and accountability
Actor   Role boundary
NCC   Defines and enforces the regulatory framework, monitors competition and
quality, and resolves matters within its authority.
Collocation/infrastructure-sharing
licensee
Provides authorised shared facilities or services under its licence and
applicable rules.
Tower company   May own or manage towers and related facilities; regulatory status depends
on the licensed activity actually performed.
Tenant operator   Installs or operates communications equipment and remains responsible for
its own licence and consumer-facing obligations.
Landlord   Provides property rights but does not automatically become a
communications licensee.
Power or maintenance contractor   Performs contracted functions without automatically acquiring regulatory
authority or the licensee's accountability.
Fibre provider   Provides route or capacity under its applicable authorisation and contract.
Outsourcing does not erase responsibility
A mobile operator may outsource tower, generator or field-maintenance work, but consumers still
experience the licensed service. Unless the legal framework provides otherwise, contractual
allocation does not prevent NCC from holding the relevant licensee accountable for regulatory
performance. The licensee can pursue contractual remedies separately.
Licence is not ownership
A party may own a tower but require the appropriate authorisation to provide regulated collocation
services. Conversely, a licensee may operate facilities it does not own. Examination answers should
distinguish title to an asset, contractual control, operational responsibility and regulatory
authorisation.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   105
A maintenance contractor is not automatically a collocation licensee, and a tower owner is
not automatically authorised to provide every active network-sharing function.

10.5 From application to operation
Stage   Evidence and decision
Request   Requester identifies site, equipment, dimensions, weight, power,
transmission, timing and service need.
Acknowledgement   Provider records the request and applicable process rather than allowing it to
disappear informally.
Site survey   Parties inspect physical space, tower loading, power, cooling, access,
transmission and safety conditions.
Feasibility   Provider documents available capacity, existing commitments, reinforcement
options and genuine constraints.
Quotation   Charges, assumptions, validity period and excluded work are stated
transparently.
Agreement   Scope, responsibilities, service levels, security, confidentiality, escalation and
exit are settled.
Design approval   Structural, electrical, radio, safety and installation designs are reviewed by
authorised persons.
Installation   Work follows method statements, access controls and change records.
Acceptance   Parties test power, alarms, transmission, safety and installed inventory before
service.
Operation   Performance, incidents, maintenance, billing and expansion are monitored.
Exit   Equipment, records, liabilities and continuity are managed without unsafe
abandonment.
Capacity is not a magic refusal
A provider claiming that a site is full should identify the limiting resource, existing committed load,
applicable safety margin and whether reasonable reinforcement or rearrangement is possible. The
requester must also provide accurate requirements. NCC can then distinguish genuine engineering
constraint from strategic exclusion.
A requester's commercial urgency does not override structural safety. Equally, an
unsupported safety claim should not shield discriminatory refusal.
NCC Promotion Study Guide   106

10.6 The sharing agreement
Clause area   Questions that must be answered
Scope   Which site, assets, positions, capacity and services are included?
Access   Who may enter, when, under what notice, identity and supervision?
Installation   Who approves designs, performs work and certifies completion?
Power   How are capacity, quality, fuel, metering, batteries and priorities controlled?
Maintenance   Who maintains shared and tenant equipment and within what response
times?
Service levels   Which availability, restoration, escalation and reporting measures apply?
Charges   What is recurring, one-off, usage-based, pass-through or adjustable?
Expansion   How are additional load, space, ports or reinforcement requested and funded?
Confidentiality   How is a rival's rollout, capacity and launch information protected?
Liability   How are damage, negligence, interruption and third-party claims allocated?
Dispute resolution   What operational escalation precedes formal regulatory or legal action?
Exit   How are removal, restoration, outstanding charges and consumer continuity
handled?
Agreement versus regulation
Commercial negotiation allows parties to tailor technical and financial details, but an agreement
cannot contract out of statutory duties, applicable guidelines, licence conditions or NCC authority. A
clause authorising discriminatory treatment does not become lawful because both parties signed it.
Confidentiality and competition
The facility provider can learn where a rival plans to launch, how much capacity it needs and when
equipment will arrive. Access to that information should be limited to operational necessity,
segregated from competitive decision-making and available to NCC where lawfully required.
A sound agreement simultaneously manages a physical asset, an operational dependency, a
wholesale commercial relationship and a competition risk.
Planned maintenance
The facility provider should give reasonable notice, coordinate maintenance windows, limit
simultaneous risk and provide emergency contacts. The tenant should disclose sensitive services
and maintain accurate contact details. Maintenance records help distinguish planned work from
avoidable outage. These arrangements should be settled before an incident, when the parties can
assess risks without the pressure of an ongoing failure.

10.7 Pricing and competition
Collocation pricing must recover legitimate costs and support investment without becoming a
mechanism for excluding competitors. The analysis should identify the service unit, cost driver, risk
allocation, comparable customers and treatment of the provider's own affiliated operator.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   107
Charge   Possible basis   Control question
Application or survey   Administrative and engineering work.   Is it reasonable and consistently applied?
Installation   Labour, materials, rigging and integration.   Does it reflect the actual scope?
Recurring space rental   Tower position, cabinet or compound
occupation.
Are comparable users treated
consistently?
Power   Metered energy, capacity reservation, fuel
and maintenance.
Are measurement and pass-through rules
transparent?
Transmission or port   Capacity and interface supplied.   Is the service distinct and correctly
authorised?
Reinforcement   Structural, electrical or civil expansion.   Who benefits and owns the
improvement?
Restoration or call-out   Emergency attendance and repair.   Is ordinary maintenance being charged
twice?
Exit   De-installation and site reinstatement.   Is the charge proportionate rather than
punitive?
Possible anti-competitive conduct
A high price is not automatically unlawful. Assess cost, scarcity, risk, comparators, market
power, discriminatory effect and justification before recommending a remedy.

10.8 Power, service quality and resilience
At Nigerian telecommunications sites, power is often the most operationally important shared service.
Grid supply may be supported by rectifiers, batteries, generators, fuel logistics and renewable
systems. Failure at the common power layer can interrupt several operators simultaneously.
Terminal and hub sites
A terminal site principally serves its local access function. A hub site aggregates or supports other
sites, so failure can affect a wider area. Power availability and Mean Time to Repair measure different
things: availability describes the proportion of the relevant measurement period during which the
service is available, while Mean Time to Repair describes average restoration time. A hub may
require stronger resilience because of its wider dependencies. Numerical compliance thresholds
must be read with the applicable service definition, exclusions and measurement method.
Risk   Necessary control
Grid failure   Battery autonomy, generator start, fuel plan and alarm response.
Shared generator failure   Standby capacity, preventive maintenance and emergency escalation.
Fuel theft or shortage   Consumption monitoring, access control and replenishment evidence.
Battery degradation   Testing, lifecycle replacement and realistic autonomy records.
Common fibre route   Physically diverse routing rather than two labels on one duct.
Planned maintenance   Notice, coordinated window, rollback and critical-service protection.
Site access delay   Twenty-four-hour contacts, escalation and emergency authority.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   108
Availability is not a feeling
Availability must be calculated from the prescribed service population, measurement interval and
exclusions. Mean Time to Repair is an average and can hide extreme incidents; NCC should
examine distributions, repeated failures, consumer impact and root cause.
Shared infrastructure improves efficiency but concentrates risk. The regulatory objective is
efficient sharing with measurable resilience, not sharing at any cost.

10.9 Disputes and regulatory response
Dispute   Evidence needed
No capacity   Structural report, loading schedule, space inventory, power headroom,
commitments and expansion options.
Delayed access   Request and response timestamps, access logs, stated reasons, work
programme and comparable cases.
Excessive charge   Rate card, cost components, contract, invoices, comparators and affiliate
treatment.
Repeated outages   Alarm logs, power and fuel records, incident timeline, affected tenants and
restoration evidence.
Equipment damage   Access record, method statement, photographs, change log, maintenance
report and custody evidence.
Confidentiality breach   Access permissions, communications, competitive use and resulting harm.
Discriminatory quality   Service-level results by tenant, prioritisation rules and technical justification.
Regulatory response
Model scenario
Three operators lose service whenever one tower company's generator fails. The regulatory
assessment should confirm the affected sites and dependency, test compliance with current
availability and repair rules, inspect maintenance and fuel evidence, determine each party's
contractual and regulatory responsibility, require immediate restoration and redundancy measures,
and verify sustained improvement. It should not assume that outsourcing power removes the mobile
operators' consumer obligations.
NCC dispute intervention must remain evidence-led and within lawful authority; it is not a
substitute for every contractual remedy between commercial parties.

10.10 Applying the regulatory framework
An infrastructure-sharing arrangement must be assessed against the Nigerian Communications Act
2003, applicable NCC guidelines, the relevant licence conditions and service-quality requirements.
The commercial agreement then specifies the facilities, charges and responsibilities between the
parties. These documents perform different functions: the Act supplies statutory authority; the
regulatory instruments and licence establish applicable obligations; the contract organises delivery
within those boundaries.
The existing material identifies the 2021 Co-location and Infrastructure Sharing Guidelines and the
Quality of Service Regulations 2024 with the 2026 Business Rules. Exact prescribed deadlines,

NCC Promotion Study Guide   109
numerical targets and procedural requirements require confirmation from the complete relevant
instruments. No contractual commitment should be described as a universal regulatory requirement
merely because it appears in one provider agreement.
A site survey, installation acceptance or negotiated service level does not authorise an activity
outside a participant's licence. Conversely, holding a licence does not establish that a particular tower
can safely carry additional equipment. Legal authorisation and site-specific engineering suitability
must both be established.

10.11 Practice questions and explained answers
Question 1. Define collocation and distinguish it from interconnection.
Answer. Collocation places one provider's equipment at another provider's site or facility under
agreed conditions. Shared support may include space, power, cooling, security and access.
Interconnection links networks so they can exchange communications traffic. Two operators can
occupy one tower without interconnecting at that site, and two networks can interconnect without
sharing a tower. The object of the arrangement is the decisive distinction: shared location and
support versus traffic exchange.
Question 2. Do collocation, co-location and colocation describe different
telecommunications arrangements?
Answer. In this context they are spelling variants, not three separate regulatory categories. An
examination answer should define the arrangement clearly and reproduce an official instrument's title
accurately. The spelling does not determine whether the facilities shared are passive or active; the
actual equipment and functions do.
Question 3. Is every infrastructure-sharing arrangement an example of collocation?
Answer. No. Infrastructure sharing is broader. A provider may lease dark fibre along a route without
sharing a tower site. Collocation concerns occupation of a common facility or location. Both can
reduce duplication, but their technical scope and contractual obligations differ.
Question 4. Why encourage sharing if it can create common points of failure?
Answer. Sharing can reduce construction costs, accelerate deployment and make better use of
scarce sites. However, several tenants depending on one generator, fibre route or access gate may
fail together. The appropriate response is to require suitable resilience and accountability, not to
assume either that all sharing is beneficial or that all shared dependencies are unacceptable.
Redundant power, genuinely diverse routes, maintenance and rapid restoration can reduce the
concentrated risk.
Question 5. A tower provider rejects a request because the site is full. What evidence
should be examined?
Answer. Identify the constrained resource: tower loading, floor space, power, cooling, transmission or
safe access. Examine the engineering assessment, current and committed loads, safety margins

because the site is full. What evidence
should be examined?
Answer. Identify the constrained resource: tower loading, floor space, power, cooling, transmission or
safe access. Examine the engineering assessment, current and committed loads, safety margins and
feasible reinforcement options. Compare treatment of similar requests and affiliated operators. The
requester must provide accurate specifications. A documented physical limit may justify refusal; an
unsupported capacity claim should not be accepted as conclusive.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   110
Question 6. Does outsourcing site power remove the mobile operator's responsibility to
consumers?
Answer. Not automatically. The contract can allocate maintenance work and financial liability between
the operator and supplier, but does not itself extinguish statutory or licence obligations. The operator
must manage the outsourced dependency and its consumer-facing responsibilities. The supplier's
own regulatory obligations must also be assessed; identifying operator accountability does not give
the supplier immunity.
Question 7. When might a high collocation charge raise competition concerns?
Answer. A high price alone is insufficient to establish a breach. Examine the service supplied, costs,
scarcity, investment risk, contractual allocation and comparable terms. Concern becomes stronger
where a provider with market power selectively inflates charges for rivals, favours an affiliate or ties
access to unnecessary purchases. The assessment should connect the conduct to its effect and test
the provider's justification.
Question 8. Three networks fail whenever their common site generator fails. Set out a
reasoned regulatory response.
Answer. First establish the affected sites, duration, customers and shared power dependency.
Preserve alarms, maintenance records, fuel records, access logs and restoration times. Assess the
applicable obligations of the site provider and tenant operators. Secure restoration and risk reduction,
including suitable standby arrangements and escalation. Investigate recurring causes rather than
accepting repeated temporary repairs. Any enforcement response must follow the governing authority
and procedure, and later monitoring should establish whether performance has actually improved.
NCC Promotion Study Guide   111

Chapter 11
Broadband, fibre infrastructure and rights of way
The previous chapters explain access to shared assets. Broadband deployment puts those
relationships into a physical network: international capacity, national transport, local access and the
practical permissions needed to build and maintain them.

11.1 Follow the connection end to end
When a user opens a service, data normally crosses several independently managed domains. A
failure in any one can dominate the experience.
Layer   Function and typical constraint
International connectivity   Submarine cable, terrestrial border link or satellite connects Nigeria to
external networks. Landing diversity and international capacity matter.
National backbone   Long-distance routes join landing stations, cities, data centres and regional
points. Long common routes can create shared failure risk.
Metropolitan network   City rings and aggregation links distribute capacity among exchanges, sites,
businesses and neighbourhoods.
Middle mile/backhaul   Carries aggregated traffic from an access node or mobile site toward the core
or Internet. Congestion here can coexist with strong radio signal.
Access/last mile   Final network segment reaches the customer: fibre, copper, cellular radio,
fixed wireless or satellite.
Premises and device   Indoor Wi-Fi, router, handset, computer, power and configuration shape
actual use.
Service platform   Domain name resolution, cloud, content delivery, application server,
cybersecurity control and peering affect response.
Forward path and return path
A request and its response may not use identical routes. Routing policy, congestion or failure can
make performance asymmetric. Therefore one successful speed test or ping does not establish
universal service quality.
Physical and logical networks
A physical route describes cable, duct, poles, radios and buildings. A logical route describes how
traffic is configured to flow. Two logical links advertised as redundant may occupy the same duct,
bridge or landing station. True resilience requires failure-domain diversity, not merely two circuit
labels.
Regulatory significance
Diagnosis should move from symptom to layer and evidence. 'Internet is slow' may require radio
measurements, backhaul utilisation, core alarms, peering paths, device tests and application data.
NCC's intervention must address the responsible layer and competent legal person.
End-to-end service quality is limited by the weakest relevant segment. Regulation should allocate
accountability without pretending one operator controls every external dependency.

11.2 How optical fibre works
Optical fibre guides pulses of light through a very thin glass core surrounded by cladding. Information
is encoded onto light, transmitted and converted back into electrical information at equipment
interfaces. Compared with copper, fibre supports very high capacity over long distances with low
attenuation and immunity to electromagnetic interference; it is not immune to cuts, poor splicing, dirty
connectors, bending, flooding, equipment failure or power loss.
Term   Plain-English meaning
Fibre strand   One glass transmission path. A cable contains multiple strands plus protective
layers.
Single-mode fibre   Small-core fibre used for long-distance and high-capacity communications;
the dominant carrier-network form.
Wavelength   A colour-like channel of light. Multiple wavelengths can carry separate
high-rate signals on one fibre pair.
Dark fibre   Installed fibre without active transmission service; it still requires equipment,
power, operation and maintenance to become useful.
Lit service   Capacity delivered over fibre using active optical equipment.
Duct/sub-duct   Protective pathway into which cables are pulled or blown; spare duct can be
shared or used for later expansion.
Splice   Permanent joining of fibre ends, commonly by fusion. Loss and quality must
be tested.
Optical distribution frame   Managed termination and cross-connection point in a facility.
Point of presence   Location where a provider houses equipment and interconnects customers or
other networks.
Capacity is engineered, not assumed
A fibre cable's theoretical potential is not the customer's purchased bandwidth. Usable capacity
depends on strand availability, optical equipment, wavelength plan, interfaces, network design,
upstream capacity, protection and commercial provisioning.
Latency, bandwidth and loss
Bandwidth is the rate at which data can be carried; latency is time for data to travel and be
processed; packet loss is data that fails to arrive. A high-bandwidth connection can still feel poor for
interactive applications if latency, jitter or loss is excessive.
'Fibre has unlimited capacity' is wrong. Fibre has very large scalable potential, but every
deployed system has finite equipment, spectrum-of-light, route and commercial limits.
NCC Promotion Study Guide   113

11.3 Architecture, topology and resilience
Topology   Strength and vulnerability
Point-to-point   Simple dedicated route; service fails if the unprotected path fails.
Star   Many endpoints connect to a hub. Efficient, but hub or feeder failure can affect
many endpoints.
Ring   Traffic can be redirected around the opposite side when the design,
equipment and physical route are genuinely diverse.
Mesh   Multiple paths improve survivability and flexibility but increase cost and
operational complexity.
Tree/branch   Efficient for access distribution; an upstream cut affects the downstream
branch.
Protection versus restoration
Protection uses pre-arranged spare capacity and often switches automatically after a fault.
Restoration finds or provisions another route after failure and may take longer. Resilience also needs
power backup, spare parts, trained field teams, network monitoring, escalation and tested recovery
procedures.
Common-mode failure
Two cables may share the same trench, bridge, pole line, manhole, power source or equipment
room. One excavation, fire or flood can therefore defeat both. Route records must identify shared
risk, and resilience claims should be verified physically.
Testing and acceptance
Method   What it establishes
Optical time-domain reflectometer   Locates loss events, joints and probable faults by analysing reflected light
along the route.
Optical power/loss test   Checks end-to-end optical loss against the engineered budget.
Route inspection   Verifies depth, markers, chambers, crossings, reinstatement and protection.
As-built record   Records actual route, depth, coordinates, ducts, strands, joints and
deviations—not merely original design.
Service test   Confirms configured bandwidth, latency, availability and failover under agreed
conditions.
Operations
A network operations centre monitors alarms and performance. Trouble tickets, dispatch times, mean
time to repair, repeat faults and unavailability show operational health. An impressive build without
accurate as-built data and maintenance funding becomes a fragile asset.
Redundancy is an evidence claim. Ask: diverse from what failure, at which layer, for how long, and
has failover been tested?
NCC Promotion Study Guide   114

11.4 Fibre, mobile networks and the last mile
Wireless access does not remove the need for fixed transport. A mobile base station uses radio to
reach devices, then normally needs fibre or microwave backhaul to carry aggregated traffic toward
the core. More radio spectrum or sites may not improve service if backhaul is constrained.
Access technology   Best use and limitation
Fibre to the premises/home   Very high, stable capacity and long upgrade life; civil works and low-density
economics can be difficult.
Fibre to the building   Fibre reaches a shared building point; internal Ethernet, fibre, coaxial cable or
Wi-Fi completes delivery.
Fixed wireless access   Rapid coverage using radio from a fixed site; capacity, line-of-sight, spectrum
and interference require engineering.
Mobile broadband   Mobility and wide reach; shared radio resources, coverage, device and indoor
conditions vary.
Microwave link   Useful high-capacity backhaul without trenching; needs spectrum, alignment,
line-of-sight and availability design.
Satellite   Reaches remote or rapidly served locations; capacity economics, terminal
view, weather bands and latency vary by orbit/system.
Legacy copper/coaxial   Can reuse installed plant, but condition, distance and upgrade ceiling affect
performance.
Fronthaul, midhaul and backhaul
In disaggregated radio networks, fronthaul connects radio units to distributed/baseband processing,
midhaul connects distributed and central processing functions, and backhaul connects the
radio-access domain toward the core. The boundaries depend on architecture; in a general exam
answer, define the function rather than reciting an acronym.
Passive optical networks
A passive optical network shares one optical feeder through passive splitters among multiple
premises. The optical line terminal is on the provider side; the optical network terminal is at or near
the user. Split ratio, distance, optical budget and contention influence design.
Coverage versus connection
Passing fibre near a community does not mean homes can order service. Distribution plant, access
equipment, permits, customer drops, addresses, installation teams, retail products and affordable
devices may still be missing.
A mast is not a broadband network, fibre kilometres are not subscriber connections, and

equipment, permits, customer drops, addresses, installation teams, retail products and affordable

A mast is not a broadband network, fibre kilometres are not subscriber connections, and a

11.5 International connectivity, data centres and local traffic
Submarine cable systems land international capacity at controlled landing stations. Resilience
depends on multiple cable systems, landing locations, terrestrial routes and upstream relationships.
Several cables landing in one area can still share coastal, power or metro risks.

metadata.section: 11.5 International connectivity, data centres and local traffic

chunks.content:
NCC Promotion Study Guide   115
Keeping local traffic local
An Internet exchange point allows participating networks to exchange appropriate traffic directly
under agreed policies. Local peering can reduce unnecessary international transit, cost and latency,
but participation alone does not guarantee optimal routing or capacity.
Element   Contribution
Internet exchange point   Neutral or governed exchange fabric for direct network-to-network traffic.
Data centre   Secure, powered, cooled environment for computing, storage and
interconnection.
Carrier-neutral facility   Allows multiple networks to meet without being locked to one carrier.
Content delivery network   Caches content nearer users, reducing repeated long-distance retrieval.
Cloud region/edge facility   Places computing closer to demand; resilience and data-governance
questions remain.
Domain name system   Translates names to addresses; failure or manipulation can make reachable
services appear unavailable.
Interconnection is not identical to Internet peering
Both join networks, but traditional telecommunications interconnection, IP transit and settlement-free
or paid peering have different technical, commercial and regulatory arrangements. A good answer
identifies the service exchanged, route, payment model, quality obligations and governing instrument.
Digital sovereignty and resilience
Local hosting can improve latency and keep some traffic within Nigeria, yet concentration in one
facility can create systemic risk. Policy should encourage competitive interconnection, secure
facilities, multiple routes and tested continuity rather than equating 'local' with automatically resilient.
Infrastructure value comes from usable interconnection. A landing cable, data centre or exchange
isolated from diverse domestic networks cannot deliver its full national benefit.

chunks.content:
11.6 What meaningful broadband requires
Meaningful connectivity shifts attention from nominal coverage to whether people can regularly use a
capable connection for valuable purposes. It is an analytical framework, not permission to invent one
universal threshold.
Dimension   Diagnostic question
Availability   Can service actually be ordered or accessed at the location?
Capacity and quality   Does it support the intended applications reliably, including busy periods?
Affordability   Can the user sustain service, device, power and installation costs?
Device   Is an appropriate, secure and capable device available?
Skills and safety   Can the person use the service confidently and manage online risks?
Relevance   Are content, language, services and opportunities useful to the user?
Continuity   Is the connection sufficiently regular, repairable and resilient?

NCC Promotion Study Guide   116
Adoption gap and usage gap
A coverage gap exists where capable infrastructure is absent. An adoption or usage gap exists where
coverage exists but people do not subscribe or use it effectively. Supply subsidy alone may not solve
affordability, trust, literacy, device or relevance barriers.
Demand aggregation
Connecting schools, hospitals, government offices, businesses and community facilities can create
anchor demand that improves a route's economics. The design should still prevent an anchor
contract from foreclosing competitive access or producing an asset usable only by one programme.
Measurement discipline
Define the service, geography, population basis and observation period.
Distinguish theoretical footprint, modelled coverage, tested coverage, serviceability, active
subscription and usage.
Use busy-hour and reliability evidence, not only peak advertised speed.
Disaggregate rural/urban, income, gender, disability and other relevant access differences without
exposing personal data.
Record methodology and uncertainty so successive figures remain comparable.
Penetration can use population, households or subscriptions as denominator;
subscriptions are not unique persons. State the definition before comparing figures.

11.7 Rights of way - the practical gateway
A right of way is the legal or authorised ability to place, operate and maintain infrastructure on, over,
under or across land or a corridor. In practice, deployment may require permits, consents, wayleaves,
environmental or traffic approvals and payment or restoration obligations. Ownership of a
communications licence does not automatically grant unrestricted entry onto every road or property.
Stakeholder   Legitimate concern
Operator/infrastructure provider   Predictable approval time, charge, route access, security and ability to
maintain.
Federal, state or local authority   Road integrity, planning, traffic, public safety, environment and lawful
revenue.
Landowner/occupier   Consent, compensation where applicable, safety, access and restoration.
Other utility   Protection of power, water, gas, drainage and existing communications plant.
Public/user   Continuity, lower deployment cost, safe streets and accountable
reinstatement.
NCC   Sector investment, non-discrimination, competition, quality and statutory
boundaries.

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.topic: 11.7 Rights of way - the practical gateway
metadata.section: 11.7 Rights of way - the practical gateway

chunks.content:
NCC Promotion Study Guide   117
Why unpredictability matters
High or inconsistent charges, duplicate approvals, uncertain timelines, arbitrary route changes and
repeated excavation raise capital cost, delay revenue and make marginal communities less
investable. The resulting cost can influence wholesale and retail prices, but a lower charge alone
does not guarantee consumer price reduction.
Good corridor governance
Published requirements, forms, service timelines, contacts and appeal/escalation route.
Geographic information system records of roads, utilities, permits and completed routes.
Coordinated roadworks, dig-once policy, spare duct and planned crossings where economical.
Proportionate, transparent charges and a clear basis for restoration deposits.
Utility detection, traffic/safety plan, public notice and supervised reinstatement.
As-built submission and emergency access for repair.
Right of way is not the same as ownership of land, duct or fibre. It is a permission or legal
access interest whose precise scope comes from the governing law and instrument.
