metadata.section: 13.10 Mobile number portability under the 2026 registration layer

chunks.content:
13.11 Churn, inactivity, recycling and number history
Subscriber control continues after activation. Churn and recycling must prevent a former subscriber's
identity, messages, credentials or liabilities from following a number to a new user.
Lifecycle event   Required reasoning
Inactivity   A Mobile Station International Subscriber Directory Number with no
revenue-generating event for 365 days is subject to delinking/barring under
the 2026 rules.
Churn   The relationship between the former subscriber and line is ended through
controlled procedures.

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.topic: 13.11 Churn, inactivity, recycling and number history
metadata.section: 13.11 Churn, inactivity, recycling and number history

chunks.content:
NCC Promotion Study Guide   145
Lifecycle event   Required reasoning
Delinking   The prior identity-number association is removed from active service records
in the required manner.
Recycling   The number is prepared and later reassigned under applicable controls; it is
not a continuation of the former subscription.
Identity purge   The former National Identification Number must not remain attached to the
recycled number.
History retention   The rules require a two-year history, supporting audit, investigation and
dispute resolution without treating the old subscriber as current.
Why recycling is risky
One-time passwords and messages may still be sent by third-party services to the old number.
A stale subscriber link can create false attribution.
Incomplete provider synchronisation can produce contradictory records.
A new subscriber may inherit reputational or fraud signals that should have been resolved.
Over-aggressive deletion can destroy evidence needed for lawful investigation or dispute resolution.
Balanced control
A sound process must separate the old and new subscriber relationships, preserve lawful history,
update relevant platforms and communicate the change through reliable interfaces. Purging a live
association and retaining an audit history are compatible; they serve different purposes.
Recycling requires both forgetting and remembering: forget the old live association, remember the
lawful historical record.

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.topic: 13.11 Churn, inactivity, recycling and number history
metadata.section: 13.11 Churn, inactivity, recycling and number history

chunks.content:
13.12 Sim swap, spoofing and account takeover
SIM replacement
A legitimate subscriber may replace a Subscriber Identity Module after loss, theft, damage or format
change while retaining the number. In SIM-swap fraud, an attacker persuades or corrupts the
provider into moving the victim's service to a SIM controlled by the attacker. Calls and one-time
passwords then reach the attacker.
Caller identity spoofing
Spoofing manipulates displayed caller or sender identity. A familiar number on the screen is therefore
not conclusive proof of origin. Controls may involve signalling integrity, traceability, blocking rules,
inter-operator coordination and consumer education. It must be distinguished from number
reassignment, where the number has genuinely moved to a new user.
Event   What changes   Principal risk
SIM swap   SIM or profile serving the same number.   Attacker captures service and
authentication messages.
Port-out fraud   Serving provider changes without valid
subscriber authority.
Attacker moves number to another
network.

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.topic: 13.12 Sim swap, spoofing and account takeover
metadata.section: 13.12 Sim swap, spoofing and account takeover

chunks.content:
NCC Promotion Study Guide   146
Event   What changes   Principal risk
Reassignment   Number is lawfully issued to a new
subscriber after lifecycle controls.
Old third-party accounts still trust it.
Spoofing   Presented identity is manipulated without
necessarily controlling the number.
Victim trusts a false display.
Fraudulent registration   Identity record is false, stolen or
improperly verified.
Anonymous or misattributed service.
Defence in depth
Strong and proportionate identity checks for replacement and porting.
Independent notification through an existing trusted channel.
Maker-checker approval for high-risk or exception transactions.
Agent authentication, location and device controls.
Velocity and anomaly detection across repeated requests.
Cooling-off or enhanced verification for sensitive downstream transactions.
Rapid consumer reporting, containment and restoration.
Evidence preservation and sanctions for insider collusion.
National Identification Number linkage reduces false identity risk but cannot alone prevent
an insider from bypassing a SIM-replacement process.

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.topic: 13.12 Sim swap, spoofing and account takeover
metadata.section: 13.12 Sim swap, spoofing and account takeover

chunks.content:
13.13 Telecom identity risk management system
The problem crosses sectors
Banks, financial-technology firms and insurers often use a mobile number for contact, authentication
or recovery. They may not know that the number has been churned, reassigned, swapped or
blacklisted. The Telecom Identity Risk Management System provides a centralised, secure interface
through which authorised telecommunications operators publish relevant status and approved service
providers verify it.
Role separation
Actor   Permitted role shown in current
documentation
Why it matters
Telecommunications
operator
Updates status for numbers it is
authorised to manage.
The source network owns the lifecycle
event evidence.
Approved service provider   Verifies status for onboarding,
authentication or transactions.
A relying organisation receives a risk
signal, not update power.
System
administrator/regulatory layer
Approves organisations, credentials and
governance.
Participation and access are controlled.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   147
Statuses are signals, not verdicts
Current documentation describes statuses such as churned, swapped, blacklisted, reassigned,
normal and null. A swapped result does not prove fraud; a legitimate customer may have replaced a
damaged card. A normal result does not prove that the person presenting the number is the lawful
subscriber. Each result should feed a proportionate decision with other evidence.
Correct status statement
Technical documentation explains implementation capability. The 9 September 2026 Board
communique separately schedules TIRMS and its business rules for October 2026. Documentation
alone does not establish completion of that planned go-live.
The system does not replace subscriber registration. Registration answers who is linked to the
service; identity-risk management adds what has happened to the number over time and whether
a relying organisation should apply caution.

13.14 Application programming interface governance
The update path
An operator detects a lifecycle event such as churn, swap, blacklist or reassignment.
Its authorised backend sends a status update through the protected application programming
interface.
The request includes the number, status and applicable event or reassignment date.
The platform validates identity, authority, format and permitted values.
The central record is updated and becomes available to authorised verification users.
Logs preserve who submitted what and when.
The verification path
An approved relying organisation faces onboarding, password-reset or sensitive-transaction risk.
Its backend submits the number in the required format using an authenticated request.
The platform returns status, verification outcome and relevant timestamps or network data.
The organisation applies its own risk rule, seeks stronger evidence, pauses or proceeds.
The decision and basis are logged for review.
Webhooks and continuous assurance
A webhook lets the system notify a registered endpoint when a previously verified number changes
status. This converts a one-time check into event-driven risk management. Delivery must still be
authenticated, retried safely, deduplicated and monitored; otherwise a missed or repeated event can
create inconsistent decisions.
Control   Failure prevented
Application-programming-interface
key protection and rotation
Impersonation of an authorised organisation.
Transport Layer Security   Interception or alteration in transit.
Range-based update authority   Operator changing a number it does not manage.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   148
Control   Failure prevented
Input and status validation   Corrupt or ambiguous central records.
Rate limits and anomaly monitoring   Abuse, scraping and denial of service.
Audit and reconciliation   Undetected omissions or conflicting feeds.
An application-programming-interface response is not self-executing regulation. The
receiving institution must interpret it lawfully and proportionately within its own decision
controls.

13.15 Consumer protection and redress
Where numbering harms become human
A routing error can isolate a business. An unauthorised SIM replacement can empty an account. A
recycled number can expose private messages. A misleading short code can create recurring
charges. Numbering administration is therefore consumer protection, not merely back-office
engineering.
Complaint   Immediate protection   Investigation focus
Number suddenly loses
service
Secure account, verify status and provide
safe restoration route.
Bar, swap, port, billing, network and
identity timestamps.
Unauthorised port or
replacement
Contain service and linked transaction
risk; preserve evidence.
Request, agent, biometrics, approvals,
notices and device/location.
Calls reach wrong person   Stop misrouting and warn affected parties
where lawful.
Assignment history, quarantine, routes
and database state.
Short-code charge disputed   Prevent continuing unwanted charge and
explain complaint path.
Consent, tariff disclosure, message logs
and service provider.
Old accounts follow recycled
number
Help current and former holders separate
identities.
Reassignment date, platform reliance and
authentication weakness.
Complaint handling principles
Authenticate the complainant without demanding the compromised channel as the only proof.
Create a traceable case and preserve volatile logs immediately.
Separate emergency containment from the final liability decision.
Coordinate operator, portability, identity and relying institutions where authorised.
Give the consumer plain-language status, realistic timelines and escalation route.
Restore service or correct records, then verify that downstream systems converge.
Analyse recurring patterns for systemic enforcement.
Shared responsibility
The telecommunications provider controls its registration and lifecycle processes, but banks and
platforms should not treat possession of a number as permanent proof of identity. Consumers should
update services and protect credentials. NCC should coordinate sector controls while respecting legal
boundaries and the mandates of other regulators.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   149
The best remedy corrects the individual case and removes the systemic weakness that allowed it.

13.16 Internal NCC workflow and data design
One resource, many regulatory records
A robust NCC numbering system should link each allocation to the licensee, licence, service purpose,
range or code, decision, effective date, conditions, utilisation returns, activation state, portability
obligations, complaints, enforcement and surrender or recovery. A scanned letter alone cannot
support modern oversight.
Role-based workflow
Applicant submits a structured request and supporting evidence.
Licensing confirms identity, authorisation and service scope.
Numbering specialists assess plan fit, demand, existing utilisation and future impact.
Technical teams assess routing, portability and interoperability readiness.
Consumer, competition, legal, finance and security units contribute where relevant.
An authorised decision maker approves, varies or refuses with recorded reasons.
The register updates through maker-checker control and the licensee is notified.
Activation, use and reporting are monitored through reconciled data.
Data model
Entity   Critical relationships
Licensee   Licences, ownership, contacts, compliance and status.
Number resource   Type, range/code, parent plan, holder and permitted purpose.
Allocation decision   Authority, date, conditions, fees and approvers.
Utilisation return   Period, status counts, certification, validation and exceptions.
Porting record   Number, donor, recipient, timestamps, result and reason.
Identity-risk event   Number, operator, event type, occurrence date and update trace.
Case or complaint   Affected resource, parties, evidence, directions and closure.
Controls for an Information Technology officer
Use least-privilege access, separation of duties, strong authentication, immutable audit, encryption,
retention schedules, monitored integrations, tested backup and disaster recovery. Reconcile source
systems rather than building dashboards over inconsistent data. Every manual override should record
who, why, authority and expiry.
Digitisation is not uploading paper forms. Regulatory digitisation requires structured data,
controlled workflow, integration, validation, audit and measurable outcomes.

13.17 TIRMS: capability, planned go-live and outcomes
The Board communique of 9 September 2026 schedules the Telecommunications Identity Risk
Management System and its associated business rules to go live in October 2026. Its technical
interfaces explain the proposed exchange of number-status information; their existence is not proof
that the scheduled go-live has already happened. A status response is a risk signal, not conclusive
identification of the person presenting a number.

13.18 Exam-application drills and model structures
Scenario 1 - activation before verification
A provider captures a claimed NIN and facial image, activates immediately, and plans to reconcile
failed verifications later. Explain the regulatory defect.
Model structure: identify the 2022 Regulations and August 2026 Rules; separate capture from
authoritative verification; explain why verification precedes activation; address provider accountability,
data alignment and audit evidence; recommend suspension, correction, investigation and control
remediation according to current authority.
Scenario 2 - recycled number
A new subscriber receives a recycled number still linked to the former subscriber's identity in one
provider interface. Explain risks and controls.
Model structure: distinguish active association from retained history; identify false attribution, privacy
and fraud risks; require purge/delinking from active systems, interface synchronisation, lawful
two-year history and evidence of correction.
Scenario 3 - corporate meter fleet
A utility claims its machine-to-machine profiles need no accountable person because the devices act
automatically.
Model structure: explain Primary Telecom Master accountability, corporate ownership, restricted
machine profiles, approved endpoints, lifecycle monitoring and the difference between subscriber
accountability and individual human use.
Scenario 4 - porting and device fraud
A bank sees a ported number used from a handset reported stolen. Explain the systems involved.
Model structure: registration verifies identity; MNP establishes current serving network and port
validity; TIRMS supplies number/identity risk; DMS supplies equipment-status evidence; type
approval is irrelevant to whether that individual handset is stolen; evidence must be combined before
intervention.
MARKING ADVANTAGE - Strong answers identify the governing layer, distinguish systems, apply
facts, name evidence and propose a proportionate response.
NCC Promotion Study Guide   151

Chapter 14
Device management and equipment conformity
Subscriber registration identifies the person or accountable entity linked to service. Device
management addresses the equipment used to obtain that service. Type approval, individual-device
registration and network treatment must be distinguished before assessing duties or outcomes.

14.1 Start with the object: what is a device?
For this subject, a device is not merely a consumer gadget. A Subscriber Identity Module-enabled
telephone, tablet, modem, router, point-of-sale terminal, tracking unit or other connected equipment
can attach to a public communications network. Once it transmits or receives through that network, its
radio behaviour, technical conformity, identity and security can affect consumers, operators and the
wider communications environment.
Model, unit and subscription are different things
Concept   Plain-language meaning   Example
Device model   A design or product type manufactured to
the same technical specification.
A particular make and model of
smartphone.
Individual device   One physical unit produced under that
model.
The particular handset in a subscriber's
hand.
Subscription   The service relationship represented by a
physical or embedded Subscriber Identity
Module profile.
A mobile line issued by an operator.
User   The human or organisation currently
possessing or operating the device.
The subscriber, employee or temporary
user.
Why the distinctions matter
Type approval ordinarily evaluates a model or product type. Device management deals with individual
equipment identities observed on networks. Subscriber registration deals with the person or entity
associated with a subscription. A lawful subscriber can place a valid Subscriber Identity Module in a
prohibited device; a compliant device can also be used with an improperly registered subscription.
One layer cannot substitute for the others.
Approval of a model does not prove that every unit claiming to be that model is genuine. A
counterfeit or altered unit may copy model information or an equipment identifier.
Level 10 regulatory lens
A strong officer separates the object being regulated before recommending action. Is the problem the
product model, the individual equipment identity, the subscription, the user, the importer, the vendor
or the operator's network control? An intervention aimed at the wrong object can punish innocent
users while leaving the actual supply-chain problem untouched.

chunks.content:
14.2 International mobile equipment identity
The International Mobile Equipment Identity is the identifier used to distinguish mobile equipment. It
answers a device question; it is not a person's National Identification Number, telephone number or
Subscriber Identity Module identity.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   152
A useful structure
The commonly taught structure is a fifteen-digit identifier. Its leading portion identifies the approved
device type through a Type Allocation Code; a following serial portion distinguishes the unit; the final
digit is used as a check digit. The examination value is not arithmetic memorisation. The value lies in
understanding why a structured identifier can connect model conformity, an individual unit and
network observations.
Identifier   Identifies   Does not by itself prove
National Identification
Number
A person within the national identity
framework.
Which handset is being used now.
Mobile Station International
Subscriber Directory Number
The public telephone number used to
reach a subscription.
The identity of the physical device.
International Mobile
Subscriber Identity
A subscription identity used inside the
mobile network.
That the equipment is genuine or
approved.
Integrated Circuit Card
Identifier
The physical Subscriber Identity Module
card or embedded profile container.
The current user or device.
International Mobile
Equipment Identity
The mobile equipment identity presented
to the network.
Ownership, lawful acquisition or
subscriber identity.
Dual-SIM and multi-radio complications
A device capable of maintaining more than one independent mobile-radio connection may have more
than one equipment identity. That does not automatically indicate fraud. The examiner may therefore
present two identifiers associated with one handset. The correct response is to investigate the
equipment design, number of radio transceivers and authoritative device records before concluding
that an identifier has been cloned.
An equipment identifier is evidence, not infallible truth. It can be malformed, duplicated,
altered or fraudulently copied. Device management must validate and correlate it rather
than accept every transmitted value at face value.

14.3 Why device management is needed
A network can technically carry traffic from equipment that presents a recognisable identifier even
when the device is stolen, counterfeit, technically non-compliant or using an identifier copied from
another handset. Without a coordinated mechanism, each operator sees only part of the national
picture. A device blocked on one network might move to another; duplicate identities observed across
networks may not be connected; and import or type-approval data may remain separate from
live-network evidence.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   153
The public-interest problems
Problem   Why it matters   Desired regulatory result
Stolen devices   The ability to reuse a stolen handset can
preserve its resale value and expose
subscribers to loss.
Enable evidence-based national
restriction and lawful restoration.
Counterfeit devices   Imitation products may misrepresent
origin, safety or technical conformity.
Detect suspect equipment identities and
disrupt non-compliant supply.
Substandard equipment   Poor radio or electrical performance may
affect safety, interference and service
quality.
Connect network admission to applicable
approval and standards.
Cloned identities   Several devices may present an identifier
assigned to one genuine unit.
Detect abnormal duplication and
investigate before action.
Fragmented operator
controls
A restriction applied by one operator may
not follow the device nationally.
Coordinate device status through a
central reference.
Weak supply-chain
traceability
Regulators may struggle to connect
devices to approved models and
responsible suppliers.
Create auditable links among approvals,
imports, vendors and network
observations.
Proportionality still matters
The existence of these risks does not justify indiscriminate blocking. A legitimate consumer may
unknowingly buy a non-compliant device; an identifier collision may arise from data or configuration
error; and an allegedly stolen device may have changed hands lawfully. A defensible system
therefore needs notice, evidence, correction, escalation and restoration procedures, not merely a
technical switch.
Device management is both a network-control system and a regulatory-governance system.
Technology identifies and enforces; governance determines authority, evidence, fairness,
accountability and remedy.

14.4 The technical architecture
The architecture can be understood as a hierarchy of equipment-identity records and decisions.
Component   Role
Device   Presents an equipment identity when it attaches to or uses a mobile network.
Operator Equipment Identity Register   Allows an operator to compare the observed identity with device-status
information and apply a network decision.
Central Equipment Identity Register   Maintains the national reference and exchanges relevant device status with
participating operators.
Device Management System   The broader platform, processes, integrations, governance and user functions
surrounding central device-identity management.
Type-approval register   Provides authoritative model-level conformity information that can support
device validation.
External authorised sources   May provide verified information about stolen devices, lawful imports,
manufacturers or other approved status events.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   154
A simplified transaction
A Subscriber Identity Module-enabled device attempts to use an operator's network.
The network obtains the equipment identity presented by the device.
The operator's equipment-identity control checks locally available status information.
The operator and central platform exchange authorised status updates according to the prescribed
interface and timing rules.
The device is permitted, monitored, restricted or referred for investigation according to its validated
status.
The event is logged so that decisions can be audited, corrected and, where justified, reversed.
Central does not mean careless concentration
A central register creates national consistency but also becomes sensitive infrastructure. Access
must follow least-privilege rules; interfaces must authenticate participating systems; data must be
protected in transit and at rest; administrative actions must be logged; and continuity arrangements
must prevent one platform failure from producing uncontrolled nationwide disruption.
The Central Equipment Identity Register is not simply a spreadsheet of telephone owners.
Its primary regulatory object is equipment identity and status; any associated personal
data must have a defined and lawful purpose.

14.5 Status lists and their consequences
Equipment-identity systems are commonly explained through white, grey and black status concepts.
Treat these as functional ideas; the controlling NCC instrument or system specification determines
the precise Nigerian labels, criteria and consequences.
Functional status   Meaning   Possible network treatment
Permitted or white   The identity is recognised as acceptable
under the applicable rules.
Ordinary access, subject to all other
subscription and network controls.
Observed or grey   The identity requires monitoring or
investigation because information is
incomplete, unusual or suspect.
Temporary access, notification, enhanced
monitoring or another prescribed
treatment.
Prohibited or black   The identity has been validly classified as
stolen, invalid, cloned, non-compliant or
otherwise barred under the rules.
Denial or restriction of access, with
logged reason and available remedy.
Classification is a decision process
A device should not move to a prohibited status merely because one data field looks unusual. The
system should determine the source of the alert, validate the identifier, test whether the same identity
is appearing implausibly across locations or device characteristics, check approval and supply-chain
records, apply the relevant rule and record the authority for the decision.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   155
Blocking is not destruction
Network blocking prevents or limits the device's access to covered communications networks. It does
not physically disable every non-radio function, determine criminal guilt, transfer ownership or
automatically recover a stolen handset. Those outcomes require different legal and operational
processes.
Emergency and safety considerations
The controlling framework should state how emergency communications, warnings, grace periods
and critical cases are handled. An officer must not assume that every prohibited device will receive
identical treatment in every circumstance unless the applicable rule says so.
Grey does not mean guilty. It is a risk or investigation status. A Level 10 answer should
preserve the difference between suspicion, validation, classification and enforcement.

14.6 Type approval and device registration
Type approval and device management are related but not interchangeable.
Feature   Type approval   Device management
Primary object   A model or type of communications
equipment.
An individual equipment identity observed
or registered in the ecosystem.
Primary question   Does this equipment type conform to
applicable technical requirements?
Should this individual device identity be
accepted, monitored or restricted?
Typical evidence   Test reports, technical construction
information, specifications, declarations
and samples where required.
Equipment identifier, approved-model
data, manufacturer/import/vendor records
and operator observations.
Regulatory result   Approval, rejection, modification control or
other model-level decision.
Registration, status classification,
notification, blocking, correction or
restoration.
What 'registration of devices' should mean
In this context, registration is the structured inclusion of relevant Subscriber Identity Module-enabled
equipment information in the device-management framework so that its identity and compliance
status can be checked. It should not be casually described as a new personal identity-registration
exercise for every consumer. NCC previously clarified that subscribers were not required to submit
their International Mobile Equipment Identity numbers personally.
Why the September 2026 announcement matters
The strengthened compliance announcement connects the previously developing Device
Management System to present type-approval enforcement for Subscriber Identity Module-enabled
devices. For examination purposes, the safest current formulation is: NCC is strengthening the
framework through which relevant devices are identified, registered or validated and checked for
type-approval compliance. Exact obligations and implementation dates must follow the official notice
and applicable Business Rules.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   156
A model can be approved while a unit is prohibited
A genuine model may have passed type approval, but a particular unit can later be reported stolen.
Conversely, a device may present a plausible individual identifier while its model lacks required
approval. The Device Management System must therefore test more than one dimension.
Do not answer that the Device Management System replaces type approval. It operationally
connects model-level conformity with individual-device identity and network enforcement.

14.7 Who does what?
Actor   Likely regulatory and operational responsibility
NCC   Establish the framework, define requirements, maintain oversight, approve
equipment, coordinate stakeholders, monitor compliance, protect consumers
and enforce applicable rules.
System operator or private partner   Design, build, finance, operate, maintain or manage assigned platform
functions under the approved public-private partnership and regulatory
controls.
Mobile network operator   Capture equipment identities, maintain operator-side controls, exchange
authorised status data, execute valid network decisions, keep logs and
support complaints or investigations.
Manufacturer   Maintain truthful model and production information, obtain required approvals
and protect the integrity of assigned device identifiers.
Importer or distributor   Ensure equipment entering the supply chain meets approval and registration
requirements and retain traceable records.
Vendor or retailer   Sell compliant equipment, provide accurate device information and support
consumer documentation and prescribed registration steps.
Consumer   Purchase through legitimate channels, retain proof of purchase, report theft
promptly and use the correction or restoration process where a device is
wrongly restricted.
Security or authorised public body   Provide or request verified status information only under lawful authority and
defined procedure.
Responsibility does not collapse upward
NCC oversight does not make the Commission the seller, importer or operator of every device.
Operator execution does not give an operator unlimited authority to invent national blocking criteria. A
private platform partner does not acquire independent regulatory power merely because it operates
technology. Each actor remains bounded by law, contract, licence, approved procedures and
accountability controls.
When answering a scenario, identify the actor who owns the data, the actor who decides status,
the actor who implements network treatment, and the actor who hears the complaint. They may be
different institutions.

14.8 Data, privacy and cybersecurity
A device register may begin with technical identifiers, but those identifiers can become personal data
when linked to a subscriber, location history, transaction, complaint or account. Privacy analysis
therefore depends on the entire data relationship, not on the label 'technical data'.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   157
Purpose limitation
Data collected to validate equipment and protect networks should not be silently repurposed for
unrelated profiling. Every collection, sharing and retention activity needs a defined regulatory or
operational purpose, a lawful basis and a documented access rule.
Control   Why it matters
Data minimisation   Collect the fields necessary for device-management purposes rather than
every available subscriber detail.
Role-based access   Separate approval, administration, investigation, complaint and audit
privileges.
Strong interface authentication   Prevent unauthorised systems from submitting or changing device status.
Encryption   Protect data moving between operators and the central platform and protect
stored records.
Immutable audit trail   Record who changed a status, when, under which authority and using what
evidence.
Retention and deletion rules   Keep information only for the period justified by law, investigation, remedy and
accountability needs.
Incident response   Contain breaches, preserve evidence, notify authorised parties and restore
trusted operation.
Continuity and recovery   Avoid uncontrolled nationwide service effects if the central platform or an
integration fails.
What the system should not become
Device management should not become an unrestricted surveillance database, an opaque
commercial blacklist or a shortcut around lawful investigative procedures. Its legitimacy depends on
necessity, proportionality, accuracy, security and meaningful remedy.
'No subscriber data is stored' does not by itself resolve privacy. Ask whether equipment
data can be linked, directly or indirectly, to identifiable people and how that linkage is
governed.

14.9 Notice, correction and restoration
A technically accurate blocking engine can still produce regulatory injustice if there is no practical
remedy. Consumers and legitimate businesses need a controlled path for resolving incorrect,
outdated or disputed device status.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   158
A defensible lifecycle
Stage   Required question
Detection   What event, report or inconsistency triggered attention?
Validation   Is the equipment identifier correctly captured and supported by authoritative
evidence?
Classification   Which rule and decision-maker justify the assigned status?
Notification   Who must be informed, by what channel and with what explanation or grace
period?
Restriction   What network treatment is authorised and proportionate?
Complaint or correction   What evidence can the affected party submit and who reviews it?
Restoration   How is a corrected or recovered device returned to permitted status across
operators?
Audit   Can the complete history and decision authority be reconstructed?
Examples of legitimate correction evidence
Proof of purchase and device packaging showing the relevant equipment identifier.
Manufacturer or authorised importer confirmation.
Police or authorised report concerning theft, recovery or mistaken classification.
Operator network records demonstrating a capture or integration error.
Type-approval and authorised supply-chain records.
Restoration must propagate
If a central status caused national restriction, correcting only one operator's local record may leave
the consumer blocked elsewhere. Restoration therefore needs coordinated propagation, confirmation
and monitoring. The same principle applies when a previously permitted device is validly moved to a
prohibited status.
Proof of purchase may support ownership and good faith, but it does not automatically
cure a technically non-compliant device. Remedy must address both the consumer's
position and the equipment's regulatory status.

14.10 Difficult technical cases
Cloned identity
A cloned identity occurs where more than one device presents the same equipment identifier.
Detection may rely on impossible or highly improbable simultaneous appearances, inconsistent
model characteristics, abnormal location patterns or other validated evidence. The genuine device
must not be assumed to be the offender merely because duplication exists.
Invalid or malformed identity
An identity may fail format, allocation or check-digit validation. That can indicate manipulation,
manufacturing error, unsupported legacy behaviour or bad network data. The system should classify
the cause rather than treating every failure as the same offence.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   159
Changed mainboard or repaired equipment
A legitimate repair may replace a component associated with equipment identity. The framework
needs rules for authorised repair, manufacturer records and updating the valid identity relationship.
Uncontrolled rewriting of identifiers, however, would undermine the system.
Roaming device
A foreign visitor's device can attach through international roaming. The framework must distinguish a
temporary roaming context from a device permanently introduced into the Nigerian market, while still
addressing stolen or internationally prohibited equipment according to applicable arrangements.
Machine-to-machine and Internet of Things equipment
Not every Subscriber Identity Module-enabled item looks like a telephone. Connected meters,
trackers, payment devices and industrial units may operate unattended and at scale. Registration,
notification and blocking procedures must account for enterprise ownership, critical services and
bulk-device management.
Legacy device
A device already active before a new enforcement phase may not have complete modern
supply-chain records. Transitional rules may allow validation, regularisation, observation or phased
restriction. Do not invent a blanket grandfathering rule; verify the controlling notice.
Hard cases reveal why the system needs classification rules, evidence thresholds and human
escalation. Automation should support regulatory judgment, not erase it.

14.11 Policy and implementation chronology
Period   Verified significance   Status treatment
May 2021   NCC clarified that subscribers were not
required to submit equipment identity
numbers and explained that a Device
Management System was being deployed
to protect against theft and identify fake
devices.
Historical policy and public clarification.
2022 procurement layer   Public-private partnership procurement
material described a partner-led design,
build, finance, operation, maintenance
and management model for the Device
Management System.
Implementation/procurement evidence;
not proof of completed national operation.
2024 Type Approval
Business Rules
The published Rules include Device
Management System registration within
the type-approval compliance framework.
Current regulatory/business-rule layer,
subject to later amendments.
1 June 2026   NCC's calendar recorded a Device
Management System stakeholder
engagement in Lagos.
Stakeholder and implementation
evidence.
10 September 2026   NCC announced strengthened
type-approval compliance for Subscriber
Identity Module-enabled devices in
Nigeria.
Current enforcement development as
recorded in the cited edition.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   160
How to write the current-status sentence
As at 15 September 2026, NCC is strengthening the registration, validation and type-approval
compliance framework for Subscriber Identity Module-enabled devices through the Device
Management System and its central equipment-identity capability. The historical policy objective
includes addressing stolen, fake and substandard devices. Exact enforcement dates and transition
rules should be quoted only from the applicable NCC notice or instrument.
Achievement versus initiative
The existence of a policy, procurement, stakeholder engagement or enforcement announcement is
an achievement in regulatory development, but it does not prove that every device in Nigeria has
already been validated or that every operator integration is complete. State precisely what the
evidence proves.
Never collapse the 2021 clarification, 2022 procurement, 2024 Business Rules, June 2026
engagement and September 2026 announcement into one undated event.

14.12 Applied level 10 scenarios
Scenario 1 - A consumer's genuine phone is blocked
Confirm the identifier presented on the network and on the device; identify the status source and
authority; check for duplication, capture error, theft report and approval record; preserve service and
security evidence; notify the consumer of the remedy; correct the central and operator records where
justified; and confirm restoration across networks. Do not simply tell the consumer to buy another
phone.
Scenario 2 - Thousands of devices share one identity
Treat the pattern as a possible cloned or improperly programmed identifier, but validate model,
geography, timing and source data. Coordinate operators, manufacturer/importer records and
enforcement units. Protect the genuine device population, contain further activation and investigate
the supply chain.
Scenario 3 - An importer presents type approval for a model
Verify that the certificate applies to the exact model and variant, remains valid under current rules,
and has not been altered. Then test whether the imported units carry legitimate identifiers and satisfy
device-registration requirements. Model approval alone does not validate every individual unit.
Scenario 4 - A stolen phone is recovered
Require the prescribed ownership and recovery evidence, validate that the request concerns the
correct identifier, remove or amend the prohibited status under authorised procedure, propagate the
update and confirm network restoration. Preserve the historical audit record rather than deleting it.
Scenario 5 - A central-platform outage
Invoke continuity arrangements, protect the last trusted status set, prevent unauthorised mass
changes, maintain emergency and critical-service considerations, notify stakeholders, reconcile
queued transactions after recovery and conduct a root-cause and control review.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   161
Scenario 6 - Privacy objection
Explain the device-integrity purpose and lawful authority; identify the data actually collected; show
purpose limitation, access control, retention and complaint routes; and correct any excessive
collection. Do not answer that privacy is irrelevant merely because the primary field is an equipment
identifier.

14.13 Examination traps and distinctions
Weak statement   Exam-standard correction
DMS registers every Nigerian citizen's
phone number.
It manages relevant device identities and compliance status; subscriber and
number registration are separate layers.
IMEI identifies the owner.   It identifies equipment presented to the network; ownership requires other
evidence.
Type approval and DMS are the
same.
Type approval is mainly model-level conformity; DMS supports
individual-device identity and network-status control.
A blacklisted phone is physically
destroyed.
Network access is restricted; ownership, recovery and physical disposition are
separate matters.
Two IMEIs in one handset prove
cloning.
Multi-radio or dual-SIM equipment may legitimately have more than one
identifier.
Every duplicate identifier makes both
devices criminals.
Duplication triggers validation and investigation; enforcement must identify the
genuine and offending circumstances.
The central register replaces operator
systems.
It coordinates national status; operator-side registers and network execution
remain necessary.
Consumers must send their IMEIs to
NCC.
NCC previously clarified that subscribers were not required to submit them
personally; follow the current prescribed registration mechanism.
The September announcement
proves nationwide completion.
It proves a current compliance development, not the completion of every
integration and device-validation outcome.
The five-part answer structure
Define the Device Management System in ordinary language.
Explain the device-identity and central-register mechanism.
Connect the mechanism to type approval, consumer protection, security and network integrity.
State the responsibilities and procedural safeguards.
Close with the controlled current status and distinguish it from historical or proposed material.
NCC Promotion Study Guide   162

14.14 Recall and short-answer bank
Question   Core answer
What problem does DMS solve?   Fragmented and unreliable device-identity control across networks, approvals
and the supply chain.
What does IMEI identify?   Mobile equipment, not the subscriber or ownership by itself.
What is CEIR?   The central national reference for relevant equipment-identity status and
exchange.
What is an operator EIR?   The operator-side function that checks equipment identity and applies
authorised network treatment.
How does type approval differ?   It establishes model-level technical conformity; DMS manages
individual-device identity and status.
What may a grey status mean?   Observation or investigation is required; it is not a finding of guilt.
What does blocking achieve?   It restricts covered network access; it does not determine ownership or
criminal guilt.
Why is remedy necessary?   Identifiers and records can be wrong, duplicated, outdated or disputed.
Must subscribers submit IMEIs
personally?
NCC's 2021 clarification said no; follow the current prescribed ecosystem
process.
What is the current exam-safe
position?
Active strengthening of device registration, validation and type-approval
compliance, without claiming universal completion.
One-minute explanation
The Device Management System is NCC's framework for identifying and managing Subscriber
Identity Module-enabled equipment that connects to Nigerian communications networks. It uses
equipment identifiers and a central equipment-identity capability to coordinate operator decisions
about whether a device should be permitted, monitored or restricted. It complements type approval:
type approval asks whether a model meets technical standards, while device management checks
the identity and status of an individual unit. Its public-interest purposes include consumer protection,
control of stolen, counterfeit and substandard devices, network integrity and supply-chain
accountability. Because wrong blocking can harm legitimate users, the system also requires accurate
data, privacy and cybersecurity controls, notification, correction and restoration procedures.

14.15 September 2026 implementation position

covering existing device stock and future imports. The Device Management System supports
automated checking through equipment identities. The announcement states that imported
SIM-enabled devices must be registered before sale and that unregistered devices will not be
permitted on Nigerian networks. This supply-chain requirement should not be rewritten as a general
instruction that every consumer must personally submit an equipment identifier. The Commission
also states that the system does not provide access to device contents or monitoring of personal
communications. Source: NCC, Strengthens Type Approval Compliance for SIM-Enabled Devices in
Nigeria, consulted 22 September 2026.

Chapter 15
Quality of Service and Quality of Experience
Once infrastructure and authorisations are in place, the service still has to perform. Start with the
difference between coverage, capacity, availability, objective quality and user experience; then
measure, diagnose, act and verify.

15.1 What quality regulation is solving
A licence is a promise of usable service
Authorisation to provide communications service does not end when a licence is issued. The
continuing regulatory relationship asks whether the licensee actually supplies service of an
acceptable standard, treats consumers fairly, reports truthfully and repairs failures. Quality regulation
converts broad licence and statutory duties into measurable performance, reporting and corrective
action.
The end-to-end path
A consumer's experience can depend on site power, antennas, radio spectrum, cell capacity,
transmission, fibre, interconnection, core-network functions, domain-name and Internet routing, the
remote application, the device and local conditions. 'Poor network' is therefore a symptom, not a
diagnosis.

causes.

cut.

verify it.

direction or sanction.
A dashboard showing a red indicator is not a complete regulatory decision. NCC still needs
valid data, an operative threshold, causation, procedural fairness, a remedy and

Full bars but slow Internet
Signal bars mainly indicate aspects of the radio link seen by the device. They do not prove sufficient
cell capacity, uncongested backhaul, a healthy core network or a fast application server. A crowded
cell can provide strong signal and poor throughput. A fibre cut can leave local radio coverage visible
while upstream service is impaired.
Good measurements but unhappy users
An operator can pass an averaged indicator while a particular community suffers. National or state
averages can conceal local failure, and a monthly average can conceal evening congestion. Quality
of Experience evidence helps reveal location, time, device, application and journey effects, but
subjective reports must be validated rather than dismissed or accepted blindly.
Technology label is not a guarantee
A fifth-generation icon indicates a radio/network condition, not guaranteed end-to-end speed or
latency. Spectrum bandwidth, configuration, backhaul, core architecture, device capability, server
location and demand all matter.
Always state the unit of analysis: which service, technology, geography, time window, subscriber
population and measurement method?

15.3 Voice service as a journey
Accessibility, retainability and integrity
A useful voice-service model asks three questions. Accessibility asks whether the user can establish
the call. Retainability asks whether an established call remains connected. Integrity asks whether the
speech is intelligible and timely enough to communicate. Mobility adds whether the network
preserves service when the user moves between cells or technologies.

For second-generation networks, the August 2026 Business Rules state busy-hour call-setup

service-, technology- and aggregation-specific values, not universal definitions of good quality.
A dropped call is an established call that terminates prematurely. A call that never
establishes is a setup failure, not automatically a dropped call.

Throughput is useful delivery, not the package name

influenced by radio conditions, scheduler share, spectrum, modulation, congestion, backhaul,
transport protocol, server capacity and the test method. The theoretical peak printed in marketing is
not the same as typical user throughput.

15.5 Coverage and capacity diagnosis
Coverage-limited pattern
A coverage problem often appears consistently at the edge of service, indoors, behind terrain or far
from a site. Measurements may show weak signal, poor signal quality or inability to camp on the
expected technology. Remedies can involve new sites, antenna adjustment, lower-frequency
spectrum, indoor systems or network optimisation.
Capacity-limited pattern
A capacity problem often varies with demand. Performance may be good late at night and poor in the
business day or evening. Radio resources, backhaul or core functions become constrained as users
compete. Remedies may include more spectrum, additional carriers or sectors, traffic balancing, site
densification, backhaul expansion, caching or core scaling.

A speed decline at busy hour suggests congestion but does not prove where it occurs. A fibre cut

Building another base station is not the automatic remedy for every slow-data complaint. If
the bottleneck is upstream fibre or core capacity, more radio coverage may not solve it.

15.6 Three evidence sources
Operator counters
Network elements continuously record attempts, successes, drops, congestion, throughput and
availability. Counters provide broad temporal coverage and can support cell-level analysis, but they
are controlled by the operator and depend on vendor definitions, configuration, completeness and
aggregation. NCC therefore needs harmonised formulae, data-integrity tests and audit access.
Drive and walk tests
A controlled test system follows a planned route or location set using defined devices, subscriptions,
servers, call scripts and measurement settings. It can compare operators under similar conditions
and capture radio and service detail. Its weakness is sampling: it observes only the selected roads,
times and environments.
Crowdsourced measurements
Measurements collected from many real users can reveal broad lived experience across places and
times that a test vehicle cannot cover. But device mix, tariff plans, indoor/outdoor location, user
selection, application version and sample density can bias results. Statistical controls and minimum
sample requirements matter.
Source   Strength   Risk

self-reporting risk.
Controlled test   Comparable method and rich diagnostics.   Limited route, time and device sample.
Crowdsourced data   Real-world breadth and user diversity.   Sampling and device-context bias.
Consumer complaints   Direct harm narratives and emerging
hotspots.

Triangulation
Confidence increases when independent sources converge. If complaints, crowdsourced speed,
operator utilisation and a controlled test all identify the same evening hotspot, the case is stronger. If
they disagree, NCC should investigate measurement scope rather than select the most convenient
result.
Evidence sources are complementary. The regulator's advantage is the ability to combine
network-wide data, independent measurement and consumer reality.

15.7 Measurement design
Define the question before collecting data
Service: voice, messaging, mobile data, fixed access, interconnection or satellite.
Technology: second, third, fourth or fifth generation, fixed wireline or another platform.
Geography: cell, cluster, Local Government Area, state, route or national level.
Time: all hours, busy hour, daily, weekly or reporting period.
Population: all users, selected plans, devices or service class.
Method: counters, active test, passive probe, survey or crowdsourced applet.
Threshold status: compliance, monitoring, contractual service level or analytical benchmark.
Sampling and representativeness
A large sample can still be biased. Testing only major roads favours outdoor mobility; testing only
premium devices may overstate experience; testing one server may measure that route rather than
the Internet generally. The plan should reflect urban, peri-urban and rural areas, indoor and outdoor
use, busy and quiet periods, relevant devices and technologies.
Averaging can hide harm
Aggregation   What it can conceal
National mean   Persistent failure in a state or rural region.
Monthly mean   Daily evening congestion or a severe multi-day outage.
Operator-wide mean   A weak cluster offset by excellent metropolitan cells.
Mean speed   A long tail of users with unusable performance.
Success percentage   Repeated harm concentrated on one route or interconnect partner.
Data integrity is itself a Key Performance Indicator
The 2026 rules include general reporting-completeness requirements and require harmonised
counters and formulae. Missing poor-performing cells can improve an apparent average. NCC should
therefore test the population of expected reporting elements, missing periods, duplicates, impossible
values and late corrections before judging service compliance.
More decimal places do not create accuracy. A precisely calculated result from a biased
sample or incomplete dataset remains unreliable.

What changed in the controlled ledger
Scope
The instrument states that it sets minimum quality and standards of service, associated
measurements and Key Performance Indicators for implementing, monitoring and managing
telecommunications Quality of Service. Its structure covers wireline, complaints, customer care,
mobile network generations, data and satellite services, colocation, a Quality of Service index,
Point-of-Interconnection indicators, major outages, reporting priority, definitions and change control.

Operator licence and approved
service offer

Business Rules can evolve without rewriting the entire regulatory architecture. The document

training slide or web snippet may therefore become obsolete even while the 2024 Regulations remain

Interpret comments and classifications
Some indicators are stated for compliance and others for monitoring. The rules also allow NCC

target, comment, formula, aggregation and exception together.

15.9 Quality of service index
Why create an index
Consumers and senior decision makers cannot interpret hundreds of technology-specific counters
easily. The 2026 Business Rules state that a Quality of Service Key Performance Indicator Index will
combine published indicators for voice, data and messaging across second-, third-, fourth- and
fifth-generation networks into a more comprehensible performance measure.
An index is designed, not discovered
Select indicators that represent important service dimensions.
Normalise unlike units such as percentages, milliseconds and megabits per second.
Set direction so higher values consistently mean better or worse performance.
Weight services, technologies, locations and indicators transparently.

Treat missing data without rewarding non-reporting.
Aggregate only after preserving drill-down to the original measures.
Validate whether the result tracks consumer and engineering reality.
Publish methodology, limitations and change history.
The masking problem
A high overall score could conceal poor rural data service if urban voice performance carries greater
sample weight. One excellent indicator can offset a critical failure if the index permits compensation.
NCC should use the index as a navigation and communication tool, while retaining threshold
compliance for underlying indicators.

15.10 Power, fibre and shared infrastructure
Power availability
A radio site needs continuous electrical power for radios, transmission, cooling and control. Grid
failure may be bridged by batteries and generators, but fuel logistics, theft, battery degradation and
maintenance affect resilience. The 2026 rules include colocation-provider power-availability targets of
at least 99.50 percent at terminal sites and 99.80 percent at hub sites, with the specified treatment for
weighting.
Mean Time to Repair
Mean Time to Repair is an average restoration duration under the prescribed population and method.
The current rules list a colocation-provider target of no more than 2.5 hours. An average can hide a
small number of extremely long outages; incident distribution and repeated failures should still be
examined.
Fibre cuts
A cut may arise from road construction, excavation, vandalism, theft, fire, flooding, poor route records
or defective work. One physical event can affect several licensees sharing the route. NCC should link
incident time, geographic path, affected sites, protection switching, restoration, customer impact and
notifications.

15.11 Major outages and incident control
Major outage is more than a long fault
Severity can depend on affected sites, subscribers, geography, critical services, duration, technology
and cascading risk. The August 2026 Business Rules include an escalation matrix based on numbers
of impacted sites and a framework for classification, reporting and publication. Staff should consult
the exact current table rather than memorise a single generic definition.
The incident lifecycle
Detect through alarms, reports or external notification.
Validate scope and establish an incident commander and contacts.
Contain the failure and activate redundancy or emergency measures.
Notify NCC and consumers through the prescribed channels.
Restore service safely and progressively.
Reconcile affected sites, services, subscribers and duration.
Perform root-cause analysis, not merely symptom description.
Direct and verify preventive action.
Assess complaint, compensation and enforcement consequences.
Information quality during crisis
An early estimate can change. The record should distinguish observed facts, working hypotheses and
confirmed cause, each with timestamps. Operators should not wait for perfect certainty before
required escalation, but must correct material inaccuracies promptly.

15.12 Complaints as regulatory evidence
The complaint chain
The consumer normally approaches the service provider first under the applicable complaint process.
The provider authenticates the account, creates a ticket, investigates, communicates and resolves or
explains. Where escalation conditions are met, NCC examines the complaint and the provider's
handling. The regulator protects redress without becoming the operator's first-line call centre for every
ordinary case.
A complaint category is not a diagnosis
'Dropped call' can arise from radio weakness, handover, congestion, core failure, device behaviour or
interconnection. 'Data depletion' may involve legitimate usage, background applications, tariff
misunderstanding or billing error. The 2026 rules provide detailed complaint categories, first- and
second-level resolution treatment and remedies, but evidence must connect the category to cause.
Evidence   Question answered
Ticket and communication history   Was the complaint acknowledged, investigated and explained?
Account, tariff and charging records   Was the charge authorised and correctly calculated?
Cell and session records   What network conditions affected the user?
Device and application context   Could the endpoint explain part of the symptom?
Comparable complaints   Is this an isolated case or systemic hotspot?
Corrective-action proof   Was the promised remedy actually implemented?
Service-level time is a control, not the whole outcome
Closing a ticket within the target while the problem remains is not resolution. NCC should distinguish
response, feedback, technical restoration, financial correction and confirmed consumer outcome.
Reopening and repeat-contact rates can expose false closure.
Accessibility
Complaint channels should account for disability, language, literacy, rural connectivity and
compromised accounts. A consumer whose SIM has been taken over should not be forced to
authenticate only through that compromised number.

15.16 Level 10 application drills
Scenario 1 - Full bars, evening buffering
Strong signal and time-dependent degradation point away from a simple coverage gap. Compare cell
resource use, user throughput, backhaul utilisation, latency and night/day performance. Test multiple
services and nearby cells. If radio or transport capacity is confirmed, require a time-bound upgrade,
monitor interim performance and assess consumer-remedy conditions.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   177
Scenario 2 - Operator passes nationally but rural complaints rise
Disaggregate by Local Government Area, settlement type, technology, hour and sample density.
Compare missing-cell reporting and crowdsourced coverage. A national mean cannot extinguish local
obligations. Validate rural results independently, identify whether coverage, site availability or
capacity drives harm, and target the remedy.
Scenario 3 - Fibre cut cited for repeated outages
Verify each incident, route, restoration and affected site. Examine physical diversity, repeat location,
protection switching, contractor coordination and preventive measures. An external cut may explain
one event; repeated unmitigated exposure can reveal resilience failure. Separate enforcement
attribution from consumer restoration and compensation.
Scenario 4 - Fifth-generation latency target quoted as a universal promise
The 2026 Business Rules list fifth-generation latency of no more than one millisecond as monitoring
in the relevant table. Determine the measurement boundary and method. Do not promise every
end-to-end Internet application will respond in one millisecond or treat a monitoring item automatically
as an identical compliance sanction.
Scenario 5 - Complaint closed after an apology
An apology may satisfy a communication step but not correct persistent call failure. Check the
complaint category, service-level requirements, network evidence and whether the consumer can
now use the service. Repeated closure without correction should be treated as a systemic
complaint-management issue.
Scenario 6 - Dashboard suddenly improves
Before celebrating, test whether the formula, counter mapping, cell population, exclusion rule or
reporting completeness changed. Recalculate from raw data, compare version history and inspect
missing poor-performing cells. A methodological break must not be presented as an operational
achievement.

THE 45-SECOND MODEL ANSWER
Quality regulation ensures that licensed communications services are usable, measurable and
accountable. Coverage asks whether service reaches a place; capacity asks whether resources
handle demand; availability measures usable time; Quality of Service compares objective
indicators with applicable standards; and Quality of Experience examines actual user experience.
NCC combines operator counters, controlled tests, crowdsourced evidence, outages and
complaints, validates the data, diagnoses causes across power, radio, transport, core,
interconnection, device and application layers, then applies restoration, consumer remedy,
compliance or enforcement and verifies the result. The operative published framework as recorded
in the cited edition is the Quality of Service Regulations 2024 with Quality of Service Business
Rules Version 2 issued in August 2026.
