17.6 Sections 115-117 - the USP board
115 - Establishment and role
The Act establishes the Board to supervise and provide broad policy directions for management of
the Fund. The Secretariat serves as its Secretariat. The President constitutes the Board on the
Minister's recommendation; the Board must collaborate and consult with NCC and remains subject to
the Act.
116 - Eleven-member composition
Position   Number
Minister - Chairman   1
NCC Board Chairman -
Vice-Chairman
1
Commissioners   2
Representative of the Ministry   1
Representative of the Minister of
Finance
1
Representative of the Chairman,
National Planning Commission
1
Private-sector representatives   4
TOTAL   11
The President, acting on the Minister's recommendations, must ensure that the four private-sector
members are persons of integrity and professional standing who can contribute meaningfully. Their
appointment is subject to Senate confirmation.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   203
117 - Proceedings
The Board makes standing orders for meetings and may establish standing or ad hoc committees.
Committees may include capable persons beyond Board membership, but must be headed by Board
members. Committee decisions do not become binding until adopted and agreed by the Board.
2007 Regulations - selected governance rules
The Board is constituted when six of the eleven members have been appointed.
It holds an ordinary meeting at least once every calendar quarter.
Unless standing orders specify otherwise, quorum is six; tied votes are decided by the Chairman.
Members disclose direct and indirect communications-sector interests on appointment and annually.
A member must not vote where the member or immediate family has a relevant financial interest,
subject to the specified waiver framework.
Do not confuse the nine-member NCC Board with the eleven-member Universal Service
Provision Board.

17.7 Section 118 - the USP secretariat
Location and administration
The Secretariat resides in NCC and handles day-to-day administration of Universal Service Provision.
NCC must staff it with suitably qualified and experienced personnel, who may be seconded from NCC
and whose terms are comparable to Commission staff.
Ten statutory functions
Function   Operational meaning
Receive applications   Accept applications for loans and grants from eligible persons, including
community-based communications operators.
Review and recommend   Assess applications and recommend those to be funded to the Board.
Licensing liaison   Work with other NCC departments to process licences for funded
applications.
Technical/managerial assistance   Help recipients with matters such as vendors and billing systems.
Project evaluation   Assess performance and act to ensure expansion and service objectives are
met.
Quality enforcement   Enforce rural and underserved-area service standards set by the Board.
Collections   Collect assessments and loan repayments and pay repayments into the Fund.
Effectiveness evaluation   Assess whether Universal Service Provision meets Government and Board
policy goals.
Development coordination   Link funded activities with other infrastructure and development efforts.
Board/Fund Manager liaison   Coordinate institutional relationships between the Board and Fund Managers.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   204
2007 Regulations additions
The Regulations require NCC to establish and staff the Secretariat and appoint an NCC employee,
seconded full-time, as Secretary. The Secretariat prepares Operating Plans, recommends standing
orders and implementation procedures, coordinates with NCC and reports to the Commission.
Contracts and payment authorisations follow approved standing orders and Board-approved budgets,
and are executed in NCC's corporate name under the prescribed arrangement.
The Secretariat is not merely a project office. Its statutory functions combine funding assessment,
licensing coordination, recipient support, quality enforcement, collections, evaluation and
inter-institutional coordination.

17.8 Section 119 - independent fund managers
Appointment
The Board, in consultation with NCC, appoints an independent and competent
investment-management firm as Fund Managers. Under the 2007 Regulations, selection is public,
transparent and competitive; the Fund Managers report quarterly on the Fund's status.
Statutory functions
Function   Purpose
Maintain accounts and records   Preserve reliable financial information for the Fund.
Support collection   Collaborate with the Secretariat on assessments and loan repayments.
Estimate annual need   Determine funding required to sustain the rate of network expansion set for
policy objectives.
Calculate required revenue/rate   Protect fiscal soundness and derive corresponding assessment needs.
Disburse approved funds   Pay eligible entities based on Board approvals.
Invest cash reserves prudently   Balance investment return with short-term disbursement liquidity.
Report financial performance   Provide regular accountability to the Board.
Support effectiveness evaluation   Assist the Secretariat in judging policy-goal attainment.

17.9 Section 120 - regulation-making power
NCC may make regulations regarding licensee contributions to the Fund and matters related or
incidental to Universal Service Provision and establishment and operation of the Fund. The Universal
Access and Universal Service Regulations 2007 expressly cite sections 70 and 120 as their enabling
powers.
Role boundary
The Board provides policy direction and approvals; the Secretariat administers programmes and
projects; the independent Fund Managers manage the financial responsibilities assigned by law;
NCC provides regulatory authority and coordination. Overlap requires collaboration, not erasure of
roles.
Fund Managers do not select public-interest projects on personal commercial preference.
Disbursement follows eligible entities and Board approvals within the legal and
operating-plan framework.
NCC Promotion Study Guide   205

17.10 The 2007 regulations - twelve-part map
Part   Regulations   Exam theme
I   1-2   Objectives, application and scope.
II   3-21   Board establishment, functions, meetings,
tenure and conflicts.
III   22-26   Secretariat staffing, Secretary, functions,
contracts and reporting.
IV   27-33   Fund Manager appointment,
transparency, reporting and standing
orders.
V   34   Coordination between Board and
Commission.
VI   35-47   Programmes, projects, strategic and
annual Operating Plans, terms, scope
and analysis.
VII   48-61   Competitive selection, minimum-subsidy
auctions, eligibility, publicity, evaluation
and disqualification.
VIII   62-69   Selection documents, notice, proposals,
bonds, project agreement and licence.
IX   70-77   Financing, contributions/levy, surplus,
restrictions, accounts and investment.
X   78-81   Financial year, records, audit, annual
report and website.
XI   82   Transitional provision.
XII   83-85   Offences, interpretation and citation.
Operating-plan architecture
A programme is the multi-year macro initiative pursuing Universal Service Provision objectives; a
project is a specific micro-level implementation activity under a programme. The Secretariat prepares
a five-year Strategic Management Plan for Board approval and review. At least annually, it prepares
an Operating Plan, and the Board approves a plan directing Board and Fund Manager operations for
specified programmes and projects.
Competitive selection
The Regulations require competitive selection processes and expressly provide for minimum-subsidy
auctions. The logic is to award service obligations to a qualified bidder requiring the least support,
subject to the defined documents, evaluation, licence, project agreement, bid bond and performance
bond. Lowest subsidy does not remove qualification, quality or sustainability tests.
A Strategic Management Plan supplies multi-year direction; an Operating Plan authorises
and directs defined annual or periodic operations. They are not synonyms.
NCC Promotion Study Guide   206

17.11 Identifying the access gap
Begin with evidence
Access-gap analysis identifies places and groups where defined communications services are absent
or inadequate. Historical USPF work mapped clusters of information and communications technology
gaps, but the number and boundaries from an earlier study should not be quoted as the current
national position without a new verification.
Data layers
Layer   Contribution
Operator coverage and site data   Shows claimed infrastructure and technology reach.
Independent radio and service
measurement
Tests whether claimed coverage is usable.
Population and settlement data   Estimates people, institutions and geographic dispersion.
Fibre, power and road maps   Reveals cost and dependency constraints.
Affordability and income evidence   Shows whether nominal availability can become adoption.
Device, skills and usage data   Tests readiness for meaningful use.
Community and stakeholder input   Adds local demand, safety and operational knowledge.
Geographic information systems
A Geographic Information System can combine settlements, population, schools, health facilities,
coverage, sites, fibre and terrain. Each layer needs a date, owner, definition and confidence level. A
visually impressive map built from stale or incomparable layers can misdirect millions of naira.
Prioritisation
Rank potential interventions using severity of gap, population and vulnerable groups, critical
institutions, expected benefits, cost, readiness, complementarity and risk. Political visibility should not
replace transparent criteria. Similar communities should receive consistent treatment or a
documented reason for difference.
An operator's coverage polygon is evidence, not final proof of usable service. Validate
signal, quality, capacity and actual availability.
NCC Promotion Study Guide   207

17.12 Choosing the intervention
Diagnose before prescribing
Gap   Possible intervention
No radio infrastructure   Targeted base-station or shared rural access support.
Sites exist but lack backhaul   Fibre, microwave or satellite transport support.
Institution has no usable access   Connectivity plus local network, equipment, power and support.
Service exists but is unaffordable   Demand-side support, shared access or cost-reducing infrastructure.
Infrastructure exists but adoption is
low
Skills, awareness, relevant content, trust and device access.
Repeated outages   Power, redundancy, security and maintenance intervention.
Technology neutrality with practical judgment
The objective should be expressed in service outcomes rather than naming a favourite technology
without analysis. Fibre may offer high capacity but be slow or costly for a remote settlement. Satellite
can reach difficult terrain but has capacity, latency, terminal and recurring-cost considerations.
Microwave needs suitable paths and spectrum. Mobile coverage may be efficient where personal
access is the goal.
Shared and open infrastructure
Where public support creates a bottleneck asset, access conditions may prevent one operator from
capturing the benefit. Open-access obligations should define eligible users, capacity, price, quality,
expansion, non-discrimination and dispute resolution without undermining sustainable operation.
Anchor demand
A school, health facility, government office or business cluster can provide initial demand that
improves viability and supports surrounding service. The project should still show how the wider
community benefits rather than treating institutional connection as automatic universal impact.
Choose the least-cost sustainable intervention that closes the evidenced gap while preserving
competition, quality and future expansion.

17.13 Project lifecycle and procurement
From need to outcome
Define target population, service gap and baseline.
Develop options and business case, including do-nothing comparison.
Approve under strategic plan, annual plan and budget.
Specify outputs, service levels, sustainability and outcome indicators.
Procure transparently using suitable competition and qualification.
Mobilise with design, permits, community and security readiness.
Build under supervised milestones and change control.
Test technically and verify inventory, location and documentation.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   208
Commission service only after acceptance criteria are met.
Operate, maintain, monitor and support beneficiaries.
Evaluate adoption, quality, outcome and additionality.
Close, renew, transfer or redesign based on evidence.
A good Terms of Reference
The Terms of Reference or technical specification should state background, objective, scope,
locations, standards, deliverables, roles, dependencies, timetable, acceptance tests, service levels,
reporting, data ownership, cybersecurity, training, warranty, sustainability, payment milestones and
evaluation. Ambiguity at procurement becomes dispute during delivery.
Weak milestone   Stronger milestone
Equipment delivered   Serialised inventory delivered to verified sites, inspected and accepted.
Installation completed   Installed, powered, configured and passed defined functional tests.
Site connected   Service meets availability, throughput and user-access tests for stated period.
Training done   Named users trained, assessed and provided materials/support.
Project successful   Output, adoption, sustainability and outcome indicators meet targets.
Change control
Site substitution, equipment change, delay or scope variation requires documented reason, technical
and financial assessment, approval and updated baseline. An informal substitution can move service
away from the intended gap.
A completion certificate proves only what its acceptance criteria tested. It does not
automatically prove years of operation or socioeconomic impact.

17.14 Sustainability
The opening-day illusion
A commissioned centre can fail when subscription expires, batteries degrade, trained staff leave,
equipment is stolen or nobody owns maintenance. Sustainability must be designed before
procurement, not added after the launch ceremony.
Dimension   Control question
Financial   Who pays bandwidth, power, security, repairs and replacement after subsidy?
Technical   Are equipment, spares, skills and remote support available?
Institutional   Which organisation owns daily operation and decisions?
Community   Do beneficiaries value, protect and use the service?
Environmental   Can the power and equipment design survive local conditions?
Security   How are theft, vandalism, cyber threats and physical access controlled?
Vendor exit   Can another maintainer operate the system with available documentation?

NCC Promotion Study Guide   209
Total cost of ownership
Purchase price is only one part of cost. Include survey, civil works, energy, bandwidth, licences, staff,
maintenance, software, security, insurance, spares, refresh, disposal and monitoring. A cheaper
tender can become the most expensive failed project if recurrent costs are unfunded.
Ownership and incentives
The host institution needs authority, budget and benefit from keeping the asset working. Community
involvement can improve protection and relevance, but responsibility should not be vague.
Service-level agreements should identify fault channels, response, escalation and consequence.
Exit and transition
Define what happens when subsidy or contract ends: transfer, continued operator service,
replacement competition or decommissioning. Protect data, assets and beneficiaries during
transition.
Sustainability is the capacity to continue delivering the intended service and outcome after initial
installation and special project attention decline.

17.15 Monitoring and impact evaluation
Results chain
Level   Example
Input   Fund money, staff, spectrum, equipment and contractor time.
Activity   Survey, build, install, connect and train.
Output   Working sites, fibre kilometres, connected schools or access points.
Outcome   Reliable use, increased adoption, lower travel cost or improved digital service.
Impact   Improved education, productivity, inclusion or institutional performance
attributable in part to intervention.
Baseline and counterfactual
Measure conditions before intervention. To estimate impact, ask what would likely have happened
without the project. Commercial rollout already planned for the area weakens additionality.
Comparable untreated locations, phased rollout or credible trend analysis can strengthen evaluation.
Monitoring dimensions
Asset exists at the approved coordinates and matches inventory.
Service is available and meets quality targets over time.
Intended beneficiaries can access it at the represented price.
Usage is genuine rather than test traffic created for inspection.
Faults are logged, restored and prevented from recurring.
Training, support and safeguarding arrangements work.
Expenditure reconciles to verified milestones and assets.
Outcomes are disaggregated by location, gender, disability and relevant target groups.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   210
Independent verification
Use geotagged evidence, remote telemetry, unannounced visits, beneficiary confirmation, network
tests, financial audit and sample inspection. Photographs alone can be staged or outdated. Every
exception should create an owned action and closure evidence.
Counting installed computers measures output, not meaningful use or learning impact.

17.16 Programme families and status
Access and connectivity programmes
Official USPF material groups work broadly around access and connectivity. Historical programmes
have included rural infrastructure, school and tertiary-institution knowledge centres, community
access, backbone or connectivity support and initiatives for persons with disabilities or other target
groups. Names, quantities and operational status must be attached to the specific plan and reporting
year.
Intervention family   Primary learning point
Rural network infrastructure   Supply-side support can extend coverage where the business case is weak.
School knowledge centre   Equipment alone is insufficient; bandwidth, power, teachers, content and
safeguarding matter.
Tertiary-institution connectivity   High-capacity access needs campus distribution, support and sustained
subscription.
Community access facility   Shared access can serve people without personal devices but needs an
operating model.
Backbone/backhaul support   Transport can unlock many downstream services if access is open and
capacity adequate.
Accessibility intervention   Technology and training should respond to specific disability and usability
barriers.
Current strategic-plan control
The official publications page lists a Revised Strategic Management Plan 2023-2027 as the current
plan. Older plans for 2007-2011, 2013-2017 and 2018-2022 are historical layers. Their project
concepts and lessons remain useful, but current priorities must be drawn from the revised plan and
current operating evidence.
Achievement wording
Say 'the annual report recorded installation or completion in that year' unless current operational
verification proves continued service. Initiative, award, delivery, commissioning, operation, adoption
and impact are separate claims.
Historical project names are exam-relevant, but a Level 10 answer controls date and status
instead of presenting an old programme count as today's position.
NCC Promotion Study Guide   211

17.17 Internal digital project control
Integrated project record
Record   Critical links
Gap and beneficiary   Coordinates, baseline, target group, institutions and evidence.
Approval and budget   Plan objective, decision, funding source and cost ceiling.
Procurement   Tender, evaluation, bidder, contract, securities and conflict declarations.
Deliverable   Specification, milestone, evidence, inspection and acceptance.
Asset   Serial number, location, custodian, warranty, status and disposal.
Service   Provider, bandwidth, tariff, availability, faults and renewal.
Payment   Invoice, certificate, deductions, approvers and reconciliation.
Outcome   Usage, beneficiary feedback, quality, sustainability and impact.
Prevent duplicate intervention
Connect the project system to coverage maps, prior projects, schools, health facilities and
government programmes. A request should flag an existing asset or planned commercial rollout.
Where another programme already supplies connectivity, funding may target power, devices, skills or
resilience rather than duplicate links.
Workflow and audit
Use role-based access, maker-checker approval, versioned documents, geospatial validation,
milestone dependency, electronic signatures, exception queues and immutable audit. Payment
should not proceed because a document is uploaded; the system must confirm authorised
certification and required preceding acceptance.
Monitoring dashboard
Show operational status, quality, utilisation, faults, recurrent-cost expiry, warranty, security incidents,
outstanding actions and outcome indicators. Separate contractor-reported and independently verified
values. A map pin should open the evidence and history behind it.
Project-management software cannot compensate for unclear ownership, weak acceptance
criteria or false data. Governance and verification remain primary.

17.18 Level 10 application drills
Scenario 1 - Connected school, no usage
Verify power, bandwidth, local network, devices, teacher capability, timetable, content, safeguarding
and fault history. Installation may be complete while adoption failed. Assign corrective actions,
redesign support and evaluate whether the intervention still fits the school's needs.
Scenario 2 - Community is marked covered but cannot connect
Compare operator polygon with independent signal, terrain, indoor/outdoor tests, technology,
capacity and available tariff. Coverage may exist only at the edge or on an unsuitable technology.
Correct the gap map and choose optimisation, new site, shared access or another proportionate
remedy.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   212
Scenario 3 - Lowest bidder cannot sustain service
Review qualification, lifecycle cost, financial capacity, operating plan and bid assumptions. Protect
continuity through contract remedies and lawful procurement action. Future evaluation should test
total cost and sustainable delivery, not price alone.
Scenario 4 - Project near commercial rollout
Determine what the operator had committed, financed and scheduled before the subsidy. Funding
should create additional coverage or quality, not pay for inevitable deployment. Consider another
gap, expanded scope or competitive open-access conditions.
Scenario 5 - Equipment exists only during inspection
Use serialised inventory, unannounced visit, telemetry, user logs and custodian confirmation.
Investigate substitution or diversion, suspend unsupported payment, preserve evidence and apply
contractual or enforcement remedies with fair process.
Scenario 6 - Fibre works but recurring fee expires
This is a sustainability-design failure. Identify the service owner, budget and contract; preserve
essential use temporarily where lawful; establish a viable operating model and incorporate
recurrent-cost verification into future approval.

17.19 Exam traps and model answer
Trap   Correct position
Universal access and universal
service are identical.
Access can be shared/community availability; service moves toward individual
availability under defined policy.
Coverage equals meaningful
connectivity.
Affordability, device, skills, quality, safety and relevance remain.
Every rural project deserves subsidy.   Evidence must show gap, additionality, value and sustainability.
Fund money belongs to operators.   It is a controlled statutory resource used for authorised public objectives.
Lowest capital cost is best value.   Total lifecycle cost, quality, risk and outcomes matter.
Delivery equals completion.   Installation, acceptance, commissioning and operation are separate.
Commissioning equals impact.   Adoption, sustained use and outcomes require evidence.
Historical project counts are current
facts.
Attach each number to its reporting date and status.
Technology should be chosen first.   Define the service gap and outcome before selecting the solution.
Photographs prove operation.   Use telemetry, tests, users, financial records and independent verification.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   213
THE 45-SECOND MODEL ANSWER
Universal access and universal service policy addresses communications gaps that commercial
markets may not close despite high social value. The Nigerian Communications Act 2003
establishes the Universal Service Provision Fund and its governance architecture, supported by
the 2007 Regulations and current strategic plans. Effective intervention begins with evidence of an
unserved or underserved population, selects a technology-neutral and competition-conscious
response, procures transparently, verifies outputs and funds only supported milestones. Success
is not equipment delivery: service must be affordable, accessible, reliable, adopted, sustainable
and linked to measurable outcomes. The Fund should monitor assets, quality, use, finances and
impact, preserve audit trails and redesign or enforce where projects fail.

17.20 Exam application and traps
Scenario 1 - Board confusion
A candidate states that the Universal Service Provision Board has nine members because the NCC
Board has nine. Correct the institutional distinction and reconstruct the eleven-member composition:
Minister, NCC Board Chairman, two Commissioners, three specified governmental representatives
and four private-sector representatives.
Scenario 2 - Fund merged with NCC operating account
Section 114 requires total separation from the Commission's Fund, transparent operation, annual
independent audit, presentation to the National Assembly and publication. Direct immediate
segregation, reconciliation, access control and audit; investigate authority and prevent recurrence.
Scenario 3 - Secretariat acts as network operator
Section 112(2) prevents a universal-service organ from constituting itself as a communications
service provider. The Secretariat should design, support, monitor and coordinate funded provision
through eligible and properly licensed actors.
Scenario 4 - Grant awarded without competitive process
Test the 2007 Regulations' competitive-selection requirements, eligibility, publicity, evaluation
evidence, any lawful exception and fair treatment. Project urgency does not create an undocumented
procurement power.
Scenario 5 - Historical plan cited as current
Plans for 2007-2011, 2013-2017 and 2018-2022 are historical. The official publications register
identifies the Revised Strategic Management Plan 2023-2027 as the current plan layer as recorded in
the cited edition. A plan proves direction, not completion of every contemplated project.
Trap   Correct answer
Fund established under section 112   Section 112 designs the system; section 114 establishes the Fund.
Section 113 establishes the Board   Section 113 defines gap categories; section 115 establishes the Board.
The Board operates the network   Universal-service organs must not constitute themselves as service providers.
Secretariat is outside NCC   Section 118 places it within NCC.
Only licensee levies fund the Fund   Sources also include appropriations, gifts, loans, aids and accruing assets.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   214
Trap   Correct answer
Committee decisions bind
immediately
They require adoption and agreement by the Board.

17.21 Section-linked recall bank
Prompt   Exam-standard answer
What does section 112 do?   Requires NCC to consider, design and determine a system promoting
widespread availability and usage of network and application services.
What does section 113 add?   Requires definitions of institutions, unserved/underserved areas and groups
using the stated statutory considerations.
Which section establishes the Fund?   Section 114.
Which section establishes the Board?   Section 115.
How many Board members?   Eleven.
Who chairs and vice-chairs?   Minister chairs; NCC Board Chairman is Vice-Chairman.
How many private-sector
representatives?
Four, subject to the statutory integrity, standing and confirmation framework.
What does section 117 cover?   Board proceedings and committees; committee decisions require Board
adoption.
Where does the Secretariat reside?   Within NCC under section 118.
Who appoints Fund Managers?   The Board, in consultation with NCC, under section 119.
What does section 120 permit?   NCC regulations on licensee contributions and matters relating or incidental to
Universal Service Provision and the Fund.
Memory spine
112 DESIGN - 113 DEFINE - 114 FUND - 115 BOARD - 116 MEMBERS - 117 PROCEED - 118
ADMINISTER - 119 MANAGE MONEY - 120 REGULATE.
Short-answer marking structure
Start with the statutory section and actor.
State the operative duty or institution accurately.
Explain why it matters in ordinary language.
Connect it to implementation, evidence or governance.
Add a controlled current/historical distinction where relevant.
Avoid unsupported project statistics or current personnel names unless specifically verified.
NCC Promotion Study Guide   215

Chapter 18
Cybersecurity, resilience and critical
infrastructure
Communications services depend on information systems and physical infrastructure. Cybersecurity
prevents and responds to digital harm; resilience preserves essential service through failures, attacks
and recovery.

18.1 Why communications cyber resilience matters
Communications infrastructure is both a service and an enabling layer for banking, emergency
response, government, energy, transport, education and ordinary social life. A failure can therefore
cascade far beyond one operator. The regulatory objective is not zero risk—an impossible
promise—but risk reduced to a defensible level, rapid detection, controlled continuity and accountable
recovery.
Dependency   Possible consequence of communications failure
Emergency services   Calls, location and dispatch coordination may be delayed.
Financial services   Authentication messages, point-of-sale links and mobile transactions may fail.
Government   Public portals, identity services and inter-agency coordination may be
impaired.
Businesses   Cloud access, logistics, customer support and payments may stop.
Citizens   Voice, data, information and access to digital services may be lost.
Other operators   Interconnection, roaming, shared towers, landing stations or upstream
providers may transmit impact.
Threat, vulnerability, likelihood and impact
A threat is a potential cause of harm: a criminal group, malicious insider, software flaw, fire, flood or
cable cut. A vulnerability is a weakness that can be exploited or triggered. Risk combines the
likelihood of the event with its consequence. A control reduces likelihood, impact or both. An incident
is an event that actually or potentially compromises security or service.
Safety and security convergence
A fibre cut caused by excavation is not necessarily a cyberattack, yet weak route diversity can make
its service impact resemble one. A compromised building-management system can disable cooling
and take network equipment offline. Resilience therefore integrates cyber, physical, power,
environmental and operational dependencies.
Risk appetite and criticality
Organisations may accept limited risk in a non-critical test system but not in subscriber identity,
emergency routing or national interconnection. Criticality should determine stronger architecture,
monitoring, recovery and assurance. Risk acceptance must be explicit, authorised, time-bound and
supported by evidence—not created silently by backlog.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   216
The regulator asks not only 'Was the operator attacked?' but 'Was the risk reasonably governed,
was critical service protected, was reporting timely, and were lessons implemented?'

18.2 Governance and the three lines
Cyber risk is a business and regulatory risk expressed through technology. The governing body
approves direction and risk appetite; executive management assigns resources and accountability;
operational teams own systems and controls; independent assurance tests whether governance
works.
Layer   Responsibility
Governing body/Board   Oversight, appetite, major investment, material incident awareness and
accountability.
Executive management   Translate direction into policy, ownership, funding, prioritisation and
consequence.
First line   Network, application, data and service owners operate controls and manage
risk daily.
Second line   Security, risk, compliance and privacy functions set frameworks, advise,
challenge and monitor.
Third line   Internal audit independently assesses design and operating effectiveness.
External assurance/regulator   Test specified obligations, evidence, sector risk and public-interest outcomes.
Essential governance artefacts
Approved cybersecurity and resilience policy architecture.
Current inventory of assets, services, information, owners and dependencies.
Risk register with treatment, accountable owner, due date and residual risk.
Service criticality and business-impact assessment.
Security architecture, standards and controlled exceptions.
Incident-response, crisis-management, business-continuity and disaster-recovery plans.
Supplier-security and assurance programme.
Metrics that reveal exposure and control effectiveness, not merely activity.
Exercise, audit, vulnerability and incident findings with closure evidence.
Segregation of duties
One person should not request, approve and implement privileged access or deploy unreviewed code
to a critical system. Where staffing makes full separation difficult, compensating
controls—independent review, logging, time limitation and alerting—must be documented.
Cybersecurity culture
Annual awareness slides are insufficient. Training should match roles: engineers need secure
configuration; executives need crisis decisions; procurement needs supplier clauses; customer-care
staff need social-engineering resistance; developers need secure design; all personnel need
reporting channels and consequences.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   217
A signed policy proves approval, not operation. Ask for configuration, logs, samples, tests,
exceptions and evidence that failures are corrected.

18.3 Know the assets, services and dependencies
An organisation cannot protect what it does not know it owns or depends upon. The inventory must
go beyond laptops. It should connect business services to applications, databases, network functions,
physical sites, cloud resources, identities, suppliers, data flows, power and transmission.
Inventory object   Important fields
Service   Owner, users, criticality, tolerance, dependencies and regulatory obligations.
Hardware/virtual asset   Identifier, location, custodian, configuration, support status and network zone.
Software   Version, licence, owner, vulnerabilities, interfaces and end-of-support date.
Information asset   Classification, purpose, lawful basis, location, retention and recovery need.
Identity   Person/service, privilege, approver, authentication, expiry and recent use.
Supplier   Service, data/access, subcontractors, location, recovery and exit dependency.
Crown jewels
Crown jewels are systems or data whose compromise would cause exceptional service, security,
legal or public harm. In communications they may include subscriber identity platforms, core-network
control, signalling, domain-name and routing functions, billing and recharge, emergency routing,
lawful-interception environments, privileged management systems and recovery infrastructure.
Classification must follow the operator's architecture rather than a generic list.
Data flow and trust boundary
Map where data originates, which interfaces transform it, where it crosses between trust zones,
where it is stored and who can retrieve it. An apparently internal application may receive internet
traffic through an application-programming interface or vendor tunnel. The boundary determines
authentication, filtering, encryption, logging and monitoring.
Legacy and end-of-support technology
Legacy equipment may be operationally stable yet lack security updates. Treatment may include
isolation, strict access, application allow-listing, enhanced monitoring, spare strategy and time-bound
replacement. 'It still works' is not evidence that risk is acceptable.
Configuration baseline
A secure baseline specifies permitted services, ports, protocols, accounts, logging and hardening.
Approved deviations need a reason, owner, compensating controls and expiry. Continuous
configuration comparison is stronger than an annual snapshot.
Build the dependency map from service outcome backwards. A redundant application is not
resilient if both copies depend on the same database, administrator, power feed or cloud region.

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.topic: 18.3 Know the assets, services and dependencies
metadata.section: 18.3 Know the assets, services and dependencies

chunks.content:
18.4 Identity, access and privilege
Most critical actions are performed through identities: employees, contractors, applications, devices
and automated services. Identity and Access Management ensures that the correct identity receives
the minimum necessary access for the minimum necessary time, and that its actions are traceable.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   218
Control   Purpose
Joiner-mover-leaver process   Create, change and remove access as employment or role changes.
Least privilege   Restrict permissions to what the task requires.
Multi-factor authentication   Reduce reliance on a stolen password.
Privileged access management   Vault, approve, time-limit, monitor and record powerful sessions.
Periodic recertification   Make owners confirm continuing need and remove accumulation.
Service-account control   Assign ownership, rotate secrets and prohibit interactive misuse.
Break-glass access   Allow emergency privilege with tight logging and after-action review.
Authentication is not authorisation
Authentication establishes who or what an identity claims to be. Authorisation determines what it may
do. A validly authenticated customer-care agent should not automatically read unrestricted call
records; a vendor should not administer every network because its account uses multi-factor
authentication.
Zero Trust
Zero Trust is a design principle: do not grant broad trust merely because a request originates inside
the network. Continuously evaluate identity, device, context, resource and policy; segment access;
verify explicitly; and assume breach. It is not one product and does not eliminate sound architecture.
Insider risk
Insider incidents may be malicious, negligent or coerced. Controls include screening proportionate to
role, conflict disclosure, segregation, monitoring, data-loss prevention, protected reporting, leave and
exit processes, and rapid credential revocation. Monitoring must remain lawful and proportionate.
Shared administrator accounts destroy accountability. Where a technical platform still
requires one, control checkout through a privileged-access system and attribute each
session to an approved individual.

18.5 Network, application and data security
Defence in depth uses several independent or complementary controls so that one failure does not
become total compromise. Prevention, detection, containment and recovery should exist across
network, endpoint, application, identity, data and physical layers.
Layer   Representative controls
Network   Segmentation, firewalls, secure routing, denial-of-service protection,
encrypted management and anomaly monitoring.
Endpoint/server   Hardening, patching, endpoint detection, application control and protected
administration.
Application   Threat modelling, secure coding, code review, dependency scanning, testing
and release control.
Data   Classification, encryption, access control, loss prevention, retention and
secure disposal.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   219
Layer   Representative controls
Email/web   Filtering, sender authentication, domain protection, sandboxing and user
reporting.
Operations   Change control, backup, logging, monitoring, incident response and tested
recovery.
Segmentation
Segmentation limits an attacker's movement. Subscriber-facing services, office users, network
management, vendors, laboratories, backups and security tools should not form one flat trust zone.
Rules must be based on required flows, reviewed and tested; a diagram without enforced controls is
decoration.
Patch and vulnerability management
Discover assets, identify vulnerabilities, validate exposure, prioritise by exploitability and service
impact, remediate, test and verify closure. A high technical score on an isolated laboratory device
may be less urgent than an actively exploited weakness on an internet-facing management system.
Unsupported assets require explicit treatment.
Secure development and interfaces
Applications should validate input, protect secrets, authenticate interfaces, restrict output, log critical
events and fail safely. Application-programming interfaces need inventory, ownership, rate limits,
schema validation, access control and version retirement. A hidden interface is not a secured
interface.
Encryption and key management
Encryption protects data in transit and at rest only if algorithms, keys, certificates and endpoints are
controlled. Manage generation, storage, access, rotation, revocation, expiry and recovery. An expired
certificate can cause a major outage; a stolen private key can undermine trust.
Availability is part of cybersecurity. A control that blocks legitimate nationwide traffic may protect
confidentiality while causing unacceptable service harm.

18.6 Supply-chain and cloud risk
A communications provider can outsource a service but not its accountability. Managed-service
providers, equipment vendors, software libraries, tower companies, cloud platforms and maintenance
contractors can introduce privileged access and concentration risk.
Lifecycle stage   Required discipline
Due diligence   Assess ownership, competence, control maturity, location, subcontractors,
incidents and financial resilience.
Contract   Specify security, audit, notification, evidence, data use, recovery,
subcontracting, vulnerability and exit duties.
Onboarding   Approve identities, routes, devices, data and access periods; establish
contacts and logging.
Operation   Monitor service, privileges, changes, vulnerabilities, incidents and assurance
findings.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   220
Lifecycle stage   Required discipline
Change   Reassess new subcontractor, hosting region, interface, product or ownership.
Exit   Revoke access, return/delete data, transfer knowledge, preserve records and
ensure continuity.
Software supply chain
A trusted update or library can carry malicious code or a vulnerable dependency. Maintain
software-component visibility, verify source and signature, scan dependencies, protect build
pipelines, restrict signing keys and test updates before critical deployment. A Software Bill of
Materials can improve visibility but does not by itself prove security.
Cloud shared responsibility
The provider secures some underlying infrastructure; the customer remains responsible for
configured identities, data, applications and services according to the model. Misconfigured storage
or excessive cloud permissions are not transferred away by the hosting contract. Recovery must
address region failure, account compromise and provider exit.
Concentration and systemic risk
Several operators may rely on the same cloud, fibre route, power provider, vendor remote-access
platform or signalling supplier. Each may appear redundant internally while the sector shares one
hidden point of failure. NCC's sector view should examine correlated dependencies and feasible
diversification.
A certification or audit report is useful evidence, not a transfer of responsibility. Define
scope, date, exclusions, tested controls and unresolved findings.

18.7 Detect, log and understand
Prevention will sometimes fail. Detection depends on meaningful telemetry collected from critical
systems, synchronised in time, protected against alteration and analysed by people and tools that
understand normal behaviour.
Log source   What it may reveal
Identity systems   Failed login, privilege change, impossible travel and dormant-account use.
Network/security devices   Unexpected flows, denied traffic, scanning and denial-of-service patterns.
Endpoints/servers   Malware, process execution, persistence and administrative actions.
Applications/databases   Fraud, abnormal queries, record changes and interface abuse.
Cloud platforms   Configuration, key use, public exposure and control-plane activity.
Physical access   Entry to sites, equipment rooms and sensitive consoles.
Security operations
A Security Operations Centre monitors, validates and escalates alerts. Effectiveness depends on
coverage, use cases, baselines, threat intelligence, skilled analysts, runbooks, escalation and
feedback. A large alert count may indicate visibility—or poorly tuned noise that hides real incidents.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   221
Detection engineering
Translate threats into observable behaviours: credential dumping, unusual signalling commands,
configuration change, mass data retrieval or disabled logging. Test whether the required telemetry
exists, whether the rule alerts, whether analysts recognise it and whether response begins in time.
Retention and integrity
Logs must be retained for operational, investigative, regulatory and legal needs under the applicable
schedule. Limit access, synchronise clocks, centralise where appropriate, protect against deletion
and document chain of custody. Excessive indiscriminate retention creates cost and privacy risk.
Threat intelligence
Useful intelligence is timely, relevant and actionable. Indicators may help block known infrastructure;
tactics and techniques help design durable detection. Information-sharing must protect source,
confidentiality and personal data while enabling sector defence.
Mean time to detect is not enough. Measure whether critical assets are visible, alerts are accurate,
containment is timely and lessons reduce recurrence.

18.8 Incident response and NCC-csirt
NCC maintains a sectoral computer security incident response capability known as NCC-CSIRT for
coordination of cybersecurity incidents in the communications sector. This sector role should be
distinguished from an operator's internal response team and from national coordination by the
national Computer Emergency Readiness and Response Team.
Phase   Key actions
Prepare   Roles, contacts, tools, playbooks, authority, exercises, backups and evidence
readiness.
Identify   Validate event, scope affected assets/data/services, establish severity and
open an incident record.
Contain   Limit spread and harm while preserving essential service and evidence.
Eradicate   Remove malicious presence, close exploited weakness and verify affected
environment.
Recover   Restore clean service in controlled stages; monitor for recurrence and validate
integrity.
Learn   Establish root causes, decisions, impact, reporting, corrective actions and
tracked closure.
Severity and materiality
Classification should consider affected service, geography, subscribers, data, critical functions,
duration, safety, attacker capability, propagation, regulatory impact and public confidence. Technical
complexity alone does not equal severity: a simple configuration error can cause national outage.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   222
Reporting
The Cyber-Resilience Framework and July 2026 Guidance Note establish the sector-specific
reporting layer. Operators should use the operative definitions, channels, templates and timelines for
immediate or periodic reporting. Do not memorise an unverified number from a summary:
examination and operational answers should distinguish initial notification, update, final/root-cause
report and quarterly sector reporting where prescribed.
Coordination does not erase ownership
The affected provider remains responsible for containment, service continuity, evidence and
consumer impact. NCC/NCC-CSIRT coordinates sector awareness and regulatory oversight; national
security, law enforcement, data protection and other bodies may have distinct statutory roles.
Reporting to one body does not automatically satisfy every obligation.
Communications during incident
Use verified facts, approved spokespersons and audience-specific messages. State known impact,
protective action and update time without disclosing details that aid attackers. Preserve every public
statement and correct material error promptly.
Do not delay notification until every fact is proven. Initial reports can state what is known,
unknown, being done and when the next update will follow, under the operative rule.

18.9 Business continuity, disaster recovery and backup
Incident response manages the event. Business continuity keeps priority activities operating. Disaster
recovery restores technology. Crisis management directs strategic decisions and stakeholder
consequences. The plans must connect but are not synonyms.
Measure   Meaning
Maximum tolerable disruption   Longest interruption the organisation can bear before unacceptable harm.
Recovery Time Objective   Target time to restore a service after disruption.
Recovery Point Objective   Maximum tolerable data loss measured in time.
Minimum business continuity
objective
Minimum acceptable level of service during disruption.
Recovery time capability   Demonstrated—not promised—time achieved by architecture and tests.
Resilient architecture
Use diversity appropriate to criticality: power, transmission, sites, regions, hardware, software,
suppliers and operational teams. Redundancy is illusory where both paths share the same duct,
exchange, cloud account or control plane. Capacity during failover must support priority traffic.
Backup principles
Define systems, data, configuration and keys required for recovery.
Use multiple copies and media/locations appropriate to threat.
Maintain an offline or immutable copy against ransomware.
Encrypt and tightly control backup administration.

metadata.topic: 18.9 Business continuity, disaster recovery and backup
metadata.section: 18.9 Business continuity, disaster recovery and backup

chunks.content:
NCC Promotion Study Guide   223
Monitor completion and investigate failed jobs.
Test restoration, application consistency and usable recovery—not merely backup status.
Protect retention, disposal and legal holds.
Recovery sequence
Identity, network control, name services, databases, applications and interfaces have dependencies.
Restoring them in the wrong order can create corruption or unsafe access. Runbooks should state
prerequisites, decision authority, integrity checks, reconciliation and rollback.
Exercises
Tabletop exercises test decisions and communication; technical simulations test tools and
procedures; failover tests demonstrate capability; red-team exercises test adversarial resilience.
Findings need accountable treatment and retest. An exercise that always succeeds on paper may be
testing courtesy, not readiness.
A backup is not a recovery capability until clean data can be restored within the required time and
the business service functions correctly.

chunks.content:
18.10 Cnii - critical national information infrastructure
Critical National Information Infrastructure comprises designated computer systems, networks, data
and associated infrastructure whose incapacity or destruction would seriously affect national security,
the economy, public health or safety, or essential services. The 2024 Designation and Protection
Order operationalises the Cybercrimes Act framework and includes communications/digital
infrastructure within Nigeria's protected critical sectors.
Designation is not merely a label
The operator must identify which critical services and supporting assets fall within the applicable
designation and protection framework, map dependencies, apply enhanced risk controls, coordinate
with competent authorities and preserve evidence of compliance. Not every office printer becomes
CNII because the organisation operates critical infrastructure.
Protection layer   Examples
Governance   Named accountable executives, risk acceptance, competent teams and
regulatory coordination.
Architecture   Segmentation, redundancy, secure management and elimination of single
points of failure.
Access   Strong authentication, privileged control, background/role checks and rapid
revocation.
Monitoring   Continuous visibility, tamper-resistant logs and priority threat detection.
Physical   Perimeter, entry control, surveillance, environment, power and route
protection.
Supply chain   Assurance, restricted remote access, component integrity, continuity and exit.
Response/recovery   Coordinated playbooks, priority restoration, reporting, exercises and
improvement.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   224
Telecommunications assets and vandalism
Physical attacks on fibre, towers, power and equipment can disrupt the same critical service
protected against cyberattack. Protection therefore needs route intelligence, lawful right-of-way
coordination, community engagement, surveillance, tamper detection, spares, rapid repair, alternate
routing and enforcement collaboration.
Proportional protection
Criticality does not justify unlimited collection or secrecy. Controls should be necessary, risk-based
and consistent with data protection, due process and lawful oversight. Public descriptions can explain
resilience objectives while restricting sensitive topology and vulnerability detail.
The CNII Order is not the Nigerian Communications Act and does not make NCC the sole
national cybersecurity authority. Explain the communications-sector role within the wider
national framework.

18.11 Data protection, evidence and regulatory oversight
Cybersecurity and data protection overlap but are not identical. Security protects systems and
information; data protection governs lawful and fair processing of personal data as well as security. A
secure database can still be unlawful if data was collected without proper purpose or retained
indefinitely.
Principle   Operational question
Purpose limitation   Why is the personal data being processed?
Data minimisation   Is every collected field necessary?
Accuracy   Can errors be corrected before they cause harm?
Storage limitation   When and how is data deleted or anonymised?
Security   Are access, transmission, storage and disposal adequately protected?
Accountability   Can the organisation demonstrate decisions and control operation?
Breach assessment
Determine what personal data and people are affected, sensitivity, volume, encryption, likely misuse,
vulnerable persons and containment. Apply the Nigeria Data Protection Act and current regulatory
guidance for notification and affected-person communication; cyber incident reporting to NCC does
not replace data-breach duties to the competent data-protection authority.
Digital evidence
Preserve original sources where possible; record who collected what, when, where and how; hash or
otherwise verify integrity; restrict access; work from forensic copies; document time zones and tools;
and maintain chain of custody. Emergency containment may take priority over perfect collection
where life or national service is at risk, but the decision and loss of evidence should be recorded.
NCC supervisory method
Identify the operative obligation and affected licence/service.
Obtain timely incident and impact information through lawful channels.

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.topic: 18.11 Data protection, evidence and regulatory oversight
metadata.section: 18.11 Data protection, evidence and regulatory oversight

chunks.content:
NCC Promotion Study Guide   225
Test service continuity, consumer harm and sector dependencies.
Review governance, control design and actual operation before the event.
Distinguish unavoidable attack sophistication from preventable control failure.
Coordinate with NCC-CSIRT and competent institutions without duplicating or exposing sensitive
evidence.
Require corrective actions, owners, deadlines, verification and proportionate enforcement.
Feed anonymised lessons and threat patterns into sector resilience.
The fact that an organisation was attacked is not proof of negligence; the fact that an attacker was
sophisticated is not proof of reasonable protection. Test obligations, risk, controls and evidence.

chunks.content:
18.12 Metrics, assurance and maturity
Useful metrics support a decision. Activity counts—alerts received, personnel trained or patches
installed—need outcome and risk context. A green dashboard built from incomplete asset coverage
can be more dangerous than an honest red finding.
Metric family   Examples and cautions
Exposure   Internet-facing assets, unsupported systems, critical vulnerabilities and
excessive privilege.
Prevention   Hardening compliance, patch coverage and blocked malicious activity; verify
denominator.
Detection   Critical telemetry coverage, alert fidelity, time to detect and adversary dwell
time.
Response   Time to contain, severity accuracy, reporting timeliness and playbook
effectiveness.
Recovery   Restoration time, recovery-point achievement, failover capacity and data
reconciliation.
Governance   Overdue high risks, expired exceptions, supplier findings and closure
verification.
Impact   Subscribers, services, geography, duration, data and financial/public-safety
consequence.
Key Risk Indicator versus Key Performance Indicator
A Key Risk Indicator signals changing exposure—for example, percentage of critical systems without
supported patches. A Key Performance Indicator measures process delivery—for example, average
remediation time. One can improve while risk worsens if the asset inventory expands or attackers
exploit a different path.
Assurance hierarchy
Management attestation: ownership statement, weakest when unsupported.
Control evidence review: configuration, logs and sampled transactions.
Technical testing: vulnerability assessment, penetration test, recovery or failover.
Independent audit/certification: useful within stated scope and date.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   226
Adversarial exercise: tests detection and response against realistic behaviour.
Regulatory inspection: links technical evidence to sector obligations and public impact.
Root cause
'Human error' is usually the starting point. Ask why one mistake could reach production, why review
or automation did not catch it, why monitoring did not alert, why recovery was slow and whether
workload, design or incentives encouraged failure. Correct systemic causes as well as the individual
action.
Closing a vulnerability ticket is not proof of remediation. Rescan, validate the configuration
or test the exploit path; then assess whether similar assets share the weakness.

18.13 Applied level 10 scenarios
Scenario 1 - Ransomware affects billing and customer care
Activate incident and crisis structures; isolate spread while preserving essential network operations;
protect identity and backups; determine data and service impact; notify through applicable sector and
data-protection channels; restore clean services in dependency order; reconcile billing; communicate
accurately; and verify root-cause actions.
Scenario 2 - Vendor account changes core configuration
Revoke and contain access, preserve session evidence, validate all changes, assess service and
signalling impact, rotate credentials and recover approved configuration. Investigate onboarding,
privilege, time limitation, monitoring, contract and supplier-control failure.
Scenario 3 - National outage after routine change
Treat impact, not maliciousness, as the first resilience concern. Roll back safely, invoke continuity,
report under the operative outage/cyber framework as applicable, establish why testing, approval,
segmentation and recovery failed, and correct similar change paths.
Scenario 4 - Subscriber database offered for sale
Validate without exposing more data; preserve evidence; investigate internal and external access;
contain credentials and interfaces; assess affected persons and fields; coordinate NCC,
data-protection and law-enforcement duties; notify lawfully; support consumers; and correct control
gaps.
Scenario 5 - Distributed denial-of-service attack
Engage upstream mitigation, rate controls and traffic engineering; protect priority services; distinguish
attack from legitimate surge; coordinate sector intelligence; provide updates; and review capacity,
architecture and provider dependencies after recovery.
Scenario 6 - Fibre routes repeatedly vandalised
Map shared physical dependencies, reroute traffic, prioritise restoration and public safety, coordinate
authorities and communities, improve route diversity and protection, and examine whether resilience
obligations were met. Physical cause does not remove cyber-resilience relevance.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   227
Scenario 7 - Backup reports green but restore fails
Escalate as a recovery-control failure; protect remaining copies; rebuild from verified sources;
document data loss; test application integrity; investigate scope, credentials, immutability and test
governance; and replace completion-rate reporting with recovery evidence.
MODEL ANSWER FORMULA
Critical service   →   threat/event   →   affected assets and dependencies   →   immediate
containment/continuity   →   legal and regulatory reporting   →   evidence and stakeholder protection   →
controlled recovery   →   root cause, corrective action and verification.
Prompt   Exam-standard response
Security versus resilience   Security reduces compromise; resilience anticipates, withstands, continues,
recovers and learns.
CIA triad   Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability.
NCC-CSIRT   NCC's sectoral incident-response capability for the communications sector.
CNII   Designated systems, networks, data and infrastructure whose disruption
would seriously affect essential national interests/services.
Incident response phases   Prepare, identify, contain, eradicate, recover and learn.
RTO/RPO   Target restoration time and maximum tolerable data loss in time.
Zero Trust   Verify explicitly, minimise privilege and assume breach; not a single product.
Defence in depth   Multiple protective, detective, containment and recovery layers.
Outsourcing rule   Service may be outsourced; regulatory accountability remains with the
regulated entity.
High-value distinctions
Do not confuse   Correct distinction
Event and incident   An event is an occurrence; an incident compromises or threatens
security/service under the applicable criteria.
Vulnerability and risk   Weakness versus likelihood-and-impact exposure in context.
Backup and disaster recovery   Protected copy versus tested restoration capability.
Business continuity and disaster
recovery
Continuing priority operations versus restoring technology.
NCC-CSIRT and operator SOC   Sector coordination versus internal monitoring and response.
Cyber reporting and data-breach
reporting
Separate duties may arise under sector and data-protection frameworks.
Compliance and security   Compliance is a required baseline; real risk can remain outside the checklist.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   228
Current-source control
For final examination memorisation, reconcile the February 2026 Cyber-Resilience Framework with
the July 2026 Guidance Note and any later NCC amendment, circular or reporting template. Verify
exact entity scope, standards mapping, maturity/assessment requirements, incident categories,
reporting periods and enforcement treatment from the official text. Preserve the 2021 national policy,
2024 CNII Order, amended Cybercrimes Act and Nigeria Data Protection Act as distinct but
connected authority layers.
A Level 10 officer does not reduce cyber resilience to antivirus or incident headlines. The officer
connects critical service, governance, architecture, people, suppliers, detection, continuity, lawful
reporting, evidence, consumer impact and verified improvement.
NCC Promotion Study Guide   229

Chapter 19
Mobile virtual networks and service business
models
Mobile service is a chain of functions, not a single indivisible business. An operator may concentrate
on customers, billing and specialised services while buying radio-network capacity from another
operator. Understanding that division connects licensing, competition, interconnection, numbering
and consumer responsibility.

19.1 What makes a mobile network virtual
A conventional mobile network operator operates a radio access network using authorised spectrum,
together with the transport, core and service arrangements needed to deliver service. A Mobile Virtual
Network Operator (MVNO) provides mobile services through an arrangement with a host network.
Virtual does not mean imaginary, unregulated or necessarily delivered only through an Internet
application. The customer still uses real radio equipment and network capacity. What changes is
which business owns or controls each function and which functions it buys wholesale.
Consider a hypothetical provider serving small agricultural businesses. It wants seasonal bundles,
local-language support and a payment arrangement suited to irregular income. Building a nationwide
radio network would require major investment before it could reach its first customer. Hosting can let
it concentrate on its service proposition. The host earns wholesale revenue from capacity, while the
virtual operator takes on the cost and risk of finding customers and running its authorised functions.
Whether the model is viable depends on wholesale prices, demand, integration costs and customer
retention; a licence alone does not create a profitable business.

chunks.content:
19.2 Follow one customer through the arrangement
At onboarding, the retail provider must ensure that the subscription is registered and activated under
the applicable rules. When the customer connects, the handset uses the host radio network.
Authentication and session handling follow the agreed technical architecture: some functions may
remain with the host and others may be controlled by a more capable virtual operator. Traffic then
reaches the called network or Internet destination through the appropriate core and interconnection
arrangements. Usage records support charging and reconciliation. Customer care must be able to
investigate the whole path even if the retail provider does not own every element.
A failed data session may therefore be a radio problem, a provisioning error, a subscriber-profile
mismatch, insufficient wholesale capacity or an application problem. The practical question is who
can see the evidence and who must act. A contract that promises good service without defining
measurements, access to fault information, escalation and restoration responsibilities leaves the
retail provider unable to fulfil its promise reliably.

19.3 The five-tier framework and the later draft rules
The published NCC licensing framework identifies five categories: Service Virtual Operator, Simple
Facilities Virtual Operator, Core Facilities Virtual Operator, Virtual Aggregator/Enabler and Unified
Virtual Operator. Increasing responsibility generally brings greater technical control and integration
obligations. The precise permissions remain those of the applicable framework, licence and
approvals. Source: NCC, Licence Framework for the Establishment of Mobile Virtual Network
Operators in Nigeria, section 4.2.
A separate public inquiry was announced for 16 July 2026 on Draft Business Rules for MVNO
licences. An inquiry and its report are stages of rule development; they do not by themselves prove
that the draft has become an operative final instrument. The tier explanations below preserve the
earlier guide’s draft-derived teaching distinctions and must not be read as a statement that every
proposed rule is in force. Source: NCC, Public Inquiry on the Draft Business Rules for Mobile Virtual
Network Operator Licences, 2026.
Tier   Teaching interpretation of the draft material
1: Service   A strongly hosted retail model; do not assume independent control over numbering,
switching or interconnection.
2: Simple facilities   Greater service-layer or subscriber-management capability does not automatically confer
independent core or interconnection authority.
3: Core facilities   More extensive core, switching and interconnection functions may be performed within
the authorised scope and approved integration.
4: Aggregator/enabler   Provides a platform or wholesale enabling arrangement for other virtual operators;
distinguish this from simply selling retail bundles.
5: Unified   Can combine authorised lower-tier capabilities; the label is not an exemption from
licence restrictions or host agreements.
The draft material in the baseline states that virtual operators do not own frequency spectrum
resources. Keep that proposition attached to its source status rather than treating a proposed clause
as an independent current legal prohibition. In every actual licensing decision, establish the granted
scope before deciding whether a particular architecture or use of infrastructure is permitted.

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.topic: 19.3 The five-tier framework and the later draft rules
metadata.section: 19.3 The five-tier framework and the later draft rules

chunks.content:
19.4 Wholesale access, cost and sustainable competition
Wholesale is the supply of network inputs to another provider; retail is the supply of services to the
end customer. The two prices perform different functions. A retail provider must recover the
wholesale input, its own customer acquisition and support costs, systems, compliance expenditure
and a sustainable margin. A cheap headline wholesale rate may be offset by minimum commitments,
integration charges, traffic restrictions or poor quality. Compare the complete arrangement rather
than a single unit price.
For illustration, assume a virtual operator receives N1,000 in retail revenue from a customer in a
month. Wholesale service costs N650 and its own variable costs are N180. The contribution is N170
before fixed overheads, taxes and other costs. If a new wholesale condition raises the first cost to
N800, contribution falls to N20. This arithmetic does not itself prove an anticompetitive practice: the
regulator would need to examine market power, costs, comparable arrangements, justification and
competitive effects. It does explain why host terms can determine whether retail competition is viable.

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.topic: 19.4 Wholesale access, cost and sustainable competition
metadata.section: 19.4 Wholesale access, cost and sustainable competition

chunks.content:
NCC Promotion Study Guide   231
A host may reasonably require accurate traffic forecasts, security testing and payment assurance.
These controls protect network operation. They become a regulatory concern when requirements are
unjustified, discriminatory or used to frustrate otherwise lawful access. Evidence should distinguish a
genuine capacity or security constraint from a commercial strategy to exclude a rival. The competition
chapter supplies that assessment method.

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master

chunks.content:
19.5 Onboarding, testing and acceptance
Implementation begins with a licensed service model and an agreed allocation of functions. The
parties then define interfaces, capacity, provisioning, subscriber data, charging records, fault
management and security responsibilities. A test environment allows defects to be corrected before
real customers depend on the arrangement. Acceptance should test the customer journey from
registration through usage, billing, complaint and termination, including failures and recovery rather
than only successful calls.
Technical visibility matters. If the retail provider cannot obtain relevant fault records or reconcile
wholesale usage with customer bills, it cannot diagnose complaints or control cost. Conversely,
unrestricted access to the host’s systems could expose other customers or commercially sensitive
information. Appropriate access is role-based, limited to the service need, logged and supported by
agreed response times. A successful test report establishes the tested conditions; it is not proof that
untested peak demand or failure modes will perform equally well.

19.6 Electronic SIMs, identity and consumer accountability
An embedded SIM, commonly called an eSIM, allows an authorised subscriber profile to be
provisioned electronically to compatible equipment. It changes the method of provisioning, not the
need to establish a lawful subscription. A downloaded profile must still be linked to valid registration,
activation controls, security and accountable records. A device capable of holding several profiles is
not the same as one subscription or one person.
The earlier draft material links remote onboarding to identity verification, fraud checks, audit trails and
record retention. These are also useful operational design questions: who verifies the person, who
authorises profile issuance, how are lost-device or replacement requests checked, and how can a
fraudulent change be investigated? Outsourcing a technical step does not automatically transfer the
regulated entity’s obligations. The host and virtual operator need an explicit responsibility map, with
consumer complaints routed to a party able to resolve them.
