Chapter 25
Compensation, leave and benefits
Pay, authorised absence and benefits are governed by specific eligibility conditions. Work through the
conditions and calculation base before applying a headline entitlement.
This section continues the employment journey by explaining how pay, authorised time away from
work and employee benefits operate under chapter 5 of the supplied handbook. The figures are the
handbook's figures. They are not a certification that no subsequent approved policy has changed
them. References use printed page numbers; numerical examples are illustrative and do not disclose
actual employee pay.

25.1 Understanding pay and eligibility
Salary compensates the employee for service in the assigned role. The handbook links salary and
other emoluments to grade, responsibilities, individual performance and applicable requirements. It
requires written notification of changes in salary or grade. Salary revision, a discretionary bonus,
reimbursement of an expense and a pension contribution are different transactions. They should not
be treated as interchangeable additions to take-home pay.
Section 5.2 says salary is paid monthly in arrears, no later than the 25th of each month. Where
payday falls on a holiday or weekend, payment is to occur on the preceding day. In arrears means
payment relates to service already rendered within the payment cycle; it does not mean an employee
is automatically owed an extra month's salary. The payslip identifies gross pay, deductions and net
pay.
Gross pay is the amount before deductions; net pay is the amount remaining after them. Basic salary
is a particular pay component, not a synonym for either total gross or net pay. This distinction matters
because the handbook calculates some benefits from basic salary and others from a broader
aggregate. Always identify the calculation base before applying a percentage.
Section 5.3 lists personal income tax, contributory pension, Commission loan repayments and
surcharges for loss or destruction of Commission property among payroll deductions. Although the
heading refers to statutory deductions, the items have different bases: a tax deduction is not the
same transaction as recovery of a staff loan. The handbook also reserves adjustments for
overpayment and specified malicious-damage cases. An examination calculation must identify which
deductions apply rather than assume every employee has every deduction.
For example, if hypothetical gross monthly pay is N500,000 and the question supplies total
deductions of N85,000, net pay is N415,000. This arithmetic does not establish the employee's basic
salary or the pensionable base. Those must be supplied separately if the question asks for a benefit
calculated from them.
Section

of N85,000, net pay is N415,000. This arithmetic does not establish the employee's basic
salary or the pensionable base. Those must be supplied separately if the question asks for a benefit
calculated from them.
Section 5.6 attaches benefits to eligibility. Full-time employees must qualify for the individual benefit;
part-time employees receive specifically designated benefits; temporary employees are described as
ineligible for benefits in this provision. Consequently, the existence of a benefit in the handbook is not
enough to determine a particular person's entitlement. Read the employment category, qualifying
conditions and approval requirements together.
Source: sections 5.1–5.3 and 5.6, printed pages 19–20.
NCC Promotion Study Guide   293

25.2 Bonuses, increments and salary reviews
Section 5.5 opens by describing the bonus as discretionary. It then describes an annual bonus of one
month's salary for permanent employees on the payroll at 31 December, with proportionate treatment
for less than one year's service and a minimum acceptable performance standard. Employees
subject to disciplinary action during the year may not be entitled. A careful answer preserves the
discretionary framing and the stated conditions rather than promising an unconditional thirteenth
payment to every employee.
A salary increment is separately described as an annual award that may be made at Management's
discretion based on the preceding year's performance assessment. A general salary review
addresses matters such as inflation, market pay and Federal Government pay-rate changes.
Promotion-related pay revision was addressed earlier. These processes can affect pay for different
reasons and need not occur together.
A candidate should therefore ask what event the question describes. An extra annual payment
concerns the bonus. Movement within a pay structure may concern an increment. A broad
adjustment to salary arrangements may concern a general review. Movement to a higher grade
engages the promotion provision. The handbook does not supply enough salary-scale data here to
calculate every one of these outcomes.
Source: sections 5.4–5.5, printed page 20. Payable overtime also requires prior explicit supervisor
approval and a designated eligible post, as explained in the employment chapter.

25.3 Annual leave: entitlement, scheduling and calculation
Leave is authorised absence for a recognised purpose. Before approval, suitable arrangements must
cover the role and business operations. Entitlement answers whether the employee qualifies;
scheduling identifies when leave can be taken; approval records permission for the proposed
absence. A leave balance in a portal does not by itself settle the latter two questions.
Section 5.7.1 applies annual leave to full-time, confirmed employees and refers to completion of 12
months' continuous service. The leave year runs from 1 February to 31 January. This differs from the
January-to-December calendar year, so an answer about the leave year must use the handbook's
dates.
The annual entitlement is 30 working days for Grade Level 7 and above, 21 working days for Grade
Levels 4–6, and 14 working days for Grade Level 3 and below. The handbook defines a workday as
excluding Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays. Thirty working days therefore does not mean 30
consecutive calendar days.
An annual roster is to be agreed at the beginning of the year. Leave should be taken as scheduled
unless operational demands prevent it. The text says leave cannot be accumulated and unused leave
within the year is forfeited. It does not provide an automatic carry-forward exception in this passage
for every operational postponement. A scenario involving an exception requires the applicable
approval or later policy, not an invented entitlement.
Promotion or demotion changes the applicable leave status from the time of the change. The text also
provides for proportionate calculation of leave or leave allowance from confirmation and specifically
refers to proportionate treatment where service in the earning period is less than six months. These
statements should not be reduced to the assertion that every new employee immediately receives a
full annual allocation.

25.4 Casual, compassionate and marriage leave
Casual leave may be granted for urgent matters after annual leave has been used. Section 5.7.2
provides seven days in a year with full pay, deductible from earned annual leave in the succeeding
year. The casual-leave passage says days, whereas the compassionate-leave passage expressly
says working days. Preserve that wording; do not casually add a unit that is absent from the particular
provision.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   295
Compassionate leave responds to critical emergencies, including natural disasters, accidents and
death in the family. The maximum is ten working days annually with full pay, and it is not deducted
from annual leave. The handbook includes permanent full-time employees whether confirmed or
unconfirmed. The reason for absence and its qualifying conditions determine which category applies.
If an eligible employee has used all annual leave and needs time for an urgent personal matter,
casual leave may be relevant, with its later deduction. If the facts concern a qualifying critical family
emergency, compassionate leave may be relevant, with no annual-leave deduction. Neither category
is an automatic extra block of annual holiday merely because the employee asks for it.
Marriage leave is five working days with pay, supported by proof of official marriage arrangements. It
can be granted only once to an employee. It should not be confused with compassionate leave or
assumed to renew every leave year.
Source: sections 5.7.2–5.7.3, printed page 22.

25.5 Maternity, antenatal and paternity provisions
The handbook provides six months' maternity leave with full pay and allowances, beginning not less
than one month before the expected delivery date. A medical certificate from a recognised healthcare
provider must confirm that date before leave starts. Expected delivery date means the date
established for planning from the medical evidence, not an officer's informal estimate.
For adoption, section 5.7.4 provides a different arrangement: a female employee adopting a baby
under four months may receive three months' leave with evidence of approval of the adoption. The
age of the child, documentation and duration are part of that particular provision. Do not transfer the
six-month birth-related duration automatically to the adoption provision.
The handbook calls maternity leave annual-leave-consuming and says no further leave is earned or
granted in the calendar year. Where annual leave has already been enjoyed, it says the equivalent
portion of maternity leave is without salary. This interaction must be taught alongside the headline
duration; omitting it would create an incomplete answer. It also uses calendar year here, while annual
leave elsewhere uses a February-to-January year. A boundary case spanning those periods needs
the relevant administrative interpretation rather than silently treating the two years as identical.
On returning from maternity leave, a nursing mother is allowed two hours off duty to nurse the child
until the child is ten months old. That is an age limit for the child, not ten months counted from the
employee's return. Antenatal care is separately supported by half a day off each week, with a medical
report confirming the appointment presented at the first appointment.
Section 5.7.6 provides eligible full-time male employees a maximum of 14 working days of paid
paternity leave in a year, within four months of the birth of a biological or adopted child. It also limits
the benefit to once in two years and a maximum of four children. These restrictions apply

leave in a year, within four months of the birth of a biological or adopted child. It also limits
the benefit to once in two years and a maximum of four children. These restrictions apply together:
the words 'in a year' do not cancel the two-year frequency condition. The entitlement cannot be
accumulated or converted to cash.
The adoption wording in the paternity passage is not precise about the timing of placement relative to
birth. For a case involving an older adopted child, do not invent a different four-month starting point.
Identify the wording and seek the applicable Human Capital interpretation or later approved policy. An
examination that supplies that clarification can then be answered on its stated facts.
Source: sections 5.7.4–5.7.6, printed pages 22–23.
NCC Promotion Study Guide   296

25.6 Study leave, leave of absence and handover
Study and examination leave were explained in the employment and promotion chapter because they
affect promotion eligibility. Their approval and evidence requirements continue to apply. Approved
examination dates, extended unpaid study and annual leave are distinct forms of absence, with
different effects on pay and other benefits.
Section 5.7.8 describes leave of absence for a specific purpose authorised by Management.
Examples include joining a spouse and specified relationships or support roles connected with
political office holders. It is unpaid; accepting paid employment during it requires express
Commission permission. The provision says it does not cover elected political appointments or
positions. It should therefore not be read as unrestricted permission to leave for any political activity.
An employee going on any type of leave must prepare a proper handover under section 5.7.9. The
useful content follows the duties being transferred: outstanding work, deadlines, decisions awaited,
records, relevant contacts and the succeeding officer's responsibilities. A handover is a continuity
record. It does not itself approve the leave or delegate powers beyond the employee's authority.
Source: sections 5.7.7–5.7.9, printed pages 23–25.

25.7 Sick leave and medical support
Section 5.8 provides sick leave for permanent employees to recuperate. It requires formal notification
of the reason for absence no later than 48 hours and a formal report from a recognised healthcare
provider on resumption. The notification and the later medical report are different steps; supplying the
report after return does not explain away failure to notify within the stated period.
The maximum aggregate sick leave described is three months in any 12-month period. Aggregate
means the total across relevant episodes, not necessarily one uninterrupted absence. If the
aggregate exceeds three months, the handbook provides for appearance before a
Commission-appointed Medical Board to assess possible invalidation from service. It also reserves
medical examination and termination powers in the stated circumstances. It does not describe an
automatic termination generated simply by a calendar counter.
Employees with recurrent or chronic conditions are encouraged to inform the Commission formally.
The text calls for speedy and compassionate handling. These are employment-policy provisions; they
are not medical advice, and an individual case requires the competent medical and administrative
processes.
Medical support includes annual allowances for employees and registered dependants, accredited or
retainer hospitals and an in-house clinic for first aid and minor conditions while on duty. Illness during
leave in Nigeria should be taken to a government hospital or recognised healthcare provider. The
passage does not itself establish that every day of illness automatically restores annual-leave days.
Overseas treatment is exceptional. The handbook connects potential payment, including appropriate
living expenses, to a need established by the Commission's doctor and an approved or designated
Nigerian referral centre. Board approval depends on the ailment and an established limit. It also
mentions possible medical leave on full pay for self-sponsored treatment supported by relevant
reports. Permission to be absent, medical support and reimbursement approval are separate
decisions.
Source: sections 5.8–5.8.3, printed pages 25–27.
NCC Promotion Study Guide   297

25.8 Pension and group life insurance
Section 5.10 describes the Commission's pension contribution as 10 percent and the employee's as
eight percent of the aggregate of basic salary, housing and transport allowances. Permanent full-time
employees must register and provide Retirement Savings Account details for remittance. These are
the supplied handbook's stated rates and base; a current payroll or legal determination requires any
applicable later rules.
Suppose a question gives monthly basic salary of N200,000, housing of N100,000 and transport of
N50,000. The stated base is N350,000. The Commission's contribution is N35,000 and the
employee's contribution is N28,000, giving combined contributions of N63,000. The combined 18
percent is not all an employee deduction. An unrelated allowance should not be added to the base
unless the question or applicable rule includes it.
Group life insurance under section 5.9 is a different benefit. The handbook describes minimum cover
of three times annual emolument. Insurance cover is not the same as the balance accumulated in a
retirement account. If a question supplies annual emolument of N4,200,000, the handbook's multiplier
gives minimum cover of N12,600,000. That calculation identifies cover, not an immediately payable
annual cash bonus.
Source: sections 5.9–5.10, printed page 27; definition of total emolument, printed page 67. These
examples teach the handbook calculations without independently certifying present statutory or
payroll treatment.

25.9 Other benefits and official travel
Long-service recognition begins at ten years and continues at five-year intervals thereafter, with a
plaque and a financial amount determined by Management. A retirement souvenir recognises
deserving retiring employees, with its value also determined by Management. Neither provision
supplies a fixed monetary figure for the learner to invent.
The club-membership provision concerns one business-oriented club for Management staff at Grade
Level 15, identified as MS3, and above. Professional membership is separately supported for
relevant bodies as determined by Management, covering registration and subscription fees within
approved rates. Payment for professional membership is not an unrestricted promise to cover every
conference, examination or activity of that body.
An ex gratia award is discretionary assistance in circumstances such as the death of a close relation.
The handbook also expresses an intention to provide an on-site creche, subject to space, for children
from four months or the mother's return from maternity leave up to two years. An expressed intention
subject to availability should not be presented as verified evidence that a facility is currently operating
at every office.
For official travel, section 5.12 covers authorised day-return and overnight assignments. It provides
for out-of-station support and reimbursement under guidelines where the employee incurs expenses
solely for Commission business. Receipts are to accompany the reimbursement form. A receipt
proves a transaction; it does not alone prove that the expense was authorised, necessary or
business-related.
Transport, accommodation, meals and incidental expenses may be provided, or prescribed
allowances may be paid instead. The handbook does not give the current rates here. It also provides
a maximum of 28 days' allowances for a newly recruited employee assuming duty outside the place
of residence. That provision is not a general duration for every duty tour or a universal transfer

NCC Promotion Study Guide   298
allowance.
An expense may be rejected if unrelated to Commission business, not pre-authorised, unsupported
by a receipt or inconsistent with policy. In a worked case, an officer who adds a private excursion to
an official journey cannot establish reimbursement merely by attaching the receipt. The answer must
connect the expense to authorised official business and the applicable travel requirements.
Source: sections 5.11–5.12, printed pages 28–29.

25.10 Applied practice with explained answers
Question 13. A Grade Level 09 employee qualifies for eight months of proportionate leave.
How many days does Appendix iii give?
Answer: 20 working days. Use the Grade Level 7-and-above column and the eight-month row.
Establishing qualification is separate from reading the table.
Question 14. Why should five months not automatically be rounded to 13 days for that
officer?
Answer: The table gives 12 days. A fraction of 30 gives 12.5, but the appendix does not consistently
apply an assumed rounding-up rule. Reproduce its specified result in a handbook question.
Question 15. An employee takes seven days of casual leave after exhausting annual
leave. What later effect does the handbook specify?
Answer: Casual leave is deductible from earned annual leave in the succeeding year. Compassionate
leave has a different rule and must not be substituted merely to avoid that deduction.
Question 16. What distinguishes ten working days of compassionate leave from five
working days of marriage leave?
Answer: Compassionate leave addresses specified critical emergencies, has an annual maximum
and is not deducted from annual leave. Marriage leave requires proof of official marriage
arrangements and is granted only once to the employee.
Question 17. Does maternity leave always sit alongside a full additional annual-leave
allocation?
Answer: No. The handbook describes maternity leave as annual-leave-consuming and provides
salary consequences for the equivalent portion where annual leave has already been enjoyed. The
interaction must accompany the headline maternity duration in the answer.
Question 18. May unused paternity leave be accumulated or paid in cash?
Answer: No. Both are expressly excluded. The 14-working-day maximum, four-month window,
two-year frequency restriction and four-child limit must also be read together.
Question 19. What is the full leave allowance on annual basic salary of N3,000,000?
Answer: N300,000, using ten percent of annual basic salary. This assumes the full allowance is due;
it is not a calculation from net pay and does not

leave allowance on annual basic salary of N3,000,000?
Answer: N300,000, using ten percent of annual basic salary. This assumes the full allowance is due;
it is not a calculation from net pay and does not settle proportionate eligibility.
Question 20. An employee's pension base is N400,000. Is the full N72,000 contribution an
employee deduction?
Answer: No. On the handbook's rates, the employer contributes N40,000 and the employee N32,000.
The combined N72,000 represents both contributions, not the employee's share alone.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   299
Question 21. Do three months of aggregate sick leave have to be one continuous
absence?
Answer: No. Aggregate refers to the total within the relevant 12-month period. Exceeding the
threshold engages the stated medical-assessment process; it should not be described as automatic
termination without that process.
Question 22. Does approved sick leave automatically approve overseas treatment
expenses?
Answer: No. Overseas treatment support has separate medical evidence, Board approval and limit
requirements. Permission to be absent and permission to incur reimbursable expenditure answer
different questions.
Question 23. A receipt is attached to an expense incurred on a private addition to an
official trip. Must it be reimbursed?
Answer: No. The handbook requires connection to Commission business and compliance with
authorisation and reimbursement rules. A receipt alone does not establish those conditions.
Question 24. Can an employee replace unused annual leave with cash while remaining in
service under section 5.7.1?
Answer: The provision rejects payment in lieu except when computing terminal pay. Do not confuse
this with the ten-percent leave allowance, which is a different benefit.
NCC Promotion Study Guide   300

Chapter 26
Employee relations, conduct and accountability
Expected conduct, safe work, confidentiality and fair treatment support reliable institutional
performance.
Good employment administration connects expected behaviour, support, evidence, fair procedure
and competent decisions. A workplace rule identifies a standard; an allegation says the standard may
have been breached; investigation establishes facts; the authorised decision applies the appropriate
response. Keeping these stages distinct is essential to answering an unfamiliar scenario.
26.1 Employee relations and communication

Chapter 6 describes discipline as supporting order, productivity, institutional objectives and fair
treatment. It places responsibility for maintaining discipline on Management. It recognises informal
oral warnings for some first instances, investigation before written warnings, possible suspension and
stronger action where the misconduct warrants it. Chapter 10 provides the more detailed procedure.
The general discussion in chapter 6 should therefore be read with the specific procedural provisions,
not treated as permission to bypass them.
The employee-relations chapter lists unacceptable conduct including theft, weapons, fighting,
deliberate damage, falsified employment information, refusal of directions, unsafe conduct, excessive
lateness, harassment, abusive language, gambling and other specified behaviour. Its general use of
'serious misconduct' is broader than the later division into categories A–D. When a question asks for
the formal category, use chapter 10's detailed classification rather than assume every example in

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6 describes discipline as supporting order, productivity, institutional objectives and fair
metadata.topic: Chapter 6 describes discipline as supporting order, productivity, institutional objectives and fair
metadata.section: Chapter 6 describes discipline as supporting order, productivity, institutional objectives and fair

chunks.content:
chapter 6 belongs to category B.
Section 6.3 gives an employee who considers a condition of service unfairly applied or who
experiences unfair treatment an opportunity to challenge it. The normal first step described is
discussion with the immediate supervisor; unresolved issues proceed through the established
grievance procedure. The section describes Management's decision as final, while section 10.15 later
expressly provides appeals against grievance decisions. The sound reading is to consider the
grievance route together with the appeal provision, rather than quote the earlier sentence as if no
internal appeal exists.
A useful grievance record identifies the act or decision complained of, relevant dates, the applicable
condition or standard, supporting records, steps already taken and the remedy sought. That is a
teaching application of an evidence-based process. It does not require the employee to speculate
about another person's motives. For example, a disputed leave decision is more readily assessed
from the request, roster, stated reason and applicable leave rule than from an unsupported assertion
that the employee is disliked.
Internal communication channels include the intranet, policies and handbook, meetings and briefings,
letters, circulars, internal memoranda, newsletters, magazines and email. Different channels serve
different purposes. A meeting can explain a policy, but a formal decision should remain traceable in
its appropriate record. An informal message is not automatically a substitute for an approval required
in writing.
External communication has an authority boundary. Section 6.4.2 requires press releases to be
approved by and issued under the authority of the Executive Vice Chairman. Knowing the technical
details of a project does not confer authority to issue an official statement. The officer should provide

NCC Promotion Study Guide   301
accurate input through the authorised communication process.
Source: chapter 6, printed pages 30–32; section 10.15, printed page 62.

26.2 Health, safety and physical security
The handbook makes workplace safety a shared responsibility. The Commission provides the safety
programme and communication, while employees must exercise care, follow safety rules and
immediately report unsafe conditions and concerns. The detailed safety policy is identified as being
with the Administration Department. A hazard does not become acceptable because it has not yet
caused injury.
Consider exposed wiring near equipment used by several staff. A responsible response identifies and
reports the condition promptly and follows the applicable safety instructions. It does not wait for an
accident before recognising an obligation. The handbook also makes failure to report hazardous
conditions potentially disciplinary. This connects prevention to accountability.
Identity cards must be displayed conspicuously on the premises and remain Commission property.
They are returned to Human Capital on leaving service. Loss must be reported immediately; the
handbook describes replacement at the employee's cost after submission of a police report and
affidavit to the Information Technology Department. The card is therefore both an identity-control item
and part of the stated dress requirement, not merely a convenient pass to lend to a colleague.
Sections 7.3.2–7.3.3 describe Commission work areas and systems as subject to inspection,
including unannounced searches, and state serious consequences for refusal. Mail sent to the
Commission's address is treated as business-related in the text. These provisions describe
institutional authority and employee obligations; they do not authorise every employee to inspect
another employee's records or possessions on personal initiative. Questions about an actual search
must identify the authorised process and applicable safeguards.
Commission property may not be removed without prior Management permission. Personal property
brought into the premises is described as being at the owner's risk, and the handbook disclaims
liability for its loss or damage. A personal laptop being present at work and a Commission laptop
being taken away from work therefore raise different questions of ownership and permission.
Visitors require authorisation. Personal visitors

liability for its loss or damage. A personal laptop being present at work and a Commission laptop
being taken away from work therefore raise different questions of ownership and permission.
Visitors require authorisation. Personal visitors register at reception and enter subject to Management
discretion; access beyond public areas is restricted to staff and authorised persons. An employee
should not turn familiarity with a vendor into permission for unrestricted office access. The vendor's
purpose, approval and access arrangements still matter.
The workplace-violence policy covers both actual violence and threats, including intimidation,
harassment and coercion affecting the Commission or its people. Threats are to be reported
immediately to Human Capital. Waiting for physical injury would miss the preventive scope of the
policy. The handbook also prohibits workplace smoking, illegal drugs and alcohol-related conduct and
misuse of prescribed or over-the-counter drugs, and requires participation when called for random
doping tests.
Employees must know the fire instructions, the location and use of extinguishers and the location of
first-aid boxes. The study point is preparedness and compliance with the safety procedure, not
improvising a hazardous response. A first-aid box provides basic supplies; its presence does not
eliminate the need to report an incident or obtain appropriate assistance.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   302
Source: chapter 7, printed pages 33–37; sections 9.2–9.4, printed page 41. The handbook refers
detailed dress and car-park arrangements to separately communicated guidance.

26.3 Confidentiality, assets and information systems
The ethical starting point in section 9.5 is that institutional integrity depends on individual conduct.
Employees must apply good judgement, devote their efforts to their work and avoid using office for
private gain or benefits for themselves or family. Seniority does not remove these duties.
Confidential information includes operator, client, vendor, employee and business records, systems
and future plans. Section 9.5.2 requires care while information is in use, secure filing when it is not,
and disclosure only to people with a legitimate business need. The restriction applies inside the
Commission as well as outside it. Being a colleague does not automatically create a need to know.
For an Information Technology officer, technical access is particularly important to distinguish from
business authority. A backup operator may be able to restore a personnel database but does not
thereby acquire permission to browse it for personal reasons. An application administrator may
resolve an access problem without distributing the underlying confidential records. The practical
control is to connect access to the approved task and preserve an appropriate record of what was
done.
Tools and equipment should be maintained in good condition. Damaged equipment is to be removed
from use and marked defective. Corporate long-distance calls must be work-related and approved by
the supervisor under the stated phone provision. Ownership of the equipment remains separate from
the employee's custody of it.
Sections 9.5.8–9.5.9 describe Commission computers, data, mail and programmes as institutional
resources for Commission business. Illegal software is prohibited. The email provision nevertheless
permits limited personal use, subject to restrictions: it must not impede productivity or business, and
the systems must not be used for religious, political or charitable solicitation or advertising personal
enterprises. Read the limited permission together with the main business-purpose rule; neither
unlimited personal use nor a claim that the text permits no personal use accurately captures both
passages.
The handbook prohibits offensive or harassing

enterprises. Read the limited permission together with the main business-purpose rule; neither
unlimited personal use nor a claim that the text permits no personal use accurately captures both
passages.
The handbook prohibits offensive or harassing messages and inappropriate sites. It says system
materials may be accessed only by authorised personnel and that personal activity on these systems
carries no guarantee of privacy. That is not an invitation for unauthorised surveillance by a colleague.
An administrator should follow authorised purposes and access controls.
The handbook refers to the Cybercrimes Act 2015 and other relevant laws. This identifies the
source's reference; it does not certify that the original 2015 text is the complete current legal position.
An examination about current legislation requires the relevant amended instrument. The handbook
lesson itself is that the employee remains accountable for what is transmitted using the system.
Source: sections 9.5.1–9.5.2 and 9.5.6–9.5.9, printed pages 42 and 45–46.

26.4 Gifts, honoraria and conflicts of interest
A bribe, as explained by the handbook, is a financial or other advantage intended to induce improper
performance or reward an improper act already done. The timing does not save the transaction: a
reward after the act can still engage the rule. Section 9.5.3 treats giving or attempting to give a bribe
as gross misconduct with potential dismissal.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   303
Section 9.5.4 uses N50,000 as its nominal-value threshold. It says gifts above that value should be
declined and reported to the immediate supervisor for approval. The wording contains both the
refusal instruction and an approval reference; it should not be rewritten as automatic permission to
keep any gift once reported. The restriction extends to immediate family members, so routing the
benefit through a spouse does not avoid the stated concern.
An honorarium is a payment for an activity such as a presentation. For presentations arising primarily
from the employee's NCC role, the handbook requires declaration above N50,000 and says no
reporting is required below that figure. It does not expressly resolve the exactly-N50,000 boundary in
those sentences. A precise examination answer should state the printed rule and avoid creating a
boundary rule that the text does not supply.
A separate legal context is essential. The official 2021 explanatory manual produced by the Technical
Unit on Governance and Anti-Corruption Reforms with the Code of Conduct Bureau explains
restrictions on benefits connected with official duties and the presumption concerning gifts from
government contractors. An internal monetary threshold is not a general exemption from those
restrictions. Source: Explanatory Manual on the Code of Conduct for Public Officers, Code 6, printed
pages 15–17, consulted 22 September 2026.
A conflict of interest occurs when personal interests or loyalties interfere, or appear to interfere, with
duty to the Commission. Section 9.5.5 addresses both the fact and appearance of conflict. Its
examples include work for contractors or suppliers, using confidential information for personal gain,
direct or indirect financial interests, private use of institutional resources and relationships that may
impair impartial decisions.
The handbook addresses transactions involving an employee's or spouse's business and requires
disclosure, while also prohibiting financial interests in transactions coming before the employee in the
course of duty. Disclosure therefore identifies the problem; it does not by itself establish that

employee's or spouse's business and requires
disclosure, while also prohibiting financial interests in transactions coming before the employee in the
course of duty. Disclosure therefore identifies the problem; it does not by itself establish that the
employee may continue to assess or approve the transaction. Doubt should be raised with the Head
of Department or Human Capital through the stated route.
Worked example: an officer involved in evaluating a supplier receives a personal gift worth N30,000
from that supplier. An answer confined to 'below N50,000, so acceptable' is incomplete. It ignores the
relationship to official duties, the anti-bribery provision and the conflict of interest. The response
should identify and disclose the issue through the competent process and avoid treating value alone
as permission.
Worked example: an officer's spouse owns a bidding business. Merely saying 'I did not personally
sign the bid' does not address indirect interest. The relevant facts include the relationship, the officer's
role and ability to influence the process, and the required disclosure and management of the conflict.
Source: sections 9.5.3–9.5.5, printed pages 43–45. The worked examples apply the supplied rules;
they are not determinations of liability in a particular case.

26.5 Discrimination, harassment and retaliation
The handbook prohibits unfair or unequal treatment on the protected grounds it lists. These include
actual or perceived age, gender, colour, marital status, disability, religion, dress and grooming,
pregnancy and related conditions, breastfeeding and association with persons in protected
categories. The protections extend to employees and independent contractors; the Commission also
undertakes to attempt protection against workplace harassment by non-employees.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   304
Harassment can be verbal, visual, physical or electronic. Examples include offensive comments,
slurs, jokes, unwanted advances, images, intimidation and interference with movement or work. The
central issue is unwelcome conduct that interferes substantially with work or creates an intimidating,
hostile or offensive environment, including conduct tied to the listed characteristics. Calling something
a joke does not settle its effect or acceptability.
The handbook identifies three important patterns: submission made a condition of employment;
submission or refusal used in employment decisions; and conduct whose purpose or effect is
substantial interference with work or creation of a hostile environment. A promised work benefit in
return for sexual favours and a threat of disadvantage for refusing them both engage the policy.
Sexual harassment includes unwelcome advances, gestures, sexual comments and requests for
sexual favours, as well as a hostile or degrading environment. The handbook says dignity may be
violated whether or not that effect was intended. The fact-finding process must therefore examine the
conduct and circumstances rather than end with the alleged actor's claim of harmless intention.
Retaliation against a person who reports with a good-faith, reasonable belief, threatens to report, or
participates in an investigation is also prohibited. This protects the reporting process. It does not
mean that every allegation is automatically proved; it means that reporting and investigation must not
themselves become grounds for punishment in breach of the policy.
A sound examination response separates the complaint, supporting evidence, protection against
further harm or retaliation and fair investigation. A record should identify what happened, when, who
was involved, witnesses and relevant communications. The purpose is to support an assessable
account while protecting confidentiality, not circulate the allegation to unrelated staff.
Source: section 9.6, printed pages 47–49.
NCC Promotion Study Guide   305

Chapter 27
Discipline, appeals and separation
Separate the allegation, investigation, recommendation, approval and appeal before considering the
effect on employment.
Discipline and separation concern different questions. Discipline addresses an alleged or established
breach and the appropriate response. Separation ends the employment relationship and can occur
without wrongdoing, as with resignation or retirement. This section follows the disciplinary process
before explaining the different exit routes.
27.1 From a report to an investigated case

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master

chunks.content:
Chapter 10 describes discipline as corrective where possible, with counselling before formal action
when suitable. Except for very extreme gross misconduct, it says an employee is not dismissed for a
first breach. It also requires investigation and establishment of facts before disciplinary action. These
safeguards must be read alongside the handbook's stronger language about serious breaches
elsewhere.
Under section 10.6, the supervisor requests a written explanation, sets a response period, examines
the reply and decides whether further attention is justified. The provision gives 48 hours as an
example of a specified response period. It is not written as an invariant deadline for every query. This
differs from the express 48-hour notification rule for sick absence.
The supervisor may close the matter if there is no sufficient reason to continue, give a verbal warning
where appropriate, or refer it to the employee's Head of Department for further procedure. A query
therefore starts a fact-finding process; it is not proof of guilt. The employee's reply must be
considered for its content rather than treated as an administrative formality before a predetermined
penalty.
Where the matter proceeds, the Head of Department passes the original request and reply to Human
Capital, which establishes an ad hoc Disciplinary Committee with a timeframe for deliberation and
reporting. Preserving the original documents matters because the committee must know the
allegation actually put to the employee and the answer actually given.
The committee has four persons. Members should, as much as possible, be on higher grades than
the employee concerned. If the employee is female, the committee includes two female employees.
The most senior member chairs it, and the secretary comes from Human Capital. The provision says
four persons; it does not say four plus a separate fifth secretary.
The employee must appear to defend the allegation. Both the employee and committee may call
witnesses and receive written and oral evidence. The committee relies on facts and makes

The employee must appear to defend the allegation. Both the employee and committee may call
witnesses and receive written and oral evidence. The committee relies on facts and makes

Head of Human Capital, who checks procedural compliance. The text aims, as much as possible, to
open and close a case within three weeks. This is a qualified timetable, not a statement that every
case automatically disappears on day 22.

27.2 Misconduct categories and proportionate consequences
Category A covers minor misconduct, including habitual lateness or unauthorised absence, failure to
follow procedures, incompetence in assigned responsibilities, poor dress or hygiene, non-adherence
to rules, clocking attendance for another employee, rudeness and conduct-code breaches. The word
minor identifies the category; it does not mean there can be no consequence.
Category B covers serious misconduct. Examples include repeated or serious category A breaches,
fighting or inciting violence, involvement in a matter leading to police arrest, action beyond one's
official powers, failure to answer lawful questioning, bringing the Commission into disrepute, partisan
politics and official-code breaches. An arrest and a conviction are different events even though both
appear in different parts of the classification.
Category C covers gross misconduct, including repeated or serious category B breaches, criminal
conviction, malicious damage, theft, unauthorised possession of Commission property, prohibited
substance use, vandalism, gambling, fraud, embezzlement, assault, sexual harassment, threats,
gross insubordination, dangerous negligence, confidentiality breaches, misuse of systems or
letterhead, unauthorised removal of property, false declarations and bribery. The examples are not
exhaustive.
Category D addresses criminal or police cases, with examples of theft, forgery, fraud, bribery, cultism
and drug offences. Some conduct appears in both institutional-misconduct and criminal categories.
The distinction concerns the process and authority as well as the behaviour. A committee's internal
finding is not a criminal conviction.
The handbook's statement that only the Police deal with criminal-code infractions is too broad to use
as a general account of Nigeria's enforcement institutions. The Independent Corrupt Practices and
Other Related Offences Commission expressly identifies investigation and prosecution of corruption
as part of its mandate. Source: that Commission's published legislative background and institutional
description, consulted 22 September 2026. Learn the handbook's referral route without converting it
into a claim that every other statutory enforcement body lacks authority.
The handbook lists different available consequences by category. Classification must follow the facts
and relevant provision. A penalty should

referral route without converting it
into a claim that every other statutory enforcement body lacks authority.
The handbook lists different available consequences by category. Classification must follow the facts
and relevant provision. A penalty should be commensurate with the offence and imposed through the
competent procedure; listing a possible sanction does not automatically require it in every case.
Category   Listed consequences
A   Written reprimand; unpaid suspension up to four weeks; withholding increment up to six
months without seniority loss.
B   Unpaid suspension up to six weeks; forfeiture of one annual increment with or without
corresponding seniority loss.
C   Surcharge; demotion up to two grades and seniority; termination with full benefits; compulsory
retirement with entitlements; dismissal.
D   Criminal-proceeding and related disciplinary provisions apply.
Notice the difference between withholding an increment and forfeiting it. The handbook describes
category A withholding for up to six months without seniority loss. Category B includes forfeiture of a
year's increment, with or without the stated seniority effect. An answer should preserve the specified
consequence rather than call every pay-related sanction a salary deduction.

one step, and the specific category C provision permitting demotion up to two grades. Do not produce
a universal one-grade limit from the earlier overview. Identify the specific sanction provision the
question engages.

27.3 Warnings, suspension and the employee's rights
A verbal warning addresses a minor failing. A first written warning may follow a more serious matter,
lack of improvement after a verbal warning or repetition; the supervisor or Head of Department invites
the employee to a hearing before the stated written-warning decision. A final written warning may
address a very serious initial offence or continuing unsatisfactory conduct, performance or
attendance after earlier warnings.
The final warning states that recurrence or similar misconduct within 12 months will result in
dismissal. Written warnings are retained in the personnel file. Read this escalation alongside the
hearing, investigation and approval requirements. It does not turn a report of recurrence into an
automatically proved offence.
Section 10.2.4 provides for full-pay suspension for a maximum of six months where dismissal may
result or the employee's presence may intimidate a witness. It says the fact of suspension is not
considered in the disciplinary proceedings. The practical distinction is between removing a risk while
a matter is examined and establishing that the employee committed the allegation. Suspension itself
is not a finding of guilt.
Section 10.2.5 separately allows suspension without pay for repeated misconduct. Section 10.7
refers to committee-requested suspension on full, half or no pay in specified investigative
circumstances. Sections 10.8.1–10.8.2 set four-week and six-week maximum unpaid suspensions for
categories A and B. These are different provisions with different contexts. Do not merge them into
one general six-month unpaid-suspension rule.
At every stage of the disciplinary procedure, section 10.3 gives the employee the right to be
accompanied by a work colleague of choice. It also provides appeal rights against disciplinary
warnings. A right to accompaniment is different from handing the colleague the employee's obligation
to answer the allegation. The handbook's specified companion is a work colleague; do not replace
that wording with a different entitlement unless an applicable instrument establishes it.
The employee is to receive a written dismissal

to answer the allegation. The handbook's specified companion is a work colleague; do not replace
that wording with a different entitlement unless an applicable instrument establishes it.
The employee is to receive a written dismissal statement under section 10.2.7 and may appeal. That
section says dismissal makes the employee ineligible for exit benefits. This is the handbook's
disciplinary description, not a complete analysis of all possible statutory pension rights. The current
treatment of a particular benefit requires its governing instrument.
Source: sections 10.2–10.3 and 10.7–10.8, printed pages 50–52 and 57–59.

27.4 Who recommends and who decides?
Section 10.4 links disciplinary authority to appointing authority and sets out delegations. The Head of
Department may reprimand employees in the department. The Executive Vice Chairman has
specified powers of reprimand, suspension, approval and recommendation. The Board approves
disciplinary action recommended to it and recommends action concerning the Executive Vice
Chairman and Executive Commissioners to the Federal Government.

NCC Promotion Study Guide   308
The detailed grade references on printed page 53 overlap and are not readily reducible to a clean
grade-by-grade chart. They are retained below as printed rather than silently normalised. These
references also should not be converted to numerical grades through an invented mapping.
Section 10.4.2(i): the Executive Vice Chairman may reprimand and suspend all employees for
offences described in Commission policies. Subparagraph (ii) refers to approval of suspension and
other actions for JS6–JS1 and SS5–SS1. Subparagraph (iii) refers to termination approval for JS6 to
SS5 and appointment of a committee to determine termination of officers on SS6 to MS2.
Subparagraph (iv) refers to recommending termination, dismissal and other disciplinary action for
SS5 to MS1 to the Board.
The overlap is material, particularly around SS5 and the relationship between broad and specific
powers. For a real decision or an examination demanding a precise disputed boundary, the approved
delegation or clarification is needed. The reliable teaching point is to distinguish recommendation
from approval, and a committee finding from the authorised final decision. It would be misleading to
invent a perfectly consistent authority table from this wording.
Lateral discipline under section 10.11 concerns an officer raising misconduct involving an employee
in another department. The initiating officer brings the matter to that employee's Head of Department,
who follows the established process. Cross-department knowledge of a problem does not
automatically confer power to impose a penalty on the other department's employee.
Section 10.14 gives the Executive Vice Chairman emergency powers where conduct may lead to a
total breakdown of discipline and order, with possible delegation to Executive Commissioners or
Directors. The text limits the scope and duration and says this is not a permanent substitute for formal
procedure. An urgent situation can justify the specified immediate response without erasing all later
accountability.
Source: sections 10.4, 10.11 and 10.14, printed pages 52–53 and 60–61.

27.5 Special situations and appeals
Where criminal proceedings are instituted, section 10.8.4 says disciplinary proceedings on grounds
involved in the charge may be taken only after conclusion of the criminal proceedings and any
appeal. It also addresses restoration of benefits after proper discharge and acquittal, and permits a
remaining disciplinary breach to be addressed under categories A–C. This is the handbook's
prescribed relationship. It should not be generalised into a legal rule governing every Nigerian
employer or every unrelated disciplinary ground.
For an unconfirmed employee found guilty, section 10.9 allows recommendation of a more stringent
punishment for the Executive Vice Chairman's approval. The phrase found guilty still matters:
probation does not make every accusation an established fact. Section 10.10 postpones disciplinary
proceedings that would otherwise occur during or after maternity leave until that leave and further
granted sick leave have expired.
A suspended employee must obtain the relevant permission before leaving the duty station and keep
the Head of Department or Executive Vice Chairman informed of an address for instructions. Under
section 10.12, failure to comply within 24 hours with an instruction delivered to that address is treated
as unauthorised absence. Permission to leave can carry conditions. Suspension is therefore not an
unrestricted holiday from every employment obligation.
Section 10.13 makes the dismissal or termination date the date approved by the disciplinary
authority. A supervisor's earlier recommendation, a committee's report date and the eventual effective

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.chapter: Chapter 10 describes discipline as corrective where possible, with counselling before formal action

chunks.content:
NCC Promotion Study Guide   309
decision date should not be treated as interchangeable.
An appeal under section 10.15 must be in writing to the person authorised to overturn the decision.
That person's details and the procedure are to be provided when the employee is told the decision.
The written appeal must be lodged within five working days of being given the decision and state the
grounds fully. Grounds may concern an unfair finding, excessive penalty, procedural irregularity or
new evidence.
A useful appeal explains the challenged decision, each ground, the supporting fact or record and the
remedy sought. For example, a procedural appeal should identify the opportunity or step said to have
been denied and why it mattered. Simply restating disagreement without addressing the finding
leaves the reviewer little to assess.
Section 10.15.1 restricts ordinary external escalation and requires use of the Commission's grievance
procedures before suit. Its wording about the Executive Vice Chairman's route through the Board,
Ministry and President is repetitive. Preserve the internal procedure lesson without teaching that the
handbook conclusively extinguishes all external legal rights. Any actual dispute requires the
governing law and competent advice; the study guide does not resolve jurisdiction or enforceability
from a handbook sentence alone.
Source: sections 10.8.4–10.15, printed pages 59–62.

chunks.content:
27.6 Resignation, retirement, termination and dismissal
Separation may be initiated by the employee or the Commission. Section 8.1 requires exit forms and
clearance before final benefits are paid. The basis for departure matters because notice, benefits,
records and approvals differ. 'The employee left' is not a sufficient classification for an examination
answer.
Resignation is initiated by the employee through written notice. For confirmed staff, section 8.2 states
one month for Junior and Senior Staff, with the printed range JS3–SS1, and three months for
Management Staff, MS3–MS1. The JS3 lower bound differs from the general Junior Staff band
JS6–JS1 printed earlier. Do not quietly alter the source range; a question about a grade outside the
stated resignation range needs clarification from the applicable conditions.
An employee leaving immediately is to pay salary in lieu of the relevant notice. Outstanding leave
may offset part of notice under the handbook. Payment in lieu concerns the missing notice period;
salary in lieu of earned leave concerns unused leave at exit. They are different calculations and may
operate in opposite directions: one may be owed by the employee, while the other may form part of
the employee's entitlement.
The handbook's compulsory-retirement rule is age 60 or 35 years in public service, whichever occurs
first, with three months' notice. It additionally states an eight-year tenure limit as Director. These are
the handbook provisions, not verification of every later government circular or individual exception.
Optional, voluntary or early retirement is described after ten years' continuous service or attaining 45
on medical or other personal grounds, with three months' notice and exceptional acceptance of
payment in lieu.
If a hypothetical officer reaches 35 years in public service at age 58, the handbook's whichever-first
formulation identifies the service limit first. Do not wait for both limits to occur. Conversely, reaching
60 first engages the age limit even where total public service is less than 35 years. The relevant
service

chunks.content:
formulation identifies the service limit first. Do not wait for both limits to occur. Conversely, reaching
60 first engages the age limit even where total public service is less than 35 years. The relevant
service record is public service as the provision says, not automatically time in NCC alone.

chunks.content:
NCC Promotion Study Guide   310
Commission-initiated termination under section 8.4 requires one month's notice, with pay in lieu
rather than working the period. Dismissal under section 8.5 concerns the disciplinary grounds and is
without notice. A disciplinary category C decision can include termination with full benefits,
compulsory retirement with entitlements or dismissal. These alternatives are not synonyms, and the
selected outcome must be supported by the competent decision.
Death ends the employment relationship. Section 8.6 provides family assistance with burial expenses
and requires a death certificate and statutory documentation for release of terminal benefits to
recorded beneficiaries. Accurate personnel records therefore matter before an emergency arises.
Naming a person in a contact field and establishing all documents for payment are not necessarily the
same thing.
Source: sections 8.1–8.6, printed pages 38–39; section 10.8.3, printed page 59.

27.7 Exit clearance, terminal pay and repatriation
An exit interview obtains feedback and supports orderly separation. Section 8.7 specifically requires it
for voluntarily departing employees, while section 8.1 refers generally to exit forms and clearance for
all modes. Commission property in the employee's possession or control is to be returned
immediately upon termination for any reason, and outstanding debts and final-pay arrangements
addressed.
For internal systems, a sound exit process also needs the responsible functions to act on the
authorised departure record: identify equipment, preserve official work, transfer ownership of
outstanding tasks and manage access through the approved process. These are practical control
applications, not an additional handbook notice period. Removing an account prematurely can disrupt
service; leaving privileged access unmanaged can expose records. The decision and implementation
should therefore be coordinated.
Section 8.9 lists salary through the last working day, salary in lieu of earned leave and gratuity as
defined in the conditions of service for employees who resign or retire. Outstanding loans and upfront
grants relating to service not rendered are deducted. The passage does not provide a gratuity
formula, so no percentage or multiplier should be invented from it.
A terminal-pay calculation needs a defined departure route, effective date, relevant salary basis,
earned leave, applicable gratuity rules and outstanding liabilities. A figure computed without those
inputs is not reliable. Nor should an employee be told that every payment is forfeited merely because
any form of separation has occurred; dismissal and ordinary resignation have different handbook
descriptions.
Repatriation under section 4.6 concerns an employee transferred away from the place of
engagement who retires or whose employment is terminated. It provides return to the permanent
home address within one month, with spouse, four children and reasonable baggage. In case of
death, the spouse and four children are to be repatriated within six months. The permanent home
address, duty station and original place of engagement must remain distinguishable.
Source: sections

27.8 Definitions that change the answer
The handbook's definitions clarify how particular words are used. Authority means Management or an
assigned officer acting for the Commission. A supervisor is the manager to whom the employee
reports and who initiates performance evaluation. Authority to perform a function must therefore not
be assumed from personal seniority alone.
Competencies comprise knowledge, skills and personal attributes. Incompetence concerns failure to
maintain prescribed or acceptable professional standards in procedures and performance
agreements. These definitions connect appraisal and development: a gap should be tied to a required
standard, not just an unsupported negative description.
Insubordination is defined with reference to an authorised, lawful instruction and unreasonable refusal
or disobedience. It should not be paraphrased as a duty to carry out any instruction whatsoever.
Similarly, a grievance is a decision or act causing perceived or actual unfairness, whereas
misconduct concerns behaviour prejudicial to service discipline or policy. A person may raise a
grievance about the handling of a misconduct allegation; the concepts can coexist.
The definition of service includes duty and duly authorised leave, but excludes unauthorised absence
and overstayed leave. This does not mean every type of authorised leave earns every benefit: the
study-leave provision separately limits benefit accrual. A general definition and a specific benefit
condition must be read together.
Dependants include spouse, four children up to 18 and wholly dependent parents in the handbook
definition. Family is separately defined as parents, spouse and four children up to 18. Close relative is
broader, including listed in-laws, step-relatives, siblings, grandchildren, aunts, uncles, nephews,
nieces and first cousins. A benefit that names one of these categories should not be widened merely
by replacing it with another.
The glossary defines total emolument as basic salary, housing and transport for pension and
terminal-benefit calculations. Its description of salary as net monthly payment must be handled
carefully where another provision expressly specifies basic salary or a different base. The specific

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.chapter: Chapter 10 describes discipline as corrective where possible, with counselling before formal action

chunks.content:
basic salary, housing and transport for pension and
terminal-benefit calculations. Its description of salary as net monthly payment must be handled
carefully where another provision expressly specifies basic salary or a different base. The specific
calculation wording controls the study exercise; using take-home pay for every calculation would be
wrong.
Appendix i summarises political appointment to the Board and labels the approving authority as
National Assembly. For the precise statutory confirmation body, section 8(1) of the Nigerian
Communications Act 2003 specifies the Senate. The handbook's broad label should not replace that
more precise statutory answer. The established nine-member composition remains the subject of the
governance chapter in the Master.
Source: Appendix i and Appendix ii, printed pages 63–67; Nigerian Communications Act 2003,
section 8(1). The signed employee acknowledgement is an administrative record and is not part of
the teaching content.

27.9 Integrated examination cases
Case 7. A vendor's gift during an evaluation
An officer assessing a vendor's deliverables receives a gift below N50,000 and proposes to retain it
without further consideration.
Model answer. The amount alone is not enough. Identify the connection to official duties and the
possibility of inducement or conflict, apply the anti-bribery and conflict provisions together with the gift

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.chapter: Chapter 10 describes discipline as corrective where possible, with counselling before formal action

chunks.content:
NCC Promotion Study Guide   312
rule, and raise the issue through the competent route. The handbook threshold must not be treated
as permission for improper influence. Keep the acceptance decision separate from the assessment of
the vendor's work.
Case 8. A query treated as proof
A supervisor says that because a written query has been issued, the employee must already be guilty
and a sanction can be imposed without reading the reply.
Model answer. Section 10.6 requires examination of the explanation to determine whether further
action is warranted. Section 10.1 requires investigation and establishment of facts. Issuing a query
identifies an allegation; it does not resolve it. The response should be considered, and closure,
warning or referral selected according to the evidence and competent procedure.
Case 9. A cross-department dispute
An officer discovers that an employee in another department has removed equipment without
permission and directly announces a suspension.
Model answer. Preserve the relevant facts and report through the lateral-discipline route in section

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.chapter: Chapter 10 describes discipline as corrective where possible, with counselling before formal action

chunks.content:
10.11 to that employee's Head of Department. The conduct may warrant investigation under the
property and misconduct provisions, but identifying a possible breach does not give the reporting
officer disciplinary approval power. Separate the allegation from authority to impose a sanction.
Case 10. Suspension described as a holiday
A suspended employee leaves the duty station without permission and stops checking the address
supplied for instructions.
Model answer. Section 10.12 imposes continuing duties concerning permission to leave, the address
for instructions and compliance after delivery. Suspension does not end employment or remove those
obligations. Establish the permission, instruction, delivery and response facts before applying the
provision; do not confuse this with the separate appeal deadline.
Case 11. A committee report treated as a termination notice
A committee recommends termination, and an administrator immediately records the employee as
terminated on the report date.
Model answer. A recommendation must be distinguished from approval by the competent authority.
Section 10.13 identifies the effective date as the date approved by that authority. Check the decision
and authorised date before changing the employment record. Preserve the committee report as
evidence of recommendation, not as a substitute for the final decision.
Case 12. An employee appeals a warning
An employee receives a disciplinary warning and is told that only dismissal may be appealed.
Model answer. Section 10.3 provides appeal rights against disciplinary warnings. Section 10.15
requires written grounds to the person authorised to overturn the decision within five working days of
notification. The employee should be given that person's details and the procedure. A useful appeal
identifies the finding or procedure challenged and supporting evidence.

27.10 Examination practice with explained answers
Question 25. Under section 10.6, what is the significance of 48 hours?
A. Every appeal must be filed within 48 hours. B. Every committee must report within 48 hours. C. It is
an example of the response period specified for a written explanation. D. Every suspension ends
after 48 hours.
Answer: C. The query provision gives an example. Other handbook provisions use different express
deadlines, including five working days for an appeal and 24 hours for compliance with a delivered
instruction during suspension.
Question 26. How many persons form the Disciplinary Committee under section 10.7?
A. Three. B. Six. C. Five plus a secretary. D. Four.
Answer: D. The text specifies four persons, with the most senior as chair and a secretary from Human
Capital. It does not add a fifth person merely by naming the secretary's role.
Question 27. Does full-pay suspension itself establish misconduct?
A. No; distinguish the interim measure from the finding. B. Yes; payment confirms guilt. C. Yes;
investigation is unnecessary after suspension. D. Only if the employee is confirmed.
Answer: A. Section 10.2.4 says the fact of suspension is not to be considered in the proceedings. The
allegation still requires examination under the applicable process.
Question 28. Which period applies to the handbook's written appeal under section 10.15?
A. Three months. B. Five working days from being given the decision. C. Six weeks from the
committee's first meeting. D. Five calendar days from any informal rumour.
Answer: B. Both the working-day unit and the notification event matter. The appeal must include its
grounds and go to the authorised reviewer.
Question 29. Can an employee inspect confidential colleague records because the
handbook calls them Commission property?
Answer: No. Institutional ownership does not confer access on every employee. The text separately
requires authorised access and a legitimate need to know.
Question 30. Why is the handbook's N50,000 gift figure not a

metadata.title: NCC_Study_Guide_Restructured_Master
metadata.chapter: Chapter 10 describes discipline as corrective where possible, with counselling before formal action

chunks.content:
property?
Answer: No. Institutional ownership does not confer access on every employee. The text separately
requires authorised access and a legitimate need to know.
Question 30. Why is the handbook's N50,000 gift figure not a complete ethics test?
Answer: Purpose, connection to official duties, conflicts and the anti-bribery rule also matter.
Reporting or being below a threshold does not turn improper influence into acceptable conduct.
Question 31. A final warning refers to similar misconduct within 12 months. May an
uninvestigated accusation be treated as a proved recurrence?
Answer: No. The warning's consequence must be read with the requirements to establish facts, hear
the matter and obtain the proper decision. A new allegation is not automatically a substantiated
breach.
Question 32. Distinguish a Head of Department's reprimand power from a Disciplinary
Committee's role.
Answer: The Head of Department has the specified departmental reprimand power. The committee
examines evidence and makes findings and recommendations through the stated process. Its
recommendation is not automatically the final approval for every sanction.

chunks.content:
NCC Promotion Study Guide   314
Question 33. Which category A and category B unpaid-suspension maxima are printed in
section 10.8?
Answer: Four weeks for category A and six weeks for category B. These must not be confused with
the six-month full-pay suspension provision in section 10.2.4, which addresses a different situation.
Question 34. What does lateral discipline require?
Answer: Bring the alleged cross-department misconduct to the employee's Head of Department, who
follows the established procedure. It does not authorise an unrelated officer to impose punishment
directly.
Question 35. What distinguishes resignation from dismissal?
Answer: Resignation is employee-initiated through the stated notice arrangement. Dismissal is a
disciplinary separation without notice under the handbook, with different stated benefit consequences
and appeal provisions. Neither should be used as a generic label for all departures.
Question 36. Under the handbook, which limit applies first to an officer aged 59 with 35
years in public service?
Answer: The 35-year public-service limit. The rule uses whichever occurs first, not a requirement to
attain both 60 years of age and 35 years of service. Any current exception would need its own
applicable authority.
Question 37. What is the difference between notice pay and earned-leave pay at exit?
Answer: Notice pay addresses a notice period that is not served. Earned-leave pay addresses eligible
unused leave in terminal computation. Their direction and calculation depend on who owes what
under the departure arrangement.
Question 38. Does the handbook supply a gratuity multiplier?
Answer: Not in section 8.9. It refers to gratuity as defined in the conditions of service. A numerical
question needs that formula or the applicable instrument; inventing one is not a valid answer.
Question 39. Is the precise statutory confirmation body for NCC Commissioners the
whole National Assembly?
Answer: Section 8(1) of the Nigerian Communications Act specifies the Senate. Use that precise
statutory answer despite the broader label in the handbook's appointment table.
Question 40. Why does this

chunks.content:
Commissioners the
whole National Assembly?
Answer: Section 8(1) of the Nigerian Communications Act specifies the Senate. Use that precise
statutory answer despite the broader label in the handbook's appointment table.
Question 40. Why does this guide distinguish handbook wording from current operative
rules?
Answer: The supplied handbook has no established edition date in the scan and expressly
anticipates amendments. It is a valuable source for its printed provisions, but a later approved policy
or governing statute may affect the current answer. The distinction prevents historical wording, an
internal rule and a legal requirement being mistaken for one another.

chunks.content:
Chapter 28
Memo, report and official writing
The written component tests whether knowledge can support a clear institutional decision. Learn
format, evidence and reasoning before practising under time pressure. The reported 30-percent
weighting is planning information supplied for preparation and remains subject to the official
examination circular.

28.1 Memo, report, minutes and brief - choose the right form
Document   Primary purpose
Memorandum   Communicates internally to seek approval, provide advice, report status or
direct action.
Report   Presents structured findings, analysis, conclusion and recommendations on
an assignment, event or investigation.
Minutes   Official record of a meeting's attendance, deliberative outcome, decisions and
actions.
Brief/briefing note   Gives a decision-maker a concise situation, key facts, risks, options and
recommended line.
Letter   Communicates formally with an external person or organisation.
Circular   Communicates a rule, instruction or information consistently to a defined
group.
Submission   Places an issue before an approving authority with analysis and decision
sought.
Format follows purpose
If instructed to 'write a memo', include memo identifiers and an approval/action request. If instructed
to 'prepare a report', use a title and report sections rather than To/From fields unless the examination
convention states otherwise. Where the prompt is ambiguous, choose the form that best serves the
audience and state purpose clearly.
Internal does not mean casual
A memorandum may be shorter than a report, but it still requires evidence, logic and record value.
Avoid conversational openings, emotional claims, unexplained abbreviations and vague requests.
Decision document versus information document
A decision document recommends and seeks authority. An information document records or updates.
Many weak answers announce information when the prompt requires approval; the final paragraph
must match the required action.
The correct format is part of the answer because it demonstrates awareness of institutional
purpose and audience.
